nytimes.com.title: I Covered the Tiananmen Square Massacre. It Still Weighs on Me.
nytimes.com.text:
This story is part of a series marking 175 years of eyewitness journalism from The New York Times. Read more here.
As I pedaled my bicycle toward the gunfire and Tiananmen Square, dodging people in crowds fleeing in the opposite direction, I kept thinking: What a crazy occupation this is.
For weeks during the spring of 1989, the question preoccupying the world had been whether the student-led Tiananmen demonstrations paralyzing China would end with a democratic revolution or with massacres. That night, June 3, the phone began ringing in the apartment in Beijing I shared with my wife and fellow New York Times correspondent, Sheryl WuDunn. We had our answer: Tens of thousands of army troops were forcing their way into central Beijing, mowing down crowds of unarmed protesters and bystanders who tried to resist.
So I jumped on my bicycle, legs pumping madly, careening around tank traps students had set up, so I could report on a modern army waging war on its people.
It was probably the most important story I’ve covered and I got at least one big thing wrong — I’ll get to that — but I did manage to reach Tiananmen Square before the troops. I parked my bicycle near the famous portrait of Chairman Mao and began interviewing people in the throng of students and workers.
Although it was already dark, the square was lit by overhead lights and by the glow of two armored personnel carriers that protesters had set ablaze. At first, the troops, arriving by the truckload, fired over our heads. Then they lowered their aim and fired right at us.

nytimes.com.title: Ukrainians Are Fighting Russians Inside Underground Gas Pipes. I Went in One.
nytimes.com.text:
Deep inside a forest in drone-infested eastern Ukraine, I stepped onto a small metal platform and descended into a postapocalyptic world of modern warfare, where the only safe place is underground.
When the elevator stopped, a vast subterranean space came into view — a logistics hub, hundreds of yards long and at least three yards high. Connected to it was a buried web of pipes that once carried natural gas between Ukraine and Russia.
Ukrainian troops cannot stand up in the pipes, which are less than four feet in diameter. Yet they spend weeks at a time inside them, fighting Russians with guns and grenades, ferrying out fellow soldiers injured or killed at the front, and carrying in critical supplies. With drones stalking the battlefield above, this is the future of war, Ukrainian strategists say.
As I approached one of the pipes, the smell of residual gas made my head spin. Soldiers caked in brown dust constantly popped out from or disappeared into the tunnel on the rusty electric buggies that roll through the underground network.
I put on protective goggles and a gas mask and sat behind troops who had been ordered to their positions. Inside the pipe, the smell would be even stronger, they said.

nytimes.com.title: Another Toll of the Violent Unrest in France: The Political Center
nytimes.com.text:
Soon after President Emmanuel Macron of France spoke to a traumatized country, in the aftermath of riots that set cities aflame on Oct. 17, Mr. Macron’s former prime minister and aspiring successor, Édouard Philippe, responded to his old boss.
“Our country needs to be commanded,” Mr. Philippe wrote, scolding Mr. Macron for what he called a failure to restore order, protect shopkeepers from looters and engage protesting high-school students in dialogue.
For Mr. Philippe, the leading presidential candidate from France’s shrinking political center, it was not the first break with Mr. Macron. But his tempered tone suggested he was speaking more in sorrow than in anger. It was all but lost in an angry cacophony, underscoring how the upheaval is reshaping France’s politics: More extreme figures are sidelining centrists.
No major candidate has lost more support in the polls than Mr. Philippe since the protests erupted last month: roughly two percentage points, leaving him between 13 percent and 15 percent. He now trails the far-left candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, and remains well behind the far-right leader, Marine Le Pen, who claims the backing of about a third of those surveyed in most polls.
As things stand, Mr. Philippe, 55, would not make it into the second round of France’s two-round election system that starts in April. That would leave voters choosing between Ms. Le Pen and Mr. Mélenchon — a race she would likely win.

nytimes.com.title: Israel’s Election Is Unlikely to Change Its Policies and Global Isolation
nytimes.com.text:
To Israelis, the two leading contenders after the election, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff, offer sharply different personalities, styles and even paths to the future.
But to the rest of the world, they don’t seem substantially different in their approach to Israel’s security or in their opposition to a Palestinian state.
If neither can form a government, Mr. Netanyahu could remain as a caretaker prime minister for weeks or months to come. In this period of instability, there is concern, analysts say, that settler violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank will increase and that Mr. Netanyahu will push President Trump to start bombing Iran again.
If Mr. Eisenkot manages to emerge as prime minister, Israel’s overall foreign policy is not expected to shift much. The tone may be more accommodating on the margins, but few expect Israel to embrace a two-state solution to establish an independent Palestine or abandon its active conflicts with Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Islamic Republic in Iran.
All that means Israel will still find itself increasingly isolated internationally.
The vote sends a message to the world that the current government’s approach to the region, which has prompted an international backlash, “is not just a Bibi problem,” said Gina Abercrombie-Winstanley, a former American diplomat now at the Atlantic Council, referring to Mr. Netanyahu. “It represents today’s Israel writ large.”

nytimes.com.title: Taking the Saga of a Criminal Gang From Page to Screen to Opera Stage
nytimes.com.text:
Plenty of novels have struck a popular chord, capturing a cultural mood, an epoch or a widespread anxiety. But few have charted the hard-boiled-to-highbrow trajectory of the 2002 Italian best seller “Romanzo Criminale.”
A bloodstained gangster saga, “Romanzo Criminale” takes place against the backdrop of “the years of lead,” the era of upheaval in the 1970s and 1980s, when bombings and murders by far-left and far-right militants terrorized Italy. It was a hit as a novel and as a 2005 film, and a cultural sensation as a television series from 2008 to 2010.
Now it has been turned into an opera, which debuted last week in Florence at one of Italy’s main opera houses, to eight minutes of curtain calls.
Written by Giancarlo De Cataldo, a judge with a literary bent, “Romanzo Criminale” follows lowlife hoodlums as they claw their way to the top of Rome’s criminal underworld, only to come crashing down. In Italy, the four main protagonists — Libano, Freddo, Dandi, Bufalo — are household names, as familiar as the four Musketeers.
Packed with greed, passion, betrayal and too many murders to count, the plot was a natural for an operatic treatment.
“Those were turbulent, violent years,” Mr. De Cataldo said in an interview last week, before the dress rehearsal at the Maggio Musicale Fiorentino theater.

nytimes.com.title: New ‘Call of Duty’ Game Draws Criticism for Using Footage of Deadly Seoul Crowd Crush
nytimes.com.text:
The latest installment in Activision’s Call of Duty video game franchise, released last week, is set in the fictional South Korean city of Hajin as it comes under a North Korean attack. But it was a reference to real life — footage of an actual tragedy — that has caused an uproar in South Korea.
The clips in question appear in the opening sequence of the game and depict the emergency response following a fictional North Korean attack.
Some of those images, such as a man performing CPR on another person, are from actual footage of the aftermath of a crowd crush in the Itaewon neighborhood of Seoul in 2022, in which nearly 160 people were killed after being trapped in a narrow alleyway during Halloween celebrations. The tragedy, which led to charged debates about bureaucratic negligence and political accountability, was one of the worst mass casualty events in South Korea’s recent history.
A group representing families of the dead has called for Activision to remove the scenes from the game, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.
“The citizens who participated in or witnessed the rescue response to the tragedy have been living through trauma and pain,” the Itaewon Tragedy Bereaved Families Association said in a statement. “Using this incident for entertainment purposes as material for a game is highly inappropriate and lacks common sense.”
The association added that many of those people were now being re-traumatized by hateful online comments about the tragedy.

nytimes.com.title: Colombia’s ‘Narcoterrorist’ Crackdown Raises Questions Over Killings
nytimes.com.text:
In Colombia’s rural Guaviare region, poor ranchers eke out a living in obscurity, surrounded by armed rebels who traffic cocaine.
But when Luis Carlos Mojica was fatally shot there last month, his death became national news.
Witnesses and his widow said Mr. Mojica, 31, was a civilian in street clothes who was shot by a soldier. The authorities said he was an armed rebel.
His killing — and at least two recent cases like it — have ignited fierce debate in Colombia.
Supporters of the country’s new right-wing president, Abelardo De La Espriella, say his iron-fisted attack on armed groups — which has involved posing with body bags and pledging to hunt down “bandidos,” or bandits — is needed after years of failed peace talks.
His critics point to the recent deaths as evidence that Mr. De La Espriella, spurred on by President Trump, is pursuing a crackdown on armed groups that is ensnaring innocent civilians, who are being falsely branded as criminals.
In Colombia, such claims evoke haunting memories.
Two decades ago, as Colombia’s army fought powerful leftist guerrillas, soldiers killed around 7,000 civilians, dressing up and planting guns on the corpses to inflate enemy body counts, a tribunal later found. The revelations became known as the False Positives scandal.

nytimes.com.title: Transylvania, Where Meadows Ripple and Dracula Legends Fade
nytimes.com.text:
I arrived in a tiny village in Transylvania after a morning of hiking through oak and beech trees. Turning onto its only street, I greeted a sun-weathered man stepping out of a Saxon home with a traditional sleepy-eyed window. We walked and he spoke, in Romanian, with the enthusiasm of being understood. He wasn’t, but I could make out enough — “Maghiara,” “Otoman,” “Sovietic” — to know I was getting a history lesson.
It was my first day on the Via Transilvanica, a long-distance trail that stretches some 1,000 miles diagonally across Romania, starting in the northeastern region of Bukovina and ending where the Danube River reaches the Serbian border. As its name suggests, most of the route lies in the central region of Transylvania, where forests and farmland meet the Carpathian Mountains.
Before visiting, the region had seemed to me less of a real place and more of a universal symbol. Since the Irish novelist Bram Stoker published “Dracula” in 1897, our popular consciousness has turned Transylvania into the default setting for Gothic horror. The destination has seen a recent resurgence in Hollywood, providing inspiration for Robert Eggers’s 2024 film “Nosferatu” and a backdrop for some parts of the Netflix series “Wednesday.”
I was curious to see Transylvania’s true character. Because I have found that long-distance hikes tend to reveal the essence of a place, I combined a few days on the Via Transilvanica with some time in the region’s gateway cities of Cluj-Napoca and Brasov.
What I discovered — beneath the storybook vistas of spired castles, hilltop citadels and pastel-colored hamlets — is a culture shaped by the influences of Huns, Saxons, Ottomans, Hapsburgs, Hungarians and, of course, post-Communist redemption.

nytimes.com.title: Rare Evacuation Announced by Melania Trump Begins in Ukrainian City of Oleshky
nytimes.com.text:
A rare local cease-fire in Ukraine took effect early Tuesday morning to allow aid delivery and evacuation in a Russian-occupied frontline city where about 2,000 civilians are trapped, threatened by starvation and constant bombardment.
The plight of the city, Oleshky, has drawn international attention. Melania Trump announced the local truce on Friday after negotiation with both the Russian and Ukrainian governments. A week earlier, Pope Leo XIV, just three days after surgery for lung cancer, spoke with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia and called for a cease-fire to enable an evacuation there.
Ukrainian officials, volunteers and relatives of people in Oleshky joined a frenzy of messages, calls and announcements to organize residents to register for transport out of the city.
“Every three minutes, people message and call me about evacuation,” said Ksenia Arkhipova, a Ukrainian volunteer worker from Oleshky who has been helping with coordination plans from elsewhere in Ukraine.
People were asking her if many others had signed up for the evacuation, and when she said they had, they asked to join, too, she said. By midday Monday, she said she had gathered 200 names on a list and had some 300 more people she wanted to contact.
“They gave us so little time,” she said of the Friday announcement.

cnn.com.title: ‘This can’t keep happening’: How divorced military spouses get trapped in foreign countries
cnn.com.text:
Christina Fuller is an American former military spouse living without legal residency in southern Spain, where a custody fight has kept her and her son for years. When her family arrived near the Strait of Gibraltar on US military orders, her son was two. Now, he’s nearly 10.
Fuller’s marriage to a US Navy sailor assigned to a guided-missile destroyer at Naval Station Rota fell apart soon after the family arrived in 2019.
When her husband filed for divorce in 2021, a Spanish court barred either parent from taking their child out of the country without the other’s permission. The next year, the Navy ordered her husband back to the US as the divorce was finalized and Fuller appealed a Spanish custody order.
She eventually won full physical custody and rights similar to legal custody in the US, but she still had to get permission from a judge or her now ex-husband to move their son. By then her son’s American passport had also expired, leaving them stuck in Spain.
Fuller says she supports her family by scrapping together an income from this odd job and that – she’s a “buscavida,” she says, what the Spanish call a hustler.
“I never came to Spain intending to make it my permanent home,” Fuller told CNN. “I don’t want to feel like a prisoner in another country any more simply because I followed military orders overseas.”
When a marriage falls apart, military spouses living overseas can find themselves stranded in foreign countries and bound by foreign custody judgments in their courts — even when those involved are American citizens who moved abroad on US orders. Spouses already made financially vulnerable by years of relocations can be left navigating unfamiliar courts, hiring lawyers in two countries and fighting simply to bring their children home.
Spouses caught in foreign courts have been largely invisible to almost everyone in military circles, including each other. But in August the issue burst into public view when the wife of a Marine Corps officer went viral with an online plea, warning that she and her children could be trapped indefinitely in Germany.
Jamie Lenio said her marriage was ending partly because her husband had an affair with a superior officer, a one-star general — a claim substantiated by a US Africa Command inspector general report obtained by CNN.
Within 48 hours, the video had drawn nearly 500,000 views, more than 30,000 likes and 2,300 comments.
Spouses facing similar circumstances contacted Lenio, leading to an informal network of women, and at least one man, who shared their stories, including on social media, in the hope they, too, can get some help.
Soon after, the military ordered Lenio’s husband to return to the US, paving the way for Lenio and her kids to return as well, before a German court could take up the family’s case. Earlier this month, Lenio arrived in Southern California with her children.
When foreign courts take control
CNN spoke to more than a dozen current or former spouses of active-duty service members, Defense Department employees or US government contractors who said they were living overseas against their wishes with their children — or had returned to the United States without them — after their marriages ended. All but one of the spouses CNN spoke to were women.
They all described debilitating financial hardship as they fought their legal battles overseas. Many racked up heavy debt, ruined their credit or relied on food banks just to feed their children. Multiple spouses said they skipped meals to get by.
“It’s heartbreaking, but it’s unfortunately the reality,” said Gilbert “Joey” Comley, a retired Army judge advocate who has represented service members and veterans in custody cases involving foreign courts. “Someone always has to have jurisdiction over child custody.”
Once a child becomes integrated into daily life abroad, courts may treat that country as the child’s “habitual residence” under the 1980 Hague Convention on international child abduction and the US law implementing it.
Legally, that can outweigh citizenship or the fact that the family moved only because of military employment, Comley said.
CNN spoke to military spouses based in Germany, Spain, the UK and Japan, all of whom expressed surprise at having an obscure, international treaty play a role in child custody during and after a divorce. Some said they were blindsided by the power of the foreign court — no matter the country they were in. And they all described incorrect or conflicting guidance from US military officials.
Ahead of deployments or overseas tours, military families often contemplate potential life-changing events, including the death of a service member or illness of a spouse in a structured Family Contingency Plan.
A number of spouses said they wished the military had armed their families with more information so they could incorporate an agreement on how they would approach custody in the event of a divorce overseas.
In response to questions for this story, individual service branches initially directed CNN to the Pentagon for information about the guidance families receive from the military when navigating divorce and child custody in foreign courts. A Pentagon spokesperson then directed CNN back to the individual service branches before highlighting a series of webpages on Military OneSource, a DOD-funded website for military personnel and families. None of the links provide direct support for navigating divorce or child custody in foreign legal systems, a reflection of the dearth of official information available to families before they may be educating themselves in the middle of a crisis.
The Air Force flagged an article that mentioned military divorce overseas, but only that it “can be more complicated than if the couple filed within a state. A US court may not recognize a divorce filed overseas, so it’s best to file in the United States.” It briefly addressed physical property but not child custody.
The Navy, like other service branches, said it doesn’t track how many families are in divorce or child custody proceedings in foreign courts but that it does give them briefings before they go overseas to “ensure service members and their dependents clearly understand host-nation jurisdiction, legal protections, and administrative responsibilities while serving abroad.”
Spokespeople for the Marine Corps and the Air Force outlined a number of resources available to military families, including legal-assistance services but with a significant caveat: they would need a private local lawyer to represent them in court.
‘A nightmare every day’
Across the cases CNN reviewed, a common pattern emerged: The higher-earning partner had an incentive to remain overseas — whether as a service member nearing retirement and eyeing a military contracting job, or as a civilian employee or contractor able to extend an at times lucrative posting long after the marriage ended. Those employment opportunities provide legal status to work in host countries.
The accompanying spouses who were stranded abroad — or felt forced to leave without their children — uniformly described custody proceedings that favored the higher-earning partner, who could afford stronger legal representation and argue that a steadier income left them better positioned to provide for the children.
“It gets expensive,” Comley explained, because finding a fair resolution requires retaining a lawyer in the US and another in the foreign country.
For many military spouses, financial independence is elusive, even more so overseas where their job opportunities are further limited by visa restrictions on where they can work. Moving every two to three years makes finding a job or maintaining a career difficult as they contort their lives around their spouse’s military service demands.
Though half of active-duty spouses have attained at least a bachelor’s degree, the military spouse unemployment rate is about four times higher and they have a median income 42% lower than civilian spouses, according to an analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data by D’Aniello Institute for Veterans and Military Families at Syracuse University.
Overseas, employment obstacles multiply as a spouse’s legal status extends through their military-connected partner. Once they lose that protection, they have to find an alternate justification for remaining and working in the country while they fight for custodial rights, a costly endeavor.
Military spouses divorcing in foreign courts can also lose out on a major marital asset: US military retirement benefits. Foreign courts may decide divorce and custody but generally do not have jurisdiction to divide those benefits as a US court can, leaving spouses little recourse if the service member refuses to share them voluntarily.
The legal fight often unfolds as an accompanying spouse loses practical support that made overseas life possible: base entry access to affordable shopping, post-office boxes and access to bank accounts or cars tied to the sponsoring spouse. Several CNN spoke with accrued significant credit card debt; one documented relying on a food bank and military-provided thrift-store vouchers.
Parents separated from children
Jose ‘Trey’ Gonzalez’s marriage deteriorated in 2023, soon after his family moved to Germany for his wife’s work with a Defense Department contractor. While a German court considered custody of their now-5-year-old son, Gonzalez’s immigration status linked to his wife expired and he left Germany. He saw his son briefly during a 2024 court hearing and visit in Stuttgart but says he has not seen him since.
“I felt like there had to be some kind of workaround because we’re all American,” Gonzalez told CNN from Florida.
“It’s been terrible. It’s been a nightmare every day. As long as the Germans have jurisdiction I have zero hope.”
In England, Air Force spouse Brandylyn Cohea is torn between staying or going in the wake of her husband filing for a divorce in the United Kingdom.
She fears being deported without her teenage son if she loses her status to work and live in the country. Meanwhile, she worries a court could rule unfavorably if she leaves. The Air Force briefly authorized her and her son to return to the US but they would have had to leave without their two beloved golden retrievers, who came from the US.
She’s working up to 55 hours a week while parenting alone, she says, receiving $1300 in child and spousal support per month.
“It’s really difficult to watch” other families leave, she says, choking up, “because I want to go home.”
A viral plea — and swift intervention
Since Lenio’s story gained national attention, military spouses facing divorce have increasingly seen public pressure as the only way to force action.
A number have taken their stories public, some appearing in social media videos. Lenio’s viral plea in August quickly reached the highest levels of the Navy Department.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, who oversees the Marine Corps and was recently nominated to permanently fill the role by President Donald Trump, responded publicly: “We hear you loud and clear. You and your family will be home soon.”
The next month, around the time of Cao’s nomination, the Marine Corps issued Lenio’s husband new orders, and she returned to the US with her children.
Lenio told CNN the video got her home. The Marine Corps said the move was underway before she went public, telling CNN it had already concluded the situation “would be best resolved in the US.”
But in short order, the Marine Corps and Navy made similar determinations in the cases of other families.
Several sources – spouses, service members and former military officials familiar with personnel decisions – said Lenio’s video was a clear catalyst.
During CNN’s reporting, another Marine Corps family facing divorce in Germany also received orders allowing them to return to the US after CNN asked the Pentagon about their situation.
Corina Acevedo, mother of four and the wife of a senior enlisted Marine, said her case began moving only after Lenio’s video. Earlier, a German court denied her the authority necessary to return to the US with her children. The Marine Corps would not discuss her case, but said every family’s circumstances and timeline are different.
‘Sucked into the German court system’
Foreign family court orders can also trump certain decisions by the US military.
Ashlee Gamble’s marriage to a Navy sailor fell apart in the summer of 2025 while the couple were living near Kaiserslautern, Germany with their two children. A German court spelled out a custody arrangement after Gamble filed, ultimately unsuccessfully, for the right to determine where her children would reside.
“You’re sucked into the German court system. And all of it is in German,” she said.
Last year, over her husband’s objections, the military granted a request for Gamble to return to the US with both children, but the German court would allow her to leave only with her eldest child. Her young son would remain in Germany with her husband.
Stars and Stripes first reported on the family earlier this month. Two days later, Gamble’s Navy-appointed legal advisor let her know the Navy had released orders to move her husband and family back to the US, more than a year after a military-provided clinical social worker first recommended Gamble return with the two children.
Gamble’s husband says the orders have upended his family’s lives in the middle of his children’s school year, and he questioned why the Navy would intervene in a private family matter.
“I think that civil matters should be handled by the civil courts and not have the military involved,” he told CNN, outlining what he sees as advantages for military spouses in the German court system.
“It’s going to cost them more in the US because here in Germany, if they can’t get a job, they’re provided access to a free lawyer for a civil case. Where in the US are you going to get a free divorce lawyer?”
But Gamble says her court-appointed lawyer is managing many cases besides hers and she is relieved to be leaving Germany and heading back to the US.
“I feel like military families have no business being in German courts unless someone broke a law. But when it comes to custody, this can’t keep happening.”
Even so, the German court order will cross the Atlantic with the family, dictating their custody arrangement unless or until the German court relinquishes jurisdiction.
Without a treaty change or a Pentagon-wide policy, commands and contractors retain broad discretion over whether a family can return home to pursue divorce and custody in an American court. Families described officials who were ill-informed or unwilling to intervene and others who were supportive and responsive but still unable to force a resolution once a foreign court became involved.
Efforts to bring attention to this specific issue have coincided with a broad new policy focus on military family struggles amid the Iran War and the early days of Trump’s Military Spouse Commission, a panel led by Jennifer Hegseth, wife of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The commission’s membership includes almost all of the spouses of the military’s top brass. The commission is tasked with, among other things, developing “policy recommendations to address … deployment-related support” and “improve the quality of life for military spouses while supporting the highest standard of military readiness,” according to the White House.
Building a life in Spain
Christina Fuller watched military interventions for other families from Spain.
“When I saw Jamie’s story come out and I saw the Secretary of the Navy saying ‘not on my watch,’ I thought, ‘OK, sir, let’s see what’s going to happen on your watch,’ because this has been happening for a long time,” she said.
Her ex-husband returned to Spain on military orders last year, she says, and now has brief regular visits and calls with their son.
However, Fuller is no longer a military dependent, limiting the Navy’s ability to resolve her case through new orders or an early return program. Her son remains a military dependent, though Fuller says he was unable to receive on-base health care for the years his father was in Hawaii.
An email Fuller provided from the naval hospital in Rota showed records incorrectly identifying the child as living in Hawaii with his father, who told CNN he included his son on his military orders.
He said it has been “extremely difficult” being separated from his son and “navigating different legal systems and military obligations presents significant challenges.”
While she still wants to return to the US, for now she is building a life for her children: play dates, basketball practice, dance classes and birthday parties. Her son now has an American half-brother, and Fuller has learned Spanish while studying European law and the Hague Convention as she works to provide other families information on social media.
“Even if it’s too late to give me those years back, it is not too late to make sure somebody else doesn’t lose theirs.”

cnn.com.title: Canada’s economic break with the US in 5 charts
cnn.com.text: For decades, the United States and Canada worked to build one of the world’s closest economic partnerships, with supply chains, businesses and trade increasingly intertwined. But now, with the two countries in the thick of a trade war, Canada is taking a dramatic step to reduce its reliance on the United States. It is forging closer economic ties with the European Union and is set to become its first-ever “associate member.” “Economic integration is now being weaponized, and tariffs are being used as a means of pressure,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told EU lawmakers last month in a parliamentary address. Carney was referring to President Donald Trump’s ramped-up trade war with Canada. Over the summer Trump levied 50% tariffs on around $20 billion worth of Canadian goods and, in some cases, imposing outright import bans. Canada matched those duties and has vowed to match any future tariffs. Forthcoming data is likely to show trade between the two nations fell as a result. It’s uncertain how the EU-Canada partnership could look and whether it will even come to fruition at all, as officials from Germany and France, key EU member states, have voiced opposition. Carney has also been met with backlash from Canadian officials who feel it compromises Canada’s sovereignty. That hasn’t stopped Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. On Thursday they invited other countries to join in the initiative they dubbed “Alliance for the Future.” “In a world of growing rivalries, sovereignty and independence are no longer just the freedom to act alone — it is the capacity to act together,” von der Leyen said in an address Thursday at this week’s two-day Canada-EU summit in Montreal. “And this is why we will build an alliance for the future,” she said. “And we start with Canada.” Few details have been shared about what Canada’s association membership with the EU could look like, though Carney said earlier this week he intends to use the summit as an opportunity to further nail down the next steps. And while trade ruptures with the US were the impetus for Carney’s push with the EU, the impact of the trade war with the US has not been limited to trade. From vacations to investments, here’s how the fallout is showing up across both economies. A trend of declining trade While Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods and Carney’s retaliatory measures against American goods over the summer likely weighed on trade, they’d represent just the latest chapter in a broader decline in trade between the two countries. The total value of trade between the US and Canada has fallen since 2022. Of those three years, the largest annual drop came last year, when Trump imposed 50% tariffs on steel and aluminum, two of the top goods the US imports from Canada. Canada is sending the smallest share of its exports to the US in nearly 30 years Most of Canada’s exports — historically between 70% and 80% — go to the US. While the US remains Canada’s largest export market by far, its share of Canadian exports has fallen sharply since Trump returned to office, reflecting heightened trade uncertainty, according to a report published last year by Global Affairs Canada’s Office of the Chief Economist. Over this period, Canada significantly increased its exports to Europe and Central Asia as it looked to wean itself off its reliance on the US market. Carney, in a statement Thursday unveiling an initiative titled “The Plan for a Stronger Canada,” said that the shift is intended “to create greater security and prosperity for Canadians.” In addition to trade, the effort is aimed at strengthening national defense and boosting public safety. Alcohol became an early casualty Alcohol accounts for a relatively small share of trade between the two countries, but it has become one of the most visible symbols of their deteriorating economic relationship. In March 2025, provincial liquor boards across Canada pulled American products from their shelves. Customers visiting the government-run liquor stores were met with empty shelves and “BUY CANADIAN INSTEAD” signs. The fallout showed up immediately in trade data, with US alcohol exports to Canada plunging and remaining well below previous levels. American spirits were hit particularly hard. Exports to Canada fell to a record low of $9.7 million in the second quarter of 2025 before rebounding to more than $20 million in each of the third and fourth quarters, according to the Distilled Spirits Council. The retaliation has since gone both ways. Last month, Trump imposed a ban on most Canadian liquor shipped to the US. Canadians are spending less time — and money — in the US Trump has repeatedly floated the idea of making Canada the 51st state, drawing the ire of many Canadians. He further inflamed tensions recently by renaming Lake Ontario “Lake Canada.” Canadians’ disdain for Trump has been apparent in travel data. Canadian visits to the US peaked at nearly 80 million in the early 1990s before settling at around 40 million a year in subsequent decades. In 2025, visits to the US fell to 29.1 million — the lowest level outside the pandemic era since records began in 1972, according to Statistics Canada. The decline is taking a bite out of US businesses. Canadians spent $16.1 billion in the US in 2024, according to Statistics Canada, but that fell to $13.4 billion in 2025, a $2.7 billion drop in a single year. Canadian investors staged a record retreat from US stocks After pouring $78.1 billion CAD (around $56 billion USD) into US stocks in the first half of 2026, Canadian investors abruptly reversed course in July, selling a record $31 billion CAD (around $22 billion USD) according to Statistics Canada. The sell-off was concentrated in shares of large US technology companies. It came as the S&P 500 edged lower in July after strong gains earlier in the year.

cnn.com.title: The push to impeach Hegseth will gain momentum if Democrats win the House
cnn.com.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s political future could be on the line if Democrats win the House majority in next week’s midterm elections. A Democrat win of the House could breathe new life into an ongoing effort to impeach Hegseth, potentially convincing more Republicans to get on board in a vote shortly after the elections. If that push fails, Democrats are planning to set their sights on the defense secretary if they have the House gavel in the new Congress, with a major push toward impeachment. GOP Rep. Thomas Massie has vowed to force a vote to impeach Hegseth when the House returns after the midterms in November if the secretary is still in office. If Republicans lose the majority, Massie is increasingly confident that there will be the bipartisan votes needed for impeachment, which just requires a simple majority. “The membership of the retirement caucus is going to swell on Election Day,” Massie told CNN. “Those members of Congress who aren’t coming back, who are Republican, might be compelled to vote their conscience when they’re no longer worried about having the support of Trump or the GOP for their election.” It is unclear how Republican leadership will handle the issue after the election. Speaker Mike Johnson sent lawmakers home early in September, staving off a vote before the midterms. He said at the time that his plan was to block a vote, calling the push to impeach Hegseth “a stunt” and saying the defense secretary has “done an extraordinary job.” But one source familiar with Republicans’ thinking told CNN that the impeachment effort is being taken seriously and that there is a real possibility some Republicans could vote in favor as many have grown increasingly frustrated with Hegseth and the Pentagon. Regardless of what happens with the impeachment push in November, Democrats are sure to intensify scrutiny on the secretary in the new Congress if they take back the House, which they are increasingly confident will happen. If their party flips the chamber, Democrats on the House and Senate Armed Services Committees are planning wide-reaching investigations into the US war with Iran and lawmakers are coalescing around Hegseth as their top target to start. Lawmakers want to press Hegseth on the decision to go to war, how the war has been conducted, and the ways they say the administration has avoided consulting Congress, including why lawmakers still have not received a full accounting of exactly how much the war has cost. “He is the lowest hanging fruit because of the animosity that seems to be both from Republican and Democratic senators and staff,” a Democratic aide told CNN. “He is going to be investigated. There is going to be oversight, and whether that turns into impeachment in the Senate is an outstanding question if Democrats win back the Senate.” President Donald Trump on Thursday praised Hegseth, decrying the effort to impeach him as “terrible.” “All they do is talking about impeaching everybody,” he told reporters, referring to Democrats. “But they’re talking about Pete Hegseth. He’s doing a great job, he’s a great warrior.” Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement, “At the War Department, we are solely focused on Peace Through Strength and ensuring our warfighters have everything they need to be successful. We are proud to serve our warriors.” Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson said in a statement, “Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War.” “By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under President Trump and Secretary Hegseth’s leadership than before. The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first.” Hegseth isn’t the only Trump cabinet secretary that Democrats want to investigate if they win the House. Democrats say that Attorney General Todd Blanche and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. would also be among top targets for oversight. Democrats hesitant to embrace Trump impeachment push Many Democrats have been much quicker to support impeaching Hegseth than Trump, at least publicly. Having impeached Trump twice, Democratic Rep. Pramila Jayapal said, “We can’t get into a situation where the American people start to believe that we can never convict an impeached president.” But the calculus for Hegseth is different. “Even if the Senate refuses to convict or take it up, I think it’s important that the country understands how dangerous he is, and then when we take back the majority, then we can actually do the investigation and the accountability that we need,” Jayapal told CNN. Even Democratic candidates on the campaign trail have vowed not to pursue a snap impeachment of Trump. “I’ve had people say that you know the first thing we should do is impeach the president, and I, my answer has been no. We need to focus on delivering for the American people,” Democrat Bob Harvie, who is trying to flip a critical battleground seat in Pennsylvania, told CNN. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has tried to take a measured stance when asked about the possibility of impeaching Trump administration officials, saying Democrats “haven’t ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out.” He has said that if Democrats win the House he wants to see how investigations play out. But Jeffries sharpened his position against Hegseth in a recent interview with CNN’s Manu Raju. “I think there’s a reason why Republicans raced out of town to avoid holding that impeachment vote because they know Pete Hegseth has been a failure,” Jeffries told CNN in an interview during a campaign stop outside of San Diego. “He’s been a failure prior to this reckless and costly war of choice, and then of course he’s badly mismanaged the whole situation over in Iran. So we’ll see what happens in terms of that vote. But I believe Pete Hegseth is in deep trouble.” Democrats vow oversight of Hegseth no matter what Many among Hegseth’s group of close advisers, which includes former Fox News producers and social media personalities, have encouraged Hegseth to consider political office — including a possible presidential run in 2028, CNN reported earlier this month. Some Trump allies told CNN they believe Hegseth would entertain a 2028 presidential bid only if Vance decided not to run. His movements have also been watched with increasing interest in Tennessee, where his family moved several years ago, though GOP sources there say he has not taken steps in the state yet that might suggest he harbors political ambitions there. But even if Hegseth were to leave his post and avoid an impeachment vote, Democrats still want to pursue oversight. Rep. Chris Deluzio, who was part of a group of Democrats who urged service members and intelligence officials to disobey illegal orders that might be issued by Trump’s administration, and a member of the House Armed Services Committee, told CNN that even if Hegseth is removed or leaves office, he still needs to be investigated. “We investigate wrongdoing, and when we’re talking about the prosecution of a war, a lack of protection for our troops and their families, that should happen no matter this being secretary or not because we need to get to the bottom of how the Pentagon failed so many patriotic Americans,” Deluzio said. Rep. Jason Crow, another member of the group who called on service members to disobey illegal orders, told reporters last week, “Pete Hegseth is a special project of mine to make sure that he does not sit in the Pentagon for any longer than he needs to, and I will do everything possible to remove him from his post because our servicemembers deserve that.” Hegseth’s political future remains in question as Congress and the Trump administration appear to be on a collision course over how to approach the Iran war and foreign policy more generally. On the campaign trial, Republicans have confronted angry voters frustrated over the war and its impact on the affordability crisis. There was bipartisan outrage over the Pentagon’s plan to livestream a firing squad execution (Trump later called off the proposal for a livestream, which faced bipartisan backlash). Republicans on the House Armed Services Committee have also publicly vented frustrations over what they have described as a lack of clarity provided by Department of Defense officials about the objectives, price tag and length of the war. Lawmakers face crowded agenda after midterms If a vote to impeach Hegseth succeeds before the start of a new Congress, Senate Majority Leader John Thune would have to contend with how to handle the situation and whether to crowd an already jam-packed floor schedule with a Senate trial. A Thune spokesperson declined to comment. Senate Democratic staff have had informal conversations about how they would handle the impeachment of Hegseth, according to a source familiar with the conversations. A lot of the calculus could come down to the results of the midterms. Once lawmakers return to session in November, the Republican-controlled House and Senate will have to contend with must-pass pieces of legislation involving the Pentagon like the annual defense policy bill and supplemental funding for the Iran war. The anger that Republicans have towards Hegseth and the president’s recent diesel deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin could further complicate that. Retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon has been outspoken in his criticism of Hegseth’s leadership, calling him “more of a performer than he is a leader.” He told CNN he has not decided how he is going to vote on the impeachment of Hegseth, but is leaning against it. “I think we should do oversight,” Bacon said. “That’s part of the problem back home. People don’t see us as being a check and a balance right now, and I think that’s going to hurt us down ballot because a lot of swing voters who tend to be Republican wanted more of an independent voice in the House.” But Bacon warned that the anger Republicans are harboring could make it difficult to deliver the funding and polices the administration is looking for. “It was on life support to begin with, but I think that plug has been pulled,” Bacon said of Trump’s agenda.

cnn.com.title: ‘BIG cheating’: This is Trump’s team on election claims and what they could do in November
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration has undertaken an unprecedented effort to inject the federal government into state elections as it hunts for voter fraud — and to help President Donald Trump continue his baseless quest to try to prove the 2020 election was rigged and stolen from him. Election officials and Democratic lawmakers fear that the Trump administration’s aggressive actions could spill into Election Day and voter intimidation — and that dubious claims of mass voter fraud will be used to cast doubt on the midterm election results if they go poorly for Trump and the GOP. CNN has reviewed what five outspoken officials leading the effort — including the president — have said in TV interviews, podcast appearances and speeches about voter fraud and their attempts to find it ahead of the midterms, how their claims about widespread issues of fraud often don’t add up, and what actions they say their agencies or the federal government may take in November. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin Who: Mullin has kept the Department of Homeland Security at the center of Trump’s election agenda — hunting for noncitizen voters and investigating election fraud, pressuring states to adopt Trump-backed election reforms and raising doubts about the security of voting machines. What are the claims: In July, Mullin claimed DHS had identified more than 250,000 noncitizens registered to vote in California, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Nevada by analyzing public voter lists as well as roughly 25,000 noncitizen registrants in more than a dozen Republican-led states that voluntarily handed over their rolls. But the headline-grabbing numbers Mullin presented as “fact” have come under immense scrutiny and, in some cases, failed to hold up. Even some Republican officials have warned that the DHS findings are misleading and dramatically inflated. Mullin has echoed Trump’s longstanding warnings that most voting machines are vulnerable to hacking, particularly because they contain foreign-made parts. “We know that [foreign adversaries] can change voter registration and your vote,” Mullin said in July. Last month, Mullin alleged there was “some trouble with some machines” but said he could not determine whether fraud was involved: “That may have had a glitch, may have been something else.” He has also warned that election officials who fail to adequately secure the midterms or prevent illegal voting could face consequences — including fines, other penalties or even prison. What can be done in November: Escalating disputes over allegations of non-citizens on voter rolls have spilled into federal court on the eve of the election and could fuel broader questions or challenges over the integrity of the results. In California, the Justice Department sued after DHS identified roughly 20,000 likely non-citizens registered, seeking to segregate their ballots until their citizenship is confirmed. A federal judge rejected the DOJ demand on Wednesday. DOJ has made similar demands in Washington State, despite concerns that last-minute investigations could disenfranchise eligible voters that may have been mistakenly flagged. Mullin’s warnings to state and local officials are part of a broader pressure campaign on election workers who have endured years of threats and baseless accusations. Some officials and voting rights advocates worry the added scrutiny could strain operations and that isolated mistakes could be used to cast doubt on otherwise valid results. He continues to press others in the administration to address what he describes as voting-machine and supply-chain vulnerabilities, including systems that use barcodes or QR codes. Other Trump allies have called for machines to be restricted or even banned ahead of the midterms, though the administration has yet to take such an action, and likely lacks the authority to do so. DHS is seeking to withhold grant funding from states that refuse to adopt sweeping Trump-backed election changes, including mandating manual paper-ballot counts after elections. It’s unclear if any states have agreed to adopt new reforms. Meanwhile, Mullin and DHS have repeatedly denied that the administration plans to widely deploy ICE agents to polling places during the midterms, saying recently: “We’re only going to be there if we’re required because there’s some type of threat.” Still, local election officials, including some Republicans, are preparing their workers in case federal officers show up. DHS has devoted extensive investigative resources to finding illegal voting, probing thousands of individuals as well as canvassing groups and nonprofit organizations. Internal department records indicate that federal agents will be monitoring the midterms in their hunt for voter fraud. Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon Who: As head of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division — which oversees voting-rights enforcement — Dhillon has become one of the administration’s most visible figures in its push to uncover election fraud. A longtime Trump ally, she supported his efforts to challenge the 2020 result. What are the claims: Dhillon has repeatedly accused local officials of enabling voter fraud and vowed to pursue cases for any and all election violations. “We’ve found hundreds of thousands of dead people on the voter rolls and tens of thousands of noncitizens on the voter rolls, which are now being investigated further,” Dhillon said on Fox Business in July. However, despite devoting massive resources to voter-fraud investigations, the administration has publicly announced only a few dozen election-related prosecutions. Dhillon’s team has sought unredacted voter rolls from the states as part of the administration’s search for noncitizen voters — and they’ve sued roughly 30 states that balked at the request. The DOJ has lost every ruling in those cases so far. Dhillon has suggested that officials who refuse to comply, which includes some Republicans, may have something to hide. Other Republican-led states have voluntarily given their voter lists to Dhillon’s department. Like Mullin, Dhillon has warned local officials they could face prosecution if they fail to adequately safeguard the midterms. This summer, she sent letters to all 50 states that even some Republican officials described as unnecessary and threatening. “My job is to enforce all of the federal laws relating to voting, and those laws include criminal penalties, not only for the people who falsely rep their citizenship to register to vote, or vote illegally, but also election officials who knowingly allow or conspire with people to vote when they have no legal right to do so, including noncitizens,” Dhillon said in a July interview on Newsmax. What can be done in November: Dhillon has championed what she calls the “biggest DOJ election observer effort in history,” with plans to deploy more than 1,000 federal monitors to polling places across all 50 states on Election Day. Federal monitors have long been part of US elections, and Dhillon says they will not interfere with voting. Instead, she says, they will document potential violations of federal law and other irregularities for review afterward. CNN found that some Justice Department monitors deployed during this year’s primaries had previously participated in legal efforts to challenge or overturn Trump’s 2020 election loss. In Wyoming, Republican officials accused two federal monitors of using “aggressive” tactics. While there’s no evidence of looming disruptions on November 3, Dhillon’s rhetoric has fueled concerns among some election officials that Trump’s Justice Department may depart from the longstanding practices and limits governing federal election monitoring. Dhillon has also said states that have refused to turn over unredacted voter rolls are “under investigation.” That warning, combined with the administration’s threats against local officials — including DOJ most recently threatening California election officials with prosecution over noncitizen voters — has stoked fears that federal authorities could target election workers and use isolated incidents to bolster claims that the results cannot be trusted. The Justice Department last week issued federal grand jury subpoenas to local election officials in Los Angeles County, a significant escalation in their battle with the state. In Alaska, DOJ filed a preemptive federal lawsuit last week to block the state from certifying the results of its Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola. DOJ alleges the campaign of another candidate — Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher — was designed to confuse and pull votes away from the incumbent, though Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled in June that both Sullivans could remain on the ballot. DOJ has also opened a criminal probe into the matter. FBI Director Kash Patel Who: Patel leads the FBI, which in January seized 700 boxes of 2020 election materials in Georgia from Fulton County’s election offices. The search warrant was obtained based on allegations in an affidavit from 2020 election denier Kurt Olsen, who has worked in the White House and Justice Department under Trump. Fulton County officials argued in court filings that those claims have long-circulated in right-wing circles and have already been investigated by the state, which found no intentional wrongdoing. In March, the FBI also subpoenaed records of the Arizona state Senate’s audit of the 2020 election, which reaffirmed Joe Biden’s victory over Trump. What are the claims: Patel has stoked Trump’s baseless claims that the 2020 election was stolen in television interviews. In April, he spoke to then-Fox Business anchor Maria Bartiromo, who pressed him about investigating Trump’s claims that the 2020 election was rigged. “Do you have anything to tell us about that?” asked Bartiromo. Patel went on about the FBI’s Russia investigation during Trump’s first term before turning to the election claims. “They not only personally attacked the presidency of the United States and President Trump, but they tried to thwart our elections and rig the entire system, and that is not something that is going to stop - that is not something I’m going to allow on my watch,” Patel said. “We’ve got all the evidence. I can announce on your show that we’ve got all the information we need,” he continued. “We’re working with our prosecutors, the Department of Justice and Attorney General Todd Blanche, and we are going to be making arrests, and it’s coming, and I promise you it’s coming soon.” It’s not clear what arrests Patel was referring to. What can be done in November: Democratic lawmakers and election officials fear the FBI could send agents to the polls on Election Day, an action they say would be an intimidation tactic that violates state election laws. At a September hearing, Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal asked Patel to commit to not sending FBI agents to the polls. “On Election Day, the FBI will follow the law,” Patel responded. “If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation of law, we will. Otherwise, we won’t.” Blumenthal followed up by asking whether Patel agreed “that deploying FBI agents to the polls on Election Day would be contrary to law?” “I don’t know that we can’t legally do it,” Patel said. “I’m telling you we’re going to house our agents and intel analysts in our field offices for election security.” White House transparency task force chairman John Solomon Who: Solomon, a conservative journalist, joined the White House in July as a special government employee leading the White House Government Transparency Task Force to declassify and release documents related to alleged election fraud as well as prior investigations into Trump. Solomon’s task force declassified the documents that fueled Trump’s July speech in which the president alleged election meddling from China in 2020, though Solomon acknowledged after the speech there was no evidence any votes were altered. What are the claims: Solomon, who runs the news site Just the News, has touted the documents as evidence of election vulnerabilities, suggesting that voting machines could be hacked, and he’s said he’s still investigating whether any votes were flipped. “The president let the American people know that for the last six years we’ve had a glass chin when it comes to election security,” Solomon said on his “Just the News: No Noise” show the day after Trump’s July speech. “We knew in 2020 our machines were potentially vulnerable to being hacked by five foreign powers.” “It doesn’t mean the machines flipped votes. It doesn’t mean that we caught widespread cheating yet. But it is absolutely certain now that the American public was in an election system that had significant vulnerabilities,” he added. Solomon has also alleged that the 2020 election was part of a broader “deep state” conspiracy that includes Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s Russia investigation into Trump during his first term and Special Counsel Jack Smith’s indictments of Trump while he was out of office. “I don’t think the intelligence committee put a thumb on the 2020 election. They threw their whole body on it,” Solomon said on the New York Post’s Pod Force One last month. “Intelligence experts with political ambition seem comfortable now using their intelligence credentials to try to hijack or influence an election.” What can be done in November: Solomon continues to release declassified documents through his White House task force, including recent files about Smith’s investigation and the FBI search of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence in 2022. While Solomon has raised concerns about the vulnerabilities of voting machines and interference from China, he’s also downplayed the notion advocated by some Trump allies that the president should declare a national emergency or take unprecedented action like seizing voting machines. After Trump’s speech, Solomon was pressed by an MS NOW reporter about the president’s claims the 2020 election was stolen and whether votes were changed. “The Intelligence Committee has zero evidence that someone, that a foreign power, flipped a vote in 2020, ’22 or ’24,” Solomon said, with a caveat that “we’re not through all the documents.” Asked about whether the 2020 election results were correct, Solomon said: “I’m still researching,” adding there was “not yet” intelligence to support the stolen election claims. President Donald Trump Who: Trump has spent years insisting, without evidence, that US elections are stacked against him and other Republicans and that widespread fraud and voting by noncitizens have affected the results of elections, falsely claiming he did not lose the 2020 election. Since retaking office last year, much of his election agenda has hit a wall. Legislation requiring proof of citizenship to register and identification to vote has stalled in the Senate. Efforts to impose new rules on mail voting and voter rolls have also been blocked by the courts. What are the claims: With the midterms approaching, he is ramping up his rhetoric. Trump claims Democrats are preparing to cheat, foreign governments can manipulate US elections and voting machines cannot be trusted. And he is urging Republicans to closely monitor the upcoming election. During California’s June primaries, as mail ballots were still being counted, Trump baselessly accused Democrats of trying to steal the races for governor and Los Angeles mayor. He claimed there was “BIG cheating” and that the count was under federal investigation. Trump later said a call he made to the Justice Department stopped the supposed fraud, but there is no evidence his call affected the results. In his July prime-time address, Trump announced the declassification of thousands of pages of records that he cast as proof of weaknesses in US elections and the threat of foreign interference. The documents included intelligence about China’s collection or analysis of American voter data. But they did not show that China altered voting systems, manipulated ballots or changed the outcome of the 2020 election. Trump has also floated extraordinary federal intervention. Earlier this year, he said Republicans “ought to nationalize the voting” and “take over” election administration in some places. At a Republican midterm convention in September, Trump led the crowd in reciting a vow that they would vote in the midterms: “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States that loves us so much he can’t even breathe, that I will go out with my family, my friends. I’ll do it any way — I don’t care if I’m registered or not, I’m going to try and cheat like hell like they do.” What can be done in November: Trump cannot simply take over the midterm elections, as some allies want him to do. States and local governments administer voting, and any major federal intervention would face steep legal and constitutional hurdles. Trump is urging supporters to vote in overwhelming numbers — including by mail — and mobilize as poll watchers. “You have to make sure that people aren’t cheating,” he has said. As demands for more aggressive action have grown among his supporters, Trump has teased the prospect of declaring a national emergency to exert greater federal control over the midterms, saying “stranger things have happened.” He’s also said he regrets not seizing voting machines after the 2020 election: “Well, I should have.” The most volatile period may come after the polls close, especially if close races remain unresolved while Trump alleges fraud. Trump will enter November in control of federal agencies with broad powers to investigate possible crimes, file lawsuits, pursue voter and citizenship records and ask judges to authorize searches for election materials. Some election officials and legal experts are preparing for the possibility that investigators could seek ballots or voting equipment while races are still being decided. Experts describe that as an extreme scenario, and any federal search warrant would require a judge’s approval. Disputes over fraud claims, ballot counting and certification drove weeks of legal battles after the 2020 election and culminated in the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol.

cnn.com.title: ‘We just have to bother the crap out of these people’: How the GOP is confronting its voter enthusiasm deficit
cnn.com.text: For Republicans, the midterm alarm bells are increasingly coming from inside their house. In Georgia, Rick Jackson, the GOP nominee for governor, has expressed concerns that rural voters had grown complacent. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis described turnout in his state as underwhelming and said, “Republicans have some work to do.” And in Texas, Bo French, the conservative firebrand running to be the state’s powerful railroad commissioner, has taken to social media to call out Republicans – especially men – in the counties he says are lagging behind Democrats. “Get off the bench,” French wrote this week. “The other side is showing up.” Across the country, in blue states and red, in marquee races and down-ballot contests, Republicans are confronting an unsettling reality: Democrats are showing a surge in enthusiasm their own party has struggled to match. A recent CNN/SSRS survey found 61% of registered voters who are leaning Democrat this year are extremely motivated to vote, up significantly from 34% four years ago. Meanwhile, Republican enthusiasm has barely budged since the last midterm election. CNN/SSRS polls in the battleground states of Texas, Kansas, Michigan and Maine found Democrats hold a significant edge in likely voters that are highly motivated. Republican voters are also less likely than Democrats to say it matters which party wins the House of Representatives in November, according to Pew Research polls. And while they were more attuned to the election than Democrats four years ago, the sentiments have flipped heading into November. One Republican National Committee official acknowledged the uphill climb facing the party. The official, who asked not to be named to discuss the midterm strategy, said Republicans have a tougher task than Democrats. They must sell voters on President Donald Trump’s accomplishments amid intensifying economic concerns, while also convincing them a Democratic takeover of Congress would be worse. “That’s harder than saying, ‘Orange man bad,’” the official said. Christina Crosby, chairwoman for the local Republican Party in Durham County, North Carolina, said Republicans in Washington haven’t adequately communicated the president’s accomplishments to voters in her state, where a US Senate seat is up for grabs. With just days remaining until the votes are counted, she said the outcome remains “hard to read” but she senses a broader weariness among the public. “There’s a fatigue across America with this political divide and I feel like there are people on both sides who are saying they’re throwing up their hands at all the texts and ads and saying, ‘I don’t want any more of this,’” she said. “It’s making it harder to get people out to the polls across the board. But the uneducated voter is the most dangerous thing.” The challenge mobilizing Trump’s coalition From the moment Trump returned to the White House, Republicans have maneuvered to overcome the historical headwinds that face the party in power and the challenge of keeping his voters engaged without him on the ballot. Trump’s political operation and Republican fundraising gave the party an unprecedented financial edge over Democrats. Meanwhile, Trump and his advisers ignited a mid-decade redistricting war intended to boost their chances of keeping the House. But those efforts now confront a political climate far more hostile than Republicans anticipated. An unpopular war, high gas prices, widespread economic unease and Trump’s sinking approval rating have threatened to overwhelm the advantages created by hundreds of millions of dollars of ad spending and a favorable electoral map. Perhaps the clearest evidence of the enthusiasm gap presenting itself at the ballot box so far is Democrats’ success turning out voters who might otherwise sit out a midterm election. In Kansas and North Carolina, for example, Democrats have opened large leads among voters who didn’t vote in one or both of the last two elections, according to a CNN analysis of early voting data. If that advantage holds — far from a guarantee — it could prove a consequential reversal of two years ago when Trump won every battleground state and the popular vote in part by picking up new support from Americans who rarely participate in elections. Hilario Deleon, chairman of the Republican Party in Milwaukee County, said his organization has spent much of the last two years focused on reaching the new voters that Trump turned out. While he believes they’ve made headway, he also acknowledged that many remain unaware of the stakes this November and why their involvement is even needed. “Politics is secondary and I don’t blame them for turning on a sports game to get a break from the world,” Deleon said. “It’s not necessarily that they’re angry at the president. But you’re going to find most people just don’t understand why it’s so important to show up in a midterm cycle.” It’s relatively new for Republicans to have to hound people on their side to cast ballots. Trump’s unique appeal in communities that tend to vote blue or not at all has transformed the party’s coalition, but it has also left Republicans struggling to replicate his success outside of presidential elections. Groups like Turning Point USA, the organization founded by the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, have recalibrated to create large ballot chasing operations to track down these irregular voters, but it remains a work in progress. “We’ve had several cycles to learn how to do it and there’s definitely a learning curve,” said Danedri Herbert, the GOP chairwoman in Kansas, the site of an unexpectedly competitive Senate race. “Democrats have been good at that for a long time, but we’re catching up to them.” The RNC official said the challenge can be as basic as informing voters when the election is taking place. “We just have to bother the crap out of these people to get them to vote,” the official said. “We’re talking 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 times to get them to action.” Rays of GOP hope Despite the troubling early indicators, some Republicans see reason for optimism heading into the final days. Herbert said any angst she felt looking at early voting returns a week ago has largely subsided and given way to confidence that the math is on her side. In Kansas, there are nearly 400,000 more registered Republicans than Democrats and she believes there are already indications they are making their presence felt. Republican gains in voter registration in recent years, particularly in key battlegrounds, have strengthened the party’s position heading into the midterms, offering a potential counterweight to the Democrats’ enthusiasm advantage. “Republicans are coming home, and they’re coming home fast,” she said. “I definitely feel a vibe shift.” Republicans are also counting on Trump’s aggressive travel schedule to help mobilize their side. For months, Trump has urged Republicans to vote as if he’s on the ballot. (Democrats, for their part, have long argued that Trump also motivates their voters wherever he goes.) Doug Deeken, chairman of the Wayne County Republican Party in Ohio, said voters in his northeast corner of the state are responding to the message. Trump and Vice President JD Vance have made multiple visits to the state as Republicans face exceptionally competitive races for Senate and governor. “If the president only had time to visit Michigan and Texas, maybe that would have worried me,” Deeken said. “But they’re spreading the love around.” Deeken said Republicans in his county are outpacing their 2022 performance. To him, it’s a sign that the polls are missing quiet Republican voters and that conventional wisdom about midterms may not apply to an election as unusual as the second midterm of a norm-busting president serving nonconsecutive terms. “Every time we think we know how politics works, especially in the era of Donald Trump, it changes,” he said. “People are trying to apply old rules to a new day.”

cnn.com.title: Three Bob Fergusons and two JFKs: A brief history of same-name ballot shenanigans
cnn.com.text: Before there were two Dan Sullivans, there were three Bob Fergusons. In 2024, Washington’s Democratic state Attorney General Bob Ferguson was joined in the gubernatorial primary race by two other Democratic hopefuls with the same name. Was it a coincidence? More like an age-old election trick that’s come up again in this year’s tightly contested Alaska US Senate race. In Washington two years ago, a Republican activist had paid the other two Bob Fergusons to run in the hopes that their names on the ballot would confuse voters — an effort to weaken the attorney general’s candidacy. But the decoys ultimately dropped out after just a few days when the first Bob Ferguson, who went on to be elected governor, threatened legal action and publicly derided their candidacy as an “attack on our democracy.” Now the tables have turned with Republicans accusing Democrats of a similar ploy in Alaska. A New York Times story Wednesday revealed that Democrats appeared to be behind having a potential Republican spoiler candidate, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan, siphon votes from incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The Justice Department has preemptively sued to block the results if the incumbent loses. Both Alaska and DOJ are investigating, and President Donald Trump has called for the criminal prosecution of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola, writing in a Truth Social post that she should “suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done.” “So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan,” Trump wrote. “Nothing else will do!” But there’s a long history of political operatives from both parties deploying the tactic — and largely getting away with it. “It’s a time-honored tradition,” said Thomas Kahn, director of the Center for Congressional and Presidential Studies at American University. “It’s not a good practice,” Kahn added, but “if trying to confuse voters was a crime, then every politician would be in jail.” The case of the spoiler grocery clerk One century-old example of same-name ballot stacking came in the 1930 Nebraska Republican US senate primary, when incumbent George W. Norris was dismayed to suddenly see another George W. Norris, a grocery clerk, running. “I’m finished unless the other George W. Norris is kept off the ballot,” the incumbent senator said at the time. It was ultimately a technicality that spoiled the candidacy for the spoiler grocer. Just as Sen. Norris prepared to withdraw from the Republican primary and run as an independent, the chief justice of the Nebraska Supreme Court ruled that the other Norris was ineligible because his petition had not been legally filed in time. Perhaps no other same-name candidate was more opportunistic than the “other JFK.” Rather than a decoy deployed by the opposite party, John Francis Kennedy, a Gillette razor factory stockroom supervisor, was a private citizen who merely capitalized on the Massachusetts name recognition of then-Sen. John Fitzgerald Kennedy. John Francis filed for state treasurer in 1954 and won without any party endorsement or public campaigning. The high school dropout from South Boston went on to win three terms. During his 1956 reelection bid, he was challenged by another political newcomer who entered the race because he was outraged that someone would pirate the good name of the Massachusetts senator. That candidate’s name was John M. Kennedy. Simply possessing the same name as a candidate is constitutionally protected under ballot access rules. Criminality occurs when operatives cross into falsifying residency documents, laundering campaign funds or offering direct payments in exchange for filing. That was the case in Florida in 2020. Authorities claimed that Republican state Sen. Frank Artiles recruited “ghost candidate” Alex Rodriguez with a $50,000 payment to run for office in the Florida legislature and to cause the Democratic incumbent with the same surname, Jose Javier Rodriguez, to lose the election by taking votes away in the razor-thin race. Alex Rodriguez received over 6,000 votes in the election, and Republican candidate Ileana Garcia beat the incumbent by just 32 votes. Artiles was ultimately convicted of excessive campaign contributions and procuring the falsification of a candidate oath form. Alex Rodriguez had sworn that he lived in the district’s limits when he actually resided in another county. While Florida law permits ghost candidates but prohibits people making excessive amounts of campaign contributions over $1,000, Bob Ferguson leaned on an 81-year-old Washington state law that makes it a felony to challenge someone with the same name “and whose political reputation is widely known, with intent to confuse and mislead the electors” to get the other two Bob Fergusons to drop their candidacies after just 72 hours when he threatened legal action. Jockeying on the Alaska ballot In Alaska, Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy said in a post on X that he would investigate if the “scheme” of recruiting a second Dan Sullivan to run “violated Alaska’s laws.” The Department of Justice last week preemptively filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate election if the incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, asking the court to potentially delay the certification of the election if the incumbent is defeated but would have won if “all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan” had “been cast instead for Senator Sullivan.” Legal experts have said the suit is unlikely to succeed. The state’s Supreme Court already ruled to keep the retired teacher on the ballot and Alaska’s Division of Elections sought to differentiate between the two Sullivans by listing the senator as the incumbent Republican and the other without a party affiliation. Alaska’s top-four primary election process — where the top four vote-getters advance to the general election regardless of their partisan affiliations — and ranked-choice voting system make the state particularly susceptible to same-name and spoiler candidate hijinks.
