The ranked-choice system, however, allows voters to show a preference for more than one candidate, so even if voters were hypothetically confused about which Dan Sullivan to vote for, they could select both, which would still favor the incumbent senator over Peltola. The August primary for Alaska’s Senate seat saw multiple efforts to boost minor candidates to hurt Peltola or the incumbent Sullivan. One group, Fair Deal Alaska, spent more than $800,000 attacking Peltola while promoting a lesser-known Democratic candidate and a Green Party candidate. A post-primary campaign finance filing revealed the group was mostly funded by the Senate Leadership Fund, the top GOP super PAC in Senate races. And in 2024, Alaska’s Democratic Party sued to keep someone off the US House ballot: Eric Hafner, who has no apparent ties to the state and is serving time in a federal prison in New York. The Democratic Party argued that it and its preferred candidate — ironically, Peltola — would be harmed because having an unaffiliated Democrat on the ballot “would confuse voters.” A divided state Supreme Court allowed Hafner to remain on the ballot. He is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the November 3 ranked vote general election ballot.

cnn.com.title: If Republicans win the midterms, Elon Musk’s money may be why
cnn.com.text: Elon Musk has plowed nearly half a billion dollars into elections in the 2026 cycle, a spending spree that makes him the single, largest disclosed donor in modern American politics and one of the Republican Party’s largest-ever benefactors. The world’s richest man has contributed more than $445 million to federal committees alone through mid-October – more than double the nearly $177 million that Democratic megadonor George Soros gave to outside groups during the 2022 cycle to become the largest known individual donor in the last midterm elections for Congress. Musk’s money could “single-handedly” alter the course of the midterms, said Brendan Glavin, who oversees research at the nonprofit OpenSecrets. The group tracks political spending. “One person is completely dominating and changing the landscape of how Republicans are able to spend money and defend themselves,” he said. Musk has donated nearly $216 million to America PAC, the super PAC at the center of his political operation. The group’s activity spans more than 40 House and Senate races this fall, according to federal campaign data. But nowhere has the billionaire spent more than in Texas, where he lives and has headquartered parts of his business empire. The key Senate contest there between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton could determine which party controls the chamber during the last two years of President Donald Trump’s tenure in the White House. America PAC has funded mailers, digital advertising and other outreach to Texas voters in an effort to defeat Talarico and other Democrats. But far more Musk money – at least $168 million so far – has been deployed in Texas through other groups. A pair of donations last month, for instance, from the SpaceX CEO to the Senate Leadership Fund, a leading Republican super PAC, were quickly funneled to a second group, Texas PAC, that has issued blistering attacks against Talarico on the airwaves, recent disclosures show. Much of the anti-Talarico messaging seeks to portray him as out of step with Texas values, with some citing his vote as a state legislator against a 2023 law banning gender surgeries and other medical interventions for minors. (Talarico’s campaign has said he does not support gender surgery for children but opposed the bill because it was overly broad.) Musk also has donated $10 million to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which as CNN’s KFILE reported this week, has underwritten AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico. A spokesperson for Musk’s America PAC declined to comment. But Republicans familiar with the strategy said the PAC is broadly focused on helping the GOP retain control of Congress next year and describe Musk’s move to shoulder some of the Texas advertising costs as freeing other GOP groups to deploy resources elsewhere to protect the Senate majority. In a statement, the Senate Leadership Fund’s executive director Alex Latcham said the donors who stepped up to fund Texas PAC “ensured that we did not have to divert any resources from other key races” and have allowed the group “to run effective campaigns across the map.” Last-minute onslaught Talarico has raised more money than any other federal candidate this cycle, $146 million through October 14, more than six times the $22.3 million collected by Paxton, according to Federal Election Commission records. And a CNN poll released Thursday shows the Democrat with a narrow lead over Paxton. But Talarico has faced an onslaught of outside spending from pro-Paxton interests, including those funded by Musk, in recent weeks. In the final four weeks of the Texas Senate campaign, Democrats have been outspent by Republicans on ads by more than 2 to 1, $118.9 million to $54.7 million, according to AdImpact data. Dave Carney, a top political adviser to Texas GOP Gov. Greg Abbott’s reelection campaign, says Republicans in the state believe the spending by Musk and other GOP groups is starting to exact a toll on Talarico. “It has taken the pretty boy, neighbor next door, cute moderate nice guy and has exposed his voting record,” Carney told CNN this week. Talarico is increasingly taking aim at Musk to highlight his outsized role in the Texas race, as Democrats work to motivate their voters to turn out in the final stretch. “Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat,” Talarico said during a recent rally as he ticked off the breadth of Musk-funded activity in the state. “In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your TV, that was Elon,” he said. “If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you’ve received a text message saying scary things about me, that was Elon, too.” A recent digital ad from Talarico reinforced the message, saying Paxton “will owe him everything” if Musk’s money helps to elect the Republican. A Paxton spokesperson did not respond to CNN’s inquiry. Democrats have sought to use Musk as a foil to spur turnout before. In Wisconsin last year, a $20 million spending blitz by Musk and aligned groups – along with his decision to campaign in the state – became a central message for Democrats who soundly defeated Musk’s preferred candidate in a state Supreme Court contest. Other Democratic ads that year used images of Musk holding a chainsaw aloft to highlight his controversial and short-lived tenure running the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency. This year, Musk has kept a lower profile, even as his political spending has soared to new heights. He has not campaigned with candidates. But he has used X, the social media platform he controls to amplify his criticism of Talarico with increasing frequency. In the last week, he’s posted more than a dozen times about the Democrat, often disparaging him as “far-left extremist.” Musk and his spending loom large over the election, said Lynda Tran, a Democratic strategist based in Washington. The billionaire may not be on stage “wielding a chainsaw and other theatrics,” she said, “but there’s no way to hide the ball on the contributions he’s making or how much he cares about various Republican races.” CNN’s David Wright contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: ‘Bravest person I know’: Father’s pride as school shooting victim leaves hospital after 262 days
cnn.com.text: A 13-year-old girl who was critically wounded in the deadly February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, Canada, has been released from hospital after 262 days, her father said Thursday. “There was never a day I stopped believing we would get here. The road ahead is still long, but this is a milestone no one thought we would reach,” David Gebala wrote in an emotional social media post addressed to his daughter Maya, calling her “the bravest person I know.” Maya was among more than two dozen people wounded in the mass shooting at a secondary school in the small mining town in northern British Columbia, which left eight people dead, including six children, in the country’s deadliest school shooting in decades. She was shot three times and airlifted to British Columbia Children’s Hospital in Vancouver, where doctors initially told her family she was unlikely to make it through the night, according to Gebala. “You refused to accept the words we heard 262 days ago when you came out of the OR. Look at you, my girl. You blew every expectation out of the water,” Gebala wrote in the post to Facebook, which included a video of Maya smiling in her wheelchair. Since February, Maya has undergone five surgeries, including receiving a prosthetic skull, Gebala said in the post, which listed challenging and hopeful milestones over the past 262 days. “251 days ago, you opened your eye, moved it, and shifted your leg only to be rushed back for emergency surgery that morning,” he wrote. “179 days ago, your prosthetic skull was placed. Your fifth surgery, and the one that finally stuck.” “145 days ago, you smiled for the first time (intentionally) while we played thumb war,” Gebala went on. “61 days ago, I heard your voice again.” “Now it’s time to leave these hospital walls behind and keep moving forward, Maya Bear,” Gebala wrote, thanking the nurses, doctors and therapists “who walked every step of this with us.” Gebala has frequently offered updates on Maya’s long recovery in posts to Facebook, including a recent excursion to see the rock band Foo Fighters and celebrate her 13th birthday. Maya, who was in the school library when the massacre unfolded on February 10, was shot three times, including in the head, which shattered parts of her skull and left her with catastrophic brain injuries, according to a criminal complaint filed by her family against OpenAI. The lawsuit, filed by Maya’s mother Cia Edmonds on her behalf, is one of dozens filed against OpenAI in both US and Canadian courts on behalf of victims, survivors and witnesses accusing the tech company of negligence after it emerged that the shooter, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The province of British Columbia is also suing OpenAI. OpenAI has pushed back against claims that it does not take safety seriously. In response to the lawsuits from the victims’ families, a company spokesperson told CNN in April that it has a “zero-tolerance policy for using our tools to assist in committing violence.” The company has said it deactivated an original account created by the shooter in June 2025 for violent activities, but Van Rootselaar made a second account to keep using the chatbot. The company’s CEO Sam Altman has previously apologized to the community of Tumbler Ridge for failing to notify authorities to the shooter’s disturbing online conversations with the AI chatbot even after staff flagged the account internally. Earlier this month, US authorities arrested a 30-year-old from Washington state who allegedly offered advice and sent money to Van Rootselaar ahead of the shooting. CNN previously reported Van Rootselaar posted about guns and hunting and her apparent mental health struggles online in the lead-up to the massacre.

cnn.com.title: After decades of boycotts, Palestinian citizens of Israel turned out to vote. It could shape what comes next
cnn.com.text: For decades, many Palestinian citizens of Israel stayed away from the polls, refusing to legitimize a system they say has oppressed their people, sidelined their concerns, and failed to represent them. But this time felt different: after four years under the most right-wing government in Israel’s history, hundreds of thousands of Arab voters decided they could not afford to sit on the sidelines. They turned out in record numbers – nearly 80% – to vote on Tuesday, compared with 53% in the last elections, according to the Mossawa Center, a civil society organization promoting equality for Palestinian citizens of Israel. That turnout gives Israel’s Arab parties unprecedented political sway with 19 seats in the 120-seat parliament. That surge was driven by a number of interlocking reasons. First, rising violent crime in the Arab community – seen as the result of negligent policing. Second, an urgent desire to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and bring an end to his right-wing coalition, which includes hardline ministers such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. No one was left in any doubt about the strength of feeling towards Israel’s national security minister, in particular, on Tuesday night, as chants of “Ben-Gvir, go home” broke out at the election headquarters of Joint List, the major Arab political alliance, as it became clear just how well the party had done. Long history Netanyahu’s coalition has overseen Israel’s devastating three-year war in the Palestinian enclave of Gaza, which has killed tens of thousands, and a yearslong campaign of settler violence in the occupied West Bank. “Our community wanted to bring down this criminal government, to change the grave reality caused by the policies of Netanyahu, Smotrich and Ben-Gvir,” said Dr. Ahmad Tibi, a leader of the Joint List. Tibi has spent nearly three decades urging the Arab community to exercise their right to vote. Now, he said, that high turnout is already having an impact: keeping Netanyahu from forming another right-wing government. Palestinian citizens of Israel – who make up 20% of the population – are descendants of Palestinians who were not expelled or forced to flee their homes when Israel was established in 1948. They were given citizenship but lived under military rule until 1966; many, though, feel that discrimination within Israeli society has continued to this day. They also include Palestinians who were born before 1948, like Mohammed Abdelhai’s 80-year-old aunt. On Tuesday, at her nephew’s urging, she became a first-time voter in the town of Tira, in central Israel. “I told her we have to vote,” Abdelhai said. “The last government was very aggressive with us, so this time we need every vote,” he said. The most important issue for him, he said, was a pervasive racism and lack of equality between Arabs and Jews in Israel. “If we can make a change, we can make a change. Why not? Why stay stuck in the same place?” Balance of power The strength of the Arab vote also means that neither Netanyahu’s governing coalition nor the opposition bloc are expected to win an outright majority. Now, Tibi’s Joint List, along with Ra’am, another Arab-majority party, appear to hold the balance of power. Tibi said the Joint List is prepared to help the opposition form a minority government, led by former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot. The Joint List would not join the government and would not seek any ministerial appointments in exchange – only a commitment to combat crime impacting the Arab community and stop the demolitions of Bedouin homes, which have risen under Netanyahu’s government. “If they want us to help, we will be there in order to help … we want to support the candidate of the opposition.” Tibi said. But doing so will require Eisenkot and his coalition to “be brave” in the face of Netanyahu’s condemnation of any attempt to form a government with the help of Israel’s Arab parties, he said. That’s because the idea of forming a government with the support of Arab parties has become politically toxic in Israel, with a majority of Jewish voters opposed. Several opposition parties have also previously ruled out such an arrangement. It remains unclear how much Eisenkot is willing to lean on the Arab parties for support. The only opposition party that supports doing that is the left-wing Democrats Party led by Yair Golan. “We have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Israel’s Arab citizens,” Golan said on Wednesday. “Now we need courage. We need leadership. We need to stop being afraid and to start taking action.” For Tibi, it’s more than fear holding some political leaders back. “It’s the pure racism against 20% of the population, Arab citizens. We are a legitimate part of parliament. We are a legitimate part of the citizens,” he said. Deligitimization efforts Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has consistently sought to delegitimize Arab voters and has repeatedly used the prospect of lawmakers from the Arab community sitting in government as a way to motivate his base to turn out and vote. In September, the CEC approved a motion to ban Arab parties to run in the election – a decision that was overturned by the High Court. As it became clear just how well Arab parties had polled on Wednesday, Netanyahu’s Likud issued a statement accusing them of “stealing the election.” This was followed on Thursday by the chair of Israel’s Central Elections Committee (CEC) sending a letter to the head of Israel’s security agency, the Shin Bet, asking him to investigate allegations of foreign interference in the election aimed at boosting turnout among Arab voters. In the letter, the CEC chair, Noam Sohlberg, admitted he could not attest to any of the suspicions, and Israeli police have said they have received nothing to back up the claims. Arab party leaders say Likud’s attacks amount to incitement and have pledged to defend the election results. Mansour Abbas, Ra’am party leader, said he would cooperate with any investigation and Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen said Netanyahu was “defeated” and “refuses to accept the voters’ decision.” ‘We belong to this country’ Many of the policies that have afflicted Palestinian citizens of Israel have been enacted under Ben-Gvir, the national security minister who was previously convicted of supporting terrorism and inciting anti-Arab racism. On Tuesday, some residents in Arab-majority towns told CNN they left polling stations without voting because of intimidation from men supporting far-right Israeli parties like Ben-Gvir’s. “People face high pressure – there was an old woman who could not stand the pressure, another one is pregnant who could not bear the situation and left … this is all because of racism,” said Taibeh resident Ulfat, who asked to be identified by her first name only. From Tibi’s point of view, the higher turnout among Arab voters compared with the Jewish majority shows that Palestinian citizens are “willing to influence and take part” in Israeli politics. “We are being blocked by the right and sometimes by the opposition. This is not a democracy. It’s an ethnic democracy. It’s a democracy for Jews,” he said. That sense of exclusion was echoed by voters across Arab communities, many of whom said it is what pushed them to the polls this time. Tira resident Munther Mansour, 60, has voted in the past, but this time he sees a real chance that his vote will count. “We never took an interest in elections before. But the level of racism and changes in our day-to-day life forced people to go out and exercise their right,” he said. “We belong to this country; we are part of the country. So we must exercise this right.”

cnn.com.title: Self-assembling magnetic tiles could build the space habitats of the future
cnn.com.text: Humans have grand plans for residing in space, from a new space station under development to a planned base on the moon. Some even hope that one day people can live on Mars. There’s work underway to figure out how to build habitats to support those ambitions. One of the innovations being tested is TESSERAE: magnetic, self-assembling tiles. Invented by Ariel Ekblaw while pursuing her PhD at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the tiles can be stacked on top of each other inside a rocket and released in space, where they can autonomously attach to each other — employing electro-permanent magnets, cameras and AI — to create a predetermined shape. Once they’re latched together, the structure can be pressurized, allowing humans to live inside. “They can self-assemble into something way bigger than the size of the rocket that they came up in,” said Ekblaw, who is now the founder and CEO of Aurelia Institute, a nonprofit space architecture research and development lab that has further refined the tiles. That could allow humans to build “science-fiction-worthy, big, grand structures” in space, she added. ‘A gold rush’ Starting in the late 1990s, it took dozens of missions to assemble the International Space Station (ISS), which rockets carried piece-by-piece to low Earth orbit. In space, robotic arms and spacewalking astronauts helped put it together. Recent years have seen a number of companies developing new kinds of space structures designed to take up minimal space in the rockets that transport them, and testing new construction methods. In 2016, Bigelow Aerospace sent an inflatable structure to the ISS. It was inflated with 25 short bursts of air over 7 hours, and it remains attached to the ISS today. Sierra Space has been testing its three-story inflatable habitat, and earlier this year, Max Space, which has a strategic partnership with Voyager Technologies, unveiled new expandable habitat modules. “We need real estate that is scalable and built for how humans will actually live and operate off Earth,” Saleem Miyan, its co-founder and CEO, told Space.com. Some are trying to reduce the need to bring material to space at all. European Space Agency (ESA) scientists have explored making LEGO-type bricks from meteorite dust and China is investigating how to make bricks with lunar soil. Sandra Häuplik-Meusburger, an architect and space researcher at the Vienna University of Technology, in Austria, told CNN that there are numerous challenges when it comes to building space habitats — from how to protect humans from radiation, to transporting materials, to how to design spaces “that can work for a long time for different kinds of people.” Adaptable architecture, like TESSERAE, could be helpful, “so that you can build something and maybe in 20 years you use it for something else,” she added. The technology’s reconfigurability is one of its key innovations, said Ekblaw. “You could absolutely pop tiles off and pop new tiles on and reconfigure them,” she said. It’s not just habitats. Some startups are looking at putting data centers and solar farms into space, to take advantage of 24/7 sunlight. Others are hoping to take manufacturing off planet Earth. “It’s like a gold rush at the moment,” said Häuplik-Meusburger. There is “a lot of interest from a lot of different players.” ISS testing TESSERAE — which stands for Tessellated Electromagnetic Space Structures for the Exploration of Reconfigurable, Adaptive Environments — have been tested on a small scale aboard the ISS in 2020 and 2022, with tiles a few inches wide. In December or January, the latest tiles — which have cameras on their edges to allow the tiles to see each other as they self-assemble — will be put to the test inside the ISS. If all goes well, the tiles will form a ball-shaped structure for the first time said Ekblaw — “maybe the size of a giant beach ball.” After that, the next test will be handled by Rendezvous Robotics, a spin off from Aurelia Institute, which will help commercialize the technology. On October 28, it announced that it had raised $20 million in funding. The tiles currently under development by Rendezvous Robotics use electromagnets and are about one to three feet wide. The company is working on scaling up the size, and it plans to do its first demo in 2028, outside the ISS, somewhere in the harsh environment of space. That will involve several tiles self-assembling into a flat shape, said Ekblaw, who is also the co-founder and board chair of Rendezvous Robotics. Grand infrastructure may be a way off. Ekblaw said that the first realistic use cases for the technology could be large antennas used for telecommunications and solar arrays. Next up, “they may be able to contribute to the future of AI data center build outs in space,” she said. “Basically, anything that’s really big infrastructure in space.”

cnn.com.title: World’s largest crypto exchange hit by world’s largest heist
cnn.com.text: Hackers stole over $6 billion in cryptocurrency on Thursday, shattering the record for the largest such heist as multiple investigators pointed the finger at North Korea. As of Thursday night in the US, a team of cryptocurrency firms had managed to freeze about $3 billion of the stolen loot amid a frenetic battle with the hackers to find and control the digital money. The hackers broke into digital wallets held at Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange. Binance said late Thursday that its initial investigation indicates that the hack went through an engineer’s laptop, “which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” On Friday, Binance co-CEO Richard Tend said on X that the attack was not a “one-click” action, but rather a complex process. He added that the investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual nor found evidence of any wallet private key leak. Binance said it would “cover all losses” from “the company’s funds” and an emergency assets fund, adding “user funds are safe.” The crypto exchange also said it had “temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed; revoked the affected address authorization; [and] engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds.” Analysts were shocked by the amount of money impacted. “It’s the biggest hack in history,” Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR’s systematic OTC business, told Reuters. Crypto-tracing firm TRM Labs attributed the heist to an elite North Korean hacking unit, “based on robust on and off-chain intelligence.” Pangolin Intelligence, another blockchain-tracking firm based in Singapore, said it also believed that a North Korean hacking unit was behind the heist. “Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]” led to the attribution, said an analyst with Pangolin Intelligence, who did not want to be named for privacy reasons. “I think the cat and mouse game has barely begun yet,” the Pangolin Intelligence analyst told CNN, adding that North Korea was likely poised to tap a network of money laundering organizations to try to cash out the stolen funds. Chainalysis, another crypto-tracking company, said it was monitoring stolen funds “moving across multiple blockchains,” including Bitcoin and Ethereum. A Chainalysis spokesperson told CNN the firm had “high confidence” North Korea was behind the hack. CNN has reached out to North Korea’s mission at the UN for comment. Pyongyang has previously denied hacking allegations. CNN has requested comment from the FBI, as well as the US Secret Service, which also investigates cybercrime. In past investigations of big crypto hacks, the FBI has had an on-call team of analysts that worked to freeze some of the money. If North Korea is proven to be the culprit, it would be little surprise to US law enforcement officials and private experts. North Korean hackers were blamed for the previous record-high crypto hack, when they allegedly stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, another major cryptocurrency exchange. In that case, the attackers stole an amount equal to a significant portion of North Korea’s reported annual gross domestic product in a matter of minutes. North Korea’s formidable hacking teams are a key source of revenue for the nuclear-armed, sanctions-battered regime, according to current and former US and South Korean officials. Pyongyang-linked hackers have stolen billions of dollars from banks and cryptocurrency firms in the last several years, according to reports from the United Nations and private firms. A 2023 CNN investigation spotlighted how the South Korean intelligence service worked with private crypto-tracking experts to seize about $1 million in cryptocurrency that North Koreans had stolen from a victim. Unlike platforms for trading stocks, cryptocurrency exchanges tend to hold digital assets on their users’ behalf, which make them more vulnerable to hackers and theft, particularly given a lack of regulatory oversight within the relatively nascent industry. Binance was co-founded in 2017 by Canadian national Changpeng Zhao, becoming the world’s largest crypto trading platform within a year of its launch. However, Zhao stepped down in 2023 after pleading guilty to violating anti-money laundering laws in the US. He was sentenced to four months in federal prison, and was pardoned by President Donald Trump in October last year. Zhao, who no longer manages the platform but remains its largest shareholder, said on X that the incident appeared to be a hack and that he expects user funds to be fully covered by the exchange. Prices of Bitcoin and Ether, the most widely-traded cryptocurrencies, plummeted following news of the Binance breach, but regained some losses to trade about 2-3% lower midday Friday in Hong Kong. This story has been updated.

cnn.com.title: The deeper question raised by the anti-Muslim attacks in Michigan’s Senate race
cnn.com.text: The Republican argument against electing Abdul El-Sayed as a senator is becoming perilously close to, Don’t vote for him because he’s a Muslim. Blistering rhetoric targeting the Democratic nominee in Michigan is among the most discriminatory — some would say bigoted — of any modern election. The goal of President Donald Trump, GOP nominee Mike Rogers and now even Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno seems clear: Portray El-Sayed as un-American and unacceptable for public office in a key race that could decide the Senate’s majority. The strategy is further polarizing a race also shaped by Trump’s unpopularity; soaring living costs; a trade war with Canada that hit border states such as Michigan especially hard; and splits between Democratic moderates and progressives. But the ugly tone of the Michigan Senate showdown runs deeper than a single tight election with enormous stakes. It is consistent with the language and actions of a president who, in one of the first official acts of his first term, tried to impose a travel ban on Muslims — and who, when speaking of his first presidential predecessor, Barack Obama, rarely drops his middle name, Hussein. Trump often seems to amplify cultural, religious and racial rhetoric at the most stressful political moments — like now, as he faces down the possibility of Democratic congressional majorities. Ultimately, it’s about portraying those who don’t share MAGA’s dogma, faith or majority-White race as somehow less authentically American. This tactic, as applied to El-Sayed, goes beyond a campaign scare. It challenges constitutional principles and reveals a divide between Trump’s movement and those with a more mainstream view of religious and racial diversity and their defining role in US identity. Trump’s comments on El-Sayed go from personal smears to mocking and stereotyping the Muslim faith — and, by implication, every American who shares it. He’s called El-Sayed a “jihadist”; said metal detectors would be needed at the Senate if he’s elected; and deliberately mangles his name as “Mohammed” and “Abdul Ramadan.” Trump seems to be equating being a Muslim with Islamist terrorism. On Thursday, he returned to one of his frequent tropes — that minorities see politics through one exclusive racial or theological lens. “If you’re Black, or if you’re Jewish, and if you vote for Abdul, you’re crazy,” the president said. Rogers is more careful to avoid maligning Islam generally, saying that he wore the uniform of the US Army to safeguard the freedom of Muslims to pray as they please. He’s stuck to questions around El-Sayed’s political affiliations, not mocking his name or faith. But in their last debate clash, Rogers said El-Sayed had links to the Muslim Brotherhood, an Egyptian Islamist group, and questioned his loyalties. “Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers asked. El-Sayed has disavowed the group. On Wednesday, Moreno stripped away all pretense, going beyond the false critique that El-Sayed may be a terrorist or a sympathizer to arguing effectively that he should be barred from office simply because of his faith. “This character Abdul El-Sayed can be nowhere near Washington, DC,” Moreno said at a Trump rally in Ohio. “Do you think he understands that concept that our rights come from God almighty, that Jesus came here for our salvation?” Moreno added. “He should be nowhere near Washington, DC, and (GOP nominee) Mike Rogers is going to kick his ass on Tuesday.” Article VI of the Constitution stipulates that “no religious Test shall ever be required as a qualification to any Office or public Trust under the United States.” The First Amendment says Congress “shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof.” Unlike El-Sayed, Moreno was not born in the US — he’s a naturalized citizen from Colombia. But he implied the Michigan Senate nominee does not deserve the same rights because he’s not a Christian. Such a view might also bar Jews, Hindus and Buddhists, all of whom are currently represented in Congress, from government service. The Constitution and the rejection of theocracy Corey Brettschneider, a Brown University professor who hosts the podcast “The Oath and the Office,” said that the anti-El-Sayed rhetoric has troubling constitutional implications. “When you are saying we can’t trust people who are Muslims and that he’s going to need to enter a metal detector — unlike everyone else in Congress — to get in, that’s nothing less than a religious test for office.” Moreno’s sympathizers might point to the use of the word “Creator” in the Declaration of Independence to argue that the founders, many of whom were believers, regarded the new United States as an officially Christian nation. But Brettschneider noted that George Washington and other founders took action specifically to ensure that the country did not have an official religion. “I don’t think Jefferson, who of course is a primary drafter of the Declaration, was a Christian nationalist, and the framers of the Constitution and the document itself are explicitly anti-Christian nationalism. It’s a rejection of theocracy,” Brettschneider said. It is appropriate for El-Sayed to be questioned about his attitude to the Muslim Brotherhood and to other foreign policy positions that many Americans oppose. And left-of-center parties in the US and elsewhere have sometimes not appreciated the concerns of voters who worry that their traditions could come under pressure from immigration or the diversification of their communities. Such omissions have created political space for populists like Trump. But much of the GOP’s rhetoric has gone beyond the cross-examination common in campaigns and ignores important context about El-Sayed’s past. The Brotherhood is a transnational Middle Eastern Sunni Islamist organization that was founded in Cairo, Egypt. Republicans have seized on old social media posts from El-Sayed’s half-sister describing how their mother — who left in El-Sayed’s early childhood — had been active in the organization in the ’70s. El-Sayed wrote an article in the HuffPost in 2011 arguing that if the Muslim Brotherhood took over Egypt, instead of its ruthless military rulers, the consequences could be more favorable than many people thought. This all came in the context of the Arab Spring uprisings, when tyrannical governments all over the Middle East were falling and long-persecuted opposition forces like the Brotherhood were emerging as alternatives. After the toppling of Egyptian dictator Hosni Mubarak in the Arab Spring uprisings, the Brotherhood’s political wing won democratic elections in Egypt under Mohamed Morsi, who became president. Hope suddenly rose that freedom would thrive in Egypt. But Morsi’s rule ended amid huge protests triggered by his economic reforms, and he was later ousted in a military coup. The Trump administration has designated some chapters of the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist organizations, including over support for Hamas. But the complex context is often missing in the Michigan furor. And since many voters are unfamiliar with the history, Republicans can use the Brotherhood as a vague proxy for Middle Eastern groups in a way that sounds threatening. El-Sayed slams dual loyalty questions In a town hall meeting earlier this month, El-Sayed rebuked a questioner for assuming “that because I am Muslim, that somehow I would have some allegiance to something that is not our Constitution.” He added, “For me, that Constitution is the guiding light.” This heated debate also comes against the backdrop of the political tumult unleashed in US politics over Israel’s response to the Hamas terror attacks on October 7, 2023, that killed around 1,200 people in Israel. Tens of thousands of Palestinians have died alongside many of the movement’s operatives in the operation. At the same time, many Democrats as well as Republicans are uneasy with El-Sayed’s positions on Israel and his calls for a change in US foreign policy toward the Jewish state. But a new CNN/SSRS poll Thursday casts doubt on whether the attacks are working in a state with a large Muslim minority and amid signs Democrats are uniting behind El-Sayed after a bruising primary. He led Rogers by 49% to 42% among likely voters. On Tuesday, Michigan’s voters will decide whether El-Sayed wins a Senate seat as America’s voters decide whether or not Democrats will control the chamber. But the race in Michigan will leave scars. It has turned into a deeper argument than the normal clashes between Republicans and Democrats, becoming a platform for a struggle over religious diversity, pluralism and the Constitution. Ultimately, it opened a new front in a perennial political question: What does it mean to be an American?

cnn.com.title: Protests and violence now go hand in hand in France. It wasn’t always like this
cnn.com.text: Lucas Petit was just 11 when hundreds of thousands of men and women wearing yellow vests poured onto the streets and occupied roundabouts across France in November 2018. His memories are hazy, though stories of clashes with police left a lasting impression. If he ever joined a demonstration, he knew what to expect. “It helped shape this whole collective image of a violent protest,” he told CNN. Petit, now 19, belongs to a generation for whom tear gas, water cannons, rubber bullets and stun grenades are par for the course when protesting. “We feel somewhat compelled to respond with violence because we’re facing social, institutional, symbolic and now physical oppression,” Petit said. “So I think violence has become normalized.” Petit has been blockading his school in eastern Paris for more than a month. He’s part of a movement that started out demanding better conditions at French schools and has since swelled into a collective cry of anger, bringing together groups with different grievances. On October 17, a day of largely peaceful nationwide protests morphed into chaotic scenes of looting and destruction: Limoges’s historic town hall went up in flames; shops were ransacked, and protesters were maimed for life. Opportunistic looters joined in, alongside young protesters from various backgrounds. According to an internal Justice Ministry document, 68% of the 186 people jailed between October 18 and 21 were 25 or younger, while 52% had no previous criminal record. Nearly half were classified as looters. Failures in the police response help explain how the situation got so out of control. Behind the tear gas and smoke, however, lies a shift in how some French protesters operate. Over the past decade, some have developed a savoir-faire for confrontation. As riot police have adapted their tactics and weapons, demonstrators have become adept at anticipating police maneuvers and exploiting gaps in security. Methods once associated with organized radical militants have spread to a younger generation. How Black Bloc tactics spread They tend to gather at the front of demonstrations, dressed head to toe in black, masked and hooded earning them the moniker “Black Bloc.” The groups first appeared in Germany in the 1980s. Associated with anarchist and anti-capitalist movements, Black Bloc is not an organization with a formal leadership; it’s a set of protest tactics. These methods gained prominence in France during the 2016 labor protests before spreading further during the Yellow Vest movement. Identities are concealed and participants often act as a group, sometimes attacking symbols of capitalism such as luxury stores. These type of protesters are often referred to as “casseurs” too, from the verb “casser,” meaning “to break” – a broad term that can be applied to anyone who vandalizes property regardless of their ideological beliefs. “Many young people who aren’t originally from the ultra-left are now adopting Black Bloc tactics,” said Thierry Vincent, an expert on radical-left movements. “It’s a way of protesting that doesn’t shock many young people anymore.” One Black Bloc tactic involves small, highly mobile groups breaking away from the main march, forcing police to spread their forces thin, making it harder for them to respond in a coordinated way. That was on display a fortnight ago when a group of protesters attempted to reach the Elysee Palace, drawing riot police away from the demonstration. The maneuver worked. Police resources were stretched, and it contributed to officers being overwhelmed that day. It’s not just their methods that have caught on. There’s also a wider willingness to confront the police. Hugo Melchior, a historian and left-wing activist who has attended demonstrations in the northwestern city of Rennes for two decades, saw that firsthand. In the sea of masked protesters, he spotted small groups of students apparently unconnected to militant organizations. “Sometimes it was four young friends, high-school or university students, probably affiliated with no network or organization, who had simply decided to come and demonstrate that way, with the intention of fighting,” he told CNN. Melchior had not seen so many people prepared for confrontation since the 2006 student riots. Police tactics are changing too Historically, France’s crowd control doctrine was all about keeping protesters at a distance. That’s become more difficult to maintain because of violent confrontations. Olivier Cappe, a former riot police officer with 25 years of experience who now represents the UN1TÉ police union, said officers are now facing threats from Molotov cocktails, fireworks mortars, pétanque balls and other projectiles. “Automatically you have to send your officers out to intervene, possibly charge and confront people,” Cappe said. “That’s where people get injured.” Staff shortages compound the problem. Cappe estimates France lacks around 800 specialist riot police officers. “The principle of French crowd control is numbers,” he said. “The more numerous you are, the more imposing you look. The more imposing you look, the less you intervene.” Outnumbered officers may resort more quickly to weapons such as rubber bullet launchers, he suggested. During both the Yellow Vest movement and more recently the student protests, officers without specialist crowd control training have been deployed with devastating results. Early in the protests, a 14-year-old boy suffered smashed teeth and a fractured jaw after a police officer fired a tear gas canister at close range, striking him in the face. A 16-year-old lost the use of an eye after being struck by a rubber bullet, while a 15-year-old lost a hand to a stun grenade, prompting the interior minister to temporarily suspend the grenade’s use. Cappe acknowledges that more forceful policing can deepen the problem. When officers confront violent groups alongside students, younger demonstrators may later come to identify with those being targeted. For student Lucas Petit, who identifies with the far left, the debate goes beyond whether violence is justified. It’s about what that violence is intended to achieve. He’s not shocked by attacks on symbols of capitalism, as he feels these acts of violence can serve a political purpose. “These are not acts of violence for the sake of violence,” he told CNN. “They have a very specific political message.” On Wednesday French President Emmanuel Macron described the escalation of violence as a collective failure. “I don’t think any high school student started pushing for their demands expecting to suffer such terrible consequences,” he said, adding police officers hadn’t signed up to face such violent confrontations either. When asked about a 15-year-old student who lost his hand, Macron said nothing could justify what had happened and reiterated his call for calm. Restoring peace to the streets is a tall order right now when so many feel that the government’s efforts to contain the violence, such as curfews, protest bans and a heavy police presence, violate their sacred right to protest and amount to a denial of democracy. And with this no longer just being a student movement, as trade unions and Yellow Vests join in, voicing grievances over the cost of living and calling on Macron to go, the anger is unlikely to subside anytime soon. On top of all that, France is heading into a deeply divisive presidential election in April, raising the stakes even further. A winter of discontent may lie ahead, with another protest on Saturday and a major demonstration scheduled for November 5, raising fears of a repeat of the extreme violence seen on October 17.

cnn.com.title: Israel’s election ended in deadlock. Here are four ways out
cnn.com.text: Israel faces weeks, possibly months, of political limbo after final results show there’s no clear winner in its elections. Neither of the two main blocs – one led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party, the other led by the centrist Yashar party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot – have reached the required 61-seat majority to form a government in Israel’s 120-seat parliament. So how could a new government be formed? Certainly, it does not look easy, with deep-rooted political and ideological divisions making any seemingly straightforward coalition almost impossible. Still, it can be done, even if the result is a tenuous alliance that survives little more than a year or so in office. If party leaders are unable to figure it out in the 12 weeks they will have available, then Israelis will be back at the polls. Here’s some potential scenarios that could avoid that. Scenario 1: An opposition government On paper, the opposition’s surest path to unseat Netanyahu is built on Jewish-Arab cooperation. And that is its biggest obstacle. Two of the opposition bloc’s right-wing party leaders, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman, oppose any government that depends on the two Arab parties in parliament – the Joint List and Raam – whether it’s from inside the coalition, or as outside supporters of a minority government. The two leaders have hardened their positions since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023. Only one government in Israel’s history has enjoyed the full participation of an Arab party. Raam was part of an eight-party coalition that succeeded in ousting Netanyahu in 2021, but it collapsed just after a year in office. Even without forming a government, the opposition parties could still work together and leverage their parliamentary majority to replace the Knesset speaker, along with other key positions, and thereby constrain Netanyahu’s caretaker government as it continued in power. But the prospects of assembling a coalition to replace him as Israel’s leader remain highly complicated and politically charged. Scenario 2: A national unity government Another option would see the implosion of the two blocs in favor of a unity government. Netanyahu’s Likud party would certainly be involved, along with some of his existing coalition partners, as well as – crucially – at least one party from the opposition bloc. Netanyahu, in this case, is believed to be willing to part ways with his far-right National Security Minister Ben-Gvir – but not from far-right Finance Minister Bezazel Smotrich and the ultra-Orthodox parties. Eisenkot, however, has ruled out sitting with Netanyahu, and it would be seen by many Israelis desperate to see the back of ‘Bibi’ as an act of betrayal if he were to change his mind. Scenario 3: A Netanyahu bloc government with defectors Another scenario could see Netanyahu encouraging defections from opposition parties or individual lawmakers. But all four opposition bloc party leaders – Eisenkot, Bennett, Liberman and Yair Golan – have declared they will not sit with him. And with Netanyahu’s bloc a full eight seats short, persuading eight individual defectors sets a high bar. Scenario 4: Another election While all these possibilities are being discussed in the background, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will hold a very public round of consultations with the leaders of the parties that have made it into parliament. Once he has solicited their opinions, he will task one of those leaders with the job of trying to form a government. Arab parties are expected to voice their support for Eisenkot, so the Yashar leader could be asked to go first. Whoever gets the nod will have 28 days to complete the job, with a possible 14-day extension if needed. If it all comes to nothing, the president will ask a second leader to have a go. They get 28 days only to sort it out. After that, a majority of Knesset members could ask the president to task a third candidate, who then has 14 days to build a coalition. If none of these produce a breakthrough, there will be another election. The person who appears best-placed to navigate this timetable is Netanyahu. As caretaker prime minister, he can afford to wait: If main rival Eisenkot gets the first shot – and fails – the mandate is likely to pass to him. And if he fails as well, the political deadlock seems certain to lead Israel to another round of elections – with Netanyahu remaining caretaker for months, until another government is formed. A repeat election – which would happen no earlier than next spring – is a real possibility, as these results look set to return Israel to a state of political paralysis and what would be the seventh general election in eight years.

cnn.com.title: Mushroom killer to be jailed for life after appeals court finds sentence too light
cnn.com.text: An attempt by murderer Erin Patterson, who killed three people with a meal of toxic mushrooms, to overturn her conviction has failed, with an appeals court finding that her original sentence was too light for her “cold and calculated” crimes. Patterson, now 52, was found guilty last July after a jury trial that attracted international attention due to the unusual method of murder – death cap mushrooms hidden inside portions of beef wellington at a family lunch in July 2023. The Australian mother was given three life sentences for the murder of three people, including her estranged husband’s parents, as well as 25 years for the attempted murder of a fourth guest, the local pastor, who recovered after weeks in hospital. She was sentenced to a non-parole period of 33 years, meaning she would have been in her 80s when freed. However, three appeals court judges instead found Friday that her crimes – which included an “elaborate series of deceptions” – were so “extraordinarily cold and calculated” that she deserved to be in prison for life. “In all the circumstances, after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period,” said Justice Stephen McLeish. Patterson’s lawyers had presented seven grounds of appeal in the hope that the mother of two would be granted a retrial. On the first ground, they took issue with the way the jury members were sequestered, which they claimed was “catastrophic” to their case. During the trial, held in the small Victorian town of Morwell, jury members shared a hotel at various times with prosecutors and witnesses. While there was no evidence that the guests interacted, Patterson’s lawyers said the possibility of interactions “cannot be excluded.” However, the three appeals court judges found “there was no objective basis for a fair-minded person to reasonably apprehend that the jury might not have discharged its function of rendering a verdict according to law.” The judges also rejected suggestions that some evidence shouldn’t have been submitted, including cellphone data that put Patterson near the location of death cap mushrooms posted to a citizen scientist website. The judges found the evidence was admissible as part of the prosecution’s “wider circumstantial case.” A fatal lunch The case has been dissected at length in books, podcasts, documentaries and feature articles since the first facts emerged in mid-2023, after Patterson invited four people to her home for a special Saturday lunch. Within hours of the meal, the guests experienced severe stomach pains and within days, three of the four were dead, including her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail’s sister Heather Wilkinson. Heather’s husband Ian Wilkinson was the sole survivor. Patterson doesn’t deny cooking the meal that ultimately killed most of her lunch guests, but she claimed she had accidentally laced the meal with death cap mushrooms as she tried to improve its flavor. However, the jury found she picked the mushrooms for the purposes of murder, drying them in a dehydrator that she dumped a few days after the meal, as her guests lay dying in hospital. Friday’s ruling means that Patterson will have no prospect of release during her lifetime. The appeals court found that the murders were “carefully planned and deliberate” and represented “a cruel breach of trust.” Patterson wasn’t in court to hear the result of her appeal, but appeared via a video link from prison. Reporters inside the court in Melbourne, Australia, said she showed no emotion when the ruling was read. Outside the court, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported that “prosecutors, police investigators and supporters” of Patterson’s ex-husband “grinned broadly.”

cnn.com.title: Bukele adds a wildcard to Haiti’s fractured security landscape
cnn.com.text: What could go wrong? For over a week, El Salvador has been quietly sending troops to Haiti, a project whose scale was only revealed publicly last night: More than 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers will be sent to the Caribbean nation, but their mission and mandate remain opaque. The deployment is a wildcard in Port-au-Prince, a city of densely-inhabited hills where battle lines constantly shift between dozens of gangs and anti-gang groups, including foreign forces, neighborhood vigilantes, and mercenaries. Two thousand soldiers is a significant arrival here. That’s more than Haiti’s entire army, and about a quarter of the urban footprint of the Haitian National Police. It’s about equal to the current staffing of the multinational UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) and far outnumbers the private military contractors on the Haitian government’s secretive “task force.” But how do they fit into Haiti’s fractured security landscape? Who is paying for it? And what exactly is their mission? For now, the Salvadoran forces’ command structure has not been established, according to a source close to the matter. On Thursday evening, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele posted online in Haitian Creole, announcing that the deployment to Haiti is “nearly completed” and that “90% of the expenses” would be shouldered by El Salvador. “This is not an operation against the Haitian people nor an invasion of Haiti… Our only goal is to bring our four aviation technicians back home. Furthermore, we intend to teach a lesson to the gangs,” he wrote. “Perhaps future generations of Haitians will remember us as friends who once came to help,” he added. The missing air technicians, catalyst for this deployment, disappeared earlier this month after an apparent gang ambush. They had been working with the GSF in a noncombat role, according to Salvadoran officials. In the immediate aftermath, 100 special forces were sent to Haiti to assist in search and rescue operations — a precursor to the now expanded force. Ten days later, local sources say it is unlikely that the missing four can be recovered. If Salvadoran forces cannot achieve that, they’ll likely seek other wins, perhaps joining one of several existing security forces for an extended push against the gangs in retaliation. A communiqué released by Haitian interim leader Alix Didier Fils-Aimé on Wednesday night described a phone call with Bukele about the deployment and operational cooperation “within the framework of the GSF.” A clue to their plans may eventually lie with the troops’ physical location; at time of reporting, the Salvadorans were not staying at the main GSF base in Port-au-Prince. Bukele has argued that he has unique bona fides to address Haiti’s crisis. His government’s own hardline crackdown on gangs back home did restore peace to what was once the most violent country in the Western Hemisphere — though critics highlight his use of mass incarceration and accusations of widespread abuses. In a message posted to X last week, he addressed the gangs in Haitian Creole: “There is still time to avoid this,” Bukele said. “Return our four countrymen to us alive and unharmed and everything will return to the way it was before the kidnapping.” Most residents of Port-au-Prince would rather see dramatic change, after years of brutal gang violence that have driven over a million people from their homes. Just two hours from Florida’s coast, the city is terrorized by frequent gang kidnappings, rape and arson, all broadcast on social media. On Thursday, Haitians nationwide were reminded again of just how much insecurity has put civil life on pause, with the news that long-deferred presidential elections are postponed yet again until next year. But experts warn about the dangers of additional players on a crowded urban battlefield. “The situation is volatile and could become more violent with innocent people being harmed,” Bill O’Neill, the UN’s human rights expert for Haiti, said. Romain LeCoeur, Haiti expert at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organized Crime, echoed the concern. “Haiti’s security response no longer rests on a single strategy, but on a juxtaposition of multilateral, national and private actors, each operating under its own rules,” he said. “As long as no one can say who decides and who is accountable, every operation risks adding to the confusion rather than to security.” Reporting contributed by CNN’s Merlin Delcid in El Salvador.

cnn.com.title: Justice Department’s Dan Sullivan criminal probe accelerates after Alaska campaign revelations
cnn.com.text: The Justice Department has dramatically accelerated a criminal probe into whether Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters by recruiting a Senate candidate intended to siphon votes from the Republican, issuing dozens of new grand jury subpoenas and homing in on new potential charges, according to people familiar with the investigation. The moves came on the heels of a New York Times report published Wednesday describing an alleged coordinated effort linked to Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign. The report provided investigators material that they hadn’t previously obtained, two officials familiar with the matter said. Federal prosecutors issued more than 40 grand jury subpoenas and record preservation notices to key targets by that evening, one of the officials said. Additional subpoenas are expected on Thursday, that person added. The Alaska activity follows an already frenetic series of Justice Department actions that have marked a stark difference with previous administrations, including the first Trump term, when it took pains to remain out of the public eye in the weeks leading up to the election. Justice Department officials claim the Alaska investigation, a highly-visible search of Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home, criminal charges against prominent critics of the president, grand jury subpoenas to California election officials and challenging voter rolls in several states, are normal and time-sensitive law enforcement activity. They also frame the election-related efforts in Alaska and other states as intended to safeguard the votes, not sway the election as critics have alleged. ‘Decoy Dan’ and Alaskan voters The federal investigation over Daniel J. Sullivan, nicknamed “Decoy Dan” by his opponents, had been moving at a slow clip, people familiar with the matter said. Republican state officials had sought to disqualify the Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot, arguing his was not a genuine candidacy but rather an attempt to confuse voters who wanted to vote for incumbent Sen. Daniel Sullivan. But the state supreme court rejected those efforts and restored the dueling Sullivans on the ballot. Michael Heyman, the US Attorney in Alaska, recused himself early in the federal criminal investigation in part because he was in discussions with Senators Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski for a judgeship nomination in the state, sources familiar with the matter said. That left the investigation to be run by career officials in his office and prosecutors from the department’s Civil Rights Division. The investigation had already roiled the US Attorney’s office in Alaska, one of the officials said, where some career prosecutors have balked at aspects of the probe and whether the effort broke federal law or simply represents electioneering dirty tricks. A department official denied the alleged backlash. Before Wednesday, prosecutors had issued some grand jury subpoenas and interviewed witnesses, one of the sources said, though at least one of the witnesses has largely gone quiet in recent months. After the Times article published, some department officials questioned why the Times appeared to have evidence that prosecutors had not yet obtained. Heymen un-recused Wednesday afternoon at the request of department leadership. “Suddenly the options in the criminal case became much wider,” a department official said Thursday. A second department official said investigators were looking to potentially bring civil rights charges, including a deprivation of rights charge that more typically is levied against law enforcement officials for wrongdoing. “I think they should be prosecuted,” President Donald Trump said Wednesday, referring to Peltola and Dan J. Sullivan. “To me, that’s voter fraud at the highest level.” The lawsuit Separately, department officials filed a long-shot lawsuit last week seeking to delay certification if Sen. Sullivan loses and the votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan under the ranked choice system would have been enough to change the outcome. Senior department attorneys worked quickly to amend that lawsuit, which proposes an undefined “investigation” into whether voters were misled, after the Times article was published. In the new version of the federal lawsuit, the department alleges that the Peltola campaign and a national Democratic Party office submitted “misleading” arguments about their knowledge of the alleged efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan. To that point, it cites twelve different excerpts from the Times report. “Although what the New York Times reports is not always true, its reporting here aligns with what the United States has been alleging on information and belief,” the new lawsuit states. “It also aligns with common sense.” Alaska’s Republican-led elections office is pressing a court to dismiss the case quickly, arguing that lawsuit seeks to sow “doubt” and will “cast a cloud over” the contest. Because of Alaska’s ranked-choice system, it could be weeks before the winner of the Senate race is declared. Critics have slammed the lawsuit as political maneuvering, particularly after Trump told reporters he directed it. Attorney General Todd Blanche tried to walk back the assertion by saying in an interview days later that Justice Department was conducting its own research, but declined to discuss his conversations with Trump, who had publicly raised the issue for months. State and federal officials briefly discussed a potential settlement in the case but have been unable to agree on what one source described as a “middle-of-the-road approach.” Among the proposals was providing additional instructions for poll workers to clarify for voters which Sullivan is which. Some inside the department privately admit that the Alaska lawsuit, which is all but destined to fail, still serves a purpose by creating headlines that warn Alaskans about what one source described as a “massive voter fraud attempt.” A state official told CNN that there are examples of voters who are well-informed about the dueling Sullivans still erroneously filling out their ballots and having to seek new ballots. It’s unclear how many of the spoiled ballots are related to the Sullivans confusion. It’s a “preservation lawsuit” one federal official told CNN. “It will allow us to challenge the election if a challenge becomes necessary.” This story has been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: Machado pushes for new elections in first news conference since returning to Venezuela
cnn.com.text: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado said she returned to the country from exile this past week to mobilize society as she pushes for new elections next year. “I have returned to finish a task and to fulfill a mandate,” she said Thursday in her first news conference since her return. The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize laureate thanked the US government for leading a democratic transition process in the South American country, saying Secretary of State Marco Rubio has outlined a sequence of events that includes holding presidential elections in 2027. “This addresses a national urgency with a sense of responsibility. It has also made clear — based on what has transpired in recent days — that the democratic transition is irreversible,” she said. Neither the United States nor the Venezuelan government have set a date for new elections. Rubio said on Monday that Venezuela’s electoral infrastructure needs to be changed in order to hold a valid election. A senior State Department official said they expect Venezuela to have a new Supreme Tribunal of Justice in place by the end of year and a new National Electoral Council (CNE) shortly thereafter. Once those institutions are replaced, Venezuela’s acting leader will have to declare a permanent vacancy in the presidency, which will trigger a six-month period for new elections, the State Department official said. The CNE will then determine a date of that election. Impact of return Machado returned on Sunday to crowds of cheering supporters, whom she said all demanded a free Venezuela. “I heard only one word, the same one: freedom,” she said Thursday. Machado left in December for Norway to accept the Nobel Peace Prize, which she was awarded for promoting democratic rights in her country. A month after she left, the United States toppled and captured her rival, strongman leader Nicolas Maduro, in a military operation on January 3. “Thanks to the actions of the United States government, Maduro is facing justice, and the floodgates of freedom have been opened,” Machado said Thursday. Within days of Maduro’s ouster, Washington began working with his successor, acting President Delcy Rodríguez, to enact political reforms and steer the nation toward a democratic transition. Rodriguez has so far met just about every demand from the US, including releasing hundreds of political prisoners, allowing some exiles to return home and making it easier for US companies to invest in the country. The US has also brokered reconciliation talks between the acting government and several high-profile opposition figures such as Dinorah Figuera. Machado reiterated on Thursday that she is not part of those talks but said she hopes they succeed. Shortly before Machado’s speech, Rodríguez also addressed the nation. She did not directly acknowledge Machado’s return, but addressed her detractors in the recorded message, saying: “To those who think differently from me, I do not ask you to change your opinion. I ask you to judge by the facts. Less fighting, more solutions.” Regarding the electoral calendar in the South American country — an open question since Maduro’s capture — Rodríguez reiterated that “there will be elections, as mandated by our Constitution.” “The election should not be a problem or make us go back to times of confrontation that no one wants anymore,” she urged. She also announced the continuation of reforms, including a promise that no one would be detained without judicial warrants, a long held demand from human rights groups. Rodríguez also revealed that the government is assessing whether non-essential assets currently held by the government will be offered to the private sector, or to former owners. The acting president said the process is “already well underway. Private property is a protected right guaranteed by our Constitution.” Machado welcomed Rodríguez’s comments, saying her commitment to new elections means the government is feeling the impact of her return. Asked if there are plans to meet with the acting president, Machado said, “No, I have not received any message from the United States or from Ms. Rodríguez.” Sidelined opposition Washington has so far sidelined Machado from the political transition process despite having a friendly relationship with the opposition leader. In January, Machado gifted US President Donald Trump her Nobel Prize, hoping the gesture would nudge him toward supporting her fight to become Venezuela’s next leader. Trump accepted the gift without endorsing her. He had previously called her a “very nice woman” but claimed she “does not have the support or the respect within the country” to lead it. Still, Machado has continued to back the Trump administration while simultaneously condemning the acting Venezuelan government that it’s been working with, which she considers a continuation of the repressive Maduro regime. During her 10 months in exile, Machado repeatedly vowed to return home and hinted that she would run for president if an election were held. She had attempted to re-enter Venezuela several times over the past few months without success, saying she was impeded by the acting government. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday the US had spoken with the interim Venezuelan authorities about Machado’s return and claimed that any “impediments” to her arrival “had nothing to do with us.” Machado didn’t provide details about how she returned, but said she received help from many people both inside and outside the country, including what she described as an “exceptionally well-qualified” team. Machado added that she had learned from her previous failed attempts to enter the country and did things differently. “And let me tell you: They didn’t see it coming,” she said of the acting government.

cnn.com.title: The range of outcomes in the 2026 battle for the Senate is enormous
cnn.com.text: Imagine when the dust settles on the 2026 midterm elections that Democrats haven’t gained a single Senate seat and are stuck at 47. Now imagine it’s a week after the election, and Democrats have won 55 seats — or even as many 57 — giving them the second-largest Senate majority for either party since 1981. The distance between those two outcomes isn’t nearly as large as you might think. With just five days left in the 2026 election, there is a huge margin of error in the battle for the Senate — with many races showing no clear leader in the polls. More than a dozen seats have polled mostly within the margin of error (six seats) or just outside of it (five seats), or the races appear competitive but there’s not high-quality polling (two others). Also looming large is the fact that Democrats are mostly chasing states that President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024 — and where it’s feasible that large numbers of conservative voters come home to their side at the very end of the election. Let’s break it down. Recent New York Times/Siena and CNN polls have filled out the picture in many key Senate races. And several races that are likely to determine the majority are well within the margin of error. The CNN poll in Michigan shows Democrat Abdul El-Sayed up by 7 points, but 6 of the last 8 quality polls there have shown no clear leader. Likewise, the CNN poll in Texas shows Democrat James Talarico ahead by 6 points, but 6 of the last 9 quality polls have shown no clear leader. The CNN poll in Kansas is now the second of two quality polls to show no clear leader. The last five quality polls in Iowa have shown no clear leader. The first quality poll in South Carolina this week was a dead heat, at 48%-48%. And CNN’s poll in Maine makes it six quality polls in a row — and 11 of the past 12 — where there has been no clear leader. Even if we assume only those races are in-play — and the rest of the races go as expected — the possible outcomes range between Democrats winning 49 seats and winning 55 seats. (That’s a one-third chance of Democrats remaining in the minority; Democrats winning 50 seats would keep Republicans in control, by virtue of Vice President JD Vance’s tie-breaking vote.) Beyond those six races: If Democrats were able to win all the margin-of-error races; plus North Carolina, Ohio and Alaska, where the polls are more in their favor; and add Florida and Mississippi, they’d be up to 57 seats. The GOP losing Nebraska would make the Democratic majority 57-42, if Osborn didn’t caucus with either party. Only once since 1981 has one side or the other controlled more of the Senate than that. That was after the 2008 election, when Democrats had 59 seats (and later won a special election to get to 60 seats). But it’s also possible Democrats could have a pretty good election, notching one of the biggest popular-vote wins in recent decades, and still come up short of a Senate majority. That could happen if they lose one or both of Maine and Michigan, or if they don’t win enough of the double-digit Trump states they’ve been chasing. Even if the popular-vote margin from the 2024 presidential race moved uniformly toward Democrats by 10 points in every state, that only gets them to 49 Senate seats. And it’s worth noting that in CNN’s polls of Michigan, Texas and Kansas, at least 1 in 8 likely voters say they could still change their minds about whom to support. In Texas and Kansas, at least 6 in 10 of those uncommitted likely voters are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, suggesting there is room for political gravity to work in the GOP’s favor as voters settle on their decisions. In other words, buckle up. The battle for the Senate could go so many different ways, with massive implications for the final two years of Trump’s second term.

cnn.com.title: Hackers claim leak of sensitive details on thousands of DHS workers
cnn.com.text: The Department of Homeland Security is investigating after hackers claimed to have stolen and leaked the sensitive personal information of tens of thousands of current and former department employees, including some that work on covert and sensitive missions. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a department spokesperson told CNN. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.” A source familiar with the data breach confirmed that the information of some undercover personnel had been exposed. A hacktivist group calling itself the Department of Peace obtained the data, and the anti-secrecy group Distributed Denial of Secrets posted it online on Wednesday, according to a statement from the latter group. The group’s co-founder, Emma Best, said that the leak “identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations.” A preliminary CNN review of the data found that at least some of the personal information attributed to DHS personnel in the leak is accurate. The data includes phone numbers, work supervisors and assignments for DHS personnel. Also in the breach is data belonging to at least three Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol officers who were involved in shootings during the second Trump administration, according to the CNN review. US officials familiar with the data leak reacted with a mix of concern and grim familiarity. One official called the leak “embarrassing,” but added “we have certainly seen worse.” They expressed concern about the possibility of phishing and doxxing stemming from the data dump. The data was taken from an “internal” DHS database linked with a “single sign-on service” used by employees, according to Distributed Denial of Secrets. DHS reiterated to its workforce Thursday that they were aware of the alleged data breach, according to an internal memo reviewed by CNN, adding that they’re “working to understand the scope of the situation, assess potential threats, and identify appropriate resources and protective measures.” In an earlier memo, employees were also pointed to previously shared resources offered to personnel for removing personally identifiable information from the internet. The leak “reveals information that can be used by hackers to target the computers and devices of DHS personnel engaged in sensitive investigations and security work,” said Thomas Warrick, a former deputy assistant secretary for counterterrorism policy at DHS. He called for a thorough investigation from Congress of how the breach occurred. “DHS can’t just lock the barn door after the horse was stolen,” Warrick added. “It needs to make sure DHS and its contractors focus more on keeping the barn locked.” “This hack has just served to put thousands of ordinary civil servants in the crosshairs of anonymous internet trolls,” said Sarah Pierce, director of social policy at the Third Way think tank, and a former official at DHS’s US Citizenship and Immigration Services agency. “Many of these employees have served the federal government for decades, under multiple administrations,” Pierce told CNN. “They didn’t design these policies, and they don’t deserve to be punished for them.” It’s just latest example of US law enforcement agencies scrambling to respond to their agents’ data being posted online. Last month, the FBI was dealing with its most serious breach in years after a cybercriminal group called ShinyHunters claimed to access data on thousands of current and former FBI personnel. That data heist included information on FBI personnel working in sensitive units focused on China and Russia, according to sources who have seen the data.

cnn.com.title: Spanish train crash yet another blow to Sánchez’s government ahead of elections in November
cnn.com.text: The deadly train crash in Spain’s Toledo province has sparked fresh criticism of Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s government and raised questions about the country’s investment in public infrastructure – just weeks before national elections in November.
