His account contradicted one given by the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi, who said: “The way is open for food, medicine, and humanitarian aid to enter the city and even for Saudi-backed groups to do so. Anyone who wants to verify that there is no siege on the city of Taiz can go to the city and see.”
Shamsan said that Houthis forces had a near-total grip on the roads into the city, adding the group had issued a choice to the more than 800,000 inside the city “either to leave or to die”.
He accused the Houthis of not waging a military battle but a battle to change the identity of Yemen, with captured villages being taken over by new religious leaders with education and religious curricula being changed. “This is not a military war but a war of vengeance,” he said.
Vowing the people of Taiz would resist until the end, he said statements of solidarity were of no use and that what was needed was access for aid agencies, including the UN, to deliver supplies to the city.
Shamsan was reluctant to divulge details of the state of the military campaign, but said shelling of the city was becoming more frequent and that communication between the city and rural areas had broken down. Houthis now controlled the mobile networks and were sending messages to citizens to end their resistance, while eavesdropping on all conversations, he said. Mobile networks were “completely disrupted”, he said, adding that he was speaking only 2-5km from the frontlines.
Most independent agencies agree that life inside the city is rapidly deteriorating. Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “Renewed efforts by the Houthis to cut off food, water, and medicine to Taiz show their utter disregard for civilian lives.
“Throughout the 12-year-long siege of Taiz, the Houthis have bombed, starved and denied humanitarian aid to a million residents of the city with scant adherence to international law.”

theguardian.com.title: Andy Burnham admits he would have liked more radical first budget
theguardian.com.text:
Andy Burnham has admitted his first budget as prime minister was not as radical as he would have liked because of the economic uncertainty facing the country.
He said he would have liked to have gone further with this week’s announcement – including with higher energy support payments – but felt hemmed in by external events such as the war in Iran, which has pushed up borrowing costs.
Burnham’s chancellor, John Healey, announced a range of relatively inexpensive measures on Wednesday, including a £100 payment for most households to help with energy bills this winter.
He has faced criticism for not doing enough on a range of issues including defence spending, welfare cuts and support for the cost of living.
Burnham told ITV: “The room for manoeuvre wasn’t what I would have hoped it to be. I guess then the question is, you know, radical within what we were able to do.
“It was quite a big call to ask the banks to repay the help they had off people 20 or so years ago. And a payment – OK, you’d like it to be more – but a payment to 20 million households is quite a significant step.”
Asked whether this was the budget he had wanted to deliver, he added: “I don’t think any prime minister and chancellor would say that, because a budget is by definition a very difficult thing.
“In the times that we’re currently in, I feel that the volatility of things means you just can’t necessarily deliver the budget that in an ideal world you would want to deliver.”
He said he wanted major changes to the benefits system that would prevent most young people having to claim benefits at all.
Burnham will spell out his plans for welfare reform in the coming months after two major reports on the system, one by the former minister Alan Milburn and one by the current minister Stephen Timms.
He told ITV on Friday the changes would not involve “brutal cuts” that would leave people in “absolute crisis”.
But he added: “I don’t actually want to see anyone in their 20s on benefits. I just don’t think that’s a good place to be, unless people can’t be in work for reasons due to disability or whatever else it might be.”
Burnham came to office this year promising an end to “40 years of neoliberalism” and a plan for sweeping change of the economy, including higher taxes on wealth and nationalisation of major utilities.
So far, however, he has made a series of smaller announcements that he and Healey say are meant to give voters “breathing space” while the government works on more radical plans for the future.
They have included tax cuts on energy bills, lower bus fares and fines for people playing music out loud on their phones on public transport.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said on Wednesday: “Most people in the country, listening to that budget, will be thinking to themselves ‘is that it?’.”
Burnham told ITV he was limited not only by geopolitical crises but also by Labour’s 2024 manifesto, which helped propel the party to a landslide victory but ruled out major policy options such as raising income tax, national insurance or VAT.
“Obviously, when the time comes, I would seek my own mandate,” he said. “If you’re asking me a very direct question, if I had held the pen on the current Labour manifesto, would I have written it exactly like it is? Well, no is the answer to that question.”
Burnham is also under to spend more on defence, with the Labour chair of the defence select committee, Tan Dhesi, accusing the government this week of inaction.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, hit back at that criticism on Friday, saying the government was investing in defence immediately and would announce more at the spending review.
“I like Tan very much,” he told BBC Breakfast. “He’s a friend, and I respect him. But I strongly disagree with him, and I don’t think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we’re funding right now.”
Streeting hinted there could be further departmental cuts next year to pay for another increase. “As the budget showed yesterday, there are choices and trade-offs,” he told Sky News. “I recognise that other government departments, as well as taxpayers, are doing some heavy lifting to make sure we prioritise defence. That’s the right thing to do.”

theguardian.com.title: North Korean group blamed for $6.3bn Binance hack in biggest ever crypto heist
theguardian.com.text:
The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by an industry-record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Binance has scrambled to freeze the affected assets, with about $3bn located so far. The company gave no update on the other $3.3bn as Binance’s co-founder Yi He said the company would cover “all hacking losses”.
Analysts attributed the attack to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of approximately $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Tokyo cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in what was the previous record crypto heist.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit. Chainalysis, another analysis outfit, also attributed the heist to TraderTraitor.
Binance did not explicitly confirm that funds had been stolen, although TRM and Chainalysis claimed more than $6bn had been taken. The company said its teams were “working around the clock” to resolve the problem.
An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.
Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.”
The company said in a statement: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”
Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368. Shares in the crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8%, while those of the bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading.
Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony in the US related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack on Binance”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.
If confirmed, the incident could be the world’s biggest crypto heist, according to Chainalysis and other industry experts. “It’s the biggest hack in history,” said Aravind Srinivasan, the head of the large crypto market maker GSR’s systematic OTC business.
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure lately because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges, as well as counterparty, solvency and liquidity risks,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.
Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website.
Bernardo Brites, the CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company, said: “It’s becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them. My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, [as it is] becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn’t cover a hack of meaningful size.”
The stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m.
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.
Binance’s Yi said $27m in stablecoins and about $2m worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350m in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability to hackers.
Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.
Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.
Coinbase said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.
In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, the prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.
With Reuters and the Associated Press

theguardian.com.title: BP profits jump as Middle East conflict drives up oil refining margins
theguardian.com.text:
BP has posted a jump in its quarterly profits as the war in the Middle East drove up oil and gas prices and led to “significantly higher” trading.
The energy company said on Friday that third-quarter underlying replacement cost profit – a key measure of its income – rose to $8.46bn, up from $2.2bn a year ago. Analysts had expected profits of $7.33bn.
The company said the jump in profits “mainly reflects significantly higher realised refining margins and significantly higher gas and marketing trading result”.
BP’s quarterly earnings were bolstered by higher profits from the oil refining business. Although global oil prices have remained below the peaks recorded during the 2022 energy crisis, the pump prices for fuels including diesel have soared to all-time highs across the UK, Europe and the US in recent months because of severe disruptions to refineries in the Gulf region and across Russia.
Meg O’Neill, the chief executive of BP, said: “These are dynamic times with volatility and disruption to trade flows continuing to define energy markets. The industry as a whole has been showing remarkable adaptability. Refineries have been running close to capacity to make up for shortfalls, shipping has been taking different and longer routes, and releases from strategic and commercial reserves are helping to bridge supply gaps.”
The jump in BP’s profits angered climate campaigners. Danny Gross, of Friends of the Earth, said: “As millions of households brace themselves for a cold winter huddling under blankets and clutching hot-water bottles as they struggle to pay their bills, BP is raking in huge profits while doubling down on gas and oil production and slashing investment in renewables.”
BP laid bare its earnings windfall after Shell and the French oil rival TotalEnergies reported their strongest profits since 2022, also in large part thanks to the profits made from refining crude into fuel products such as diesel.
The US-Israeli war on Iran has boosted profits for oil majors, leading to questions over how they will allocate the extra cash. BP said on Friday it would use the excess cashflow generated by earnings to address remaining liabilities in full from the Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010.
Deepwater Horizon oil spill payables and provisions stood at $5.94bn, according to BP data.
BP is expected to set out its first major strategy update under O’Neill on 15 December, which market observers expect will outline the company’s plans to grow its oil and gas production and potentially restart share buybacks from next year.

theguardian.com.title: Are Trump’s global actions, from Ukraine to Iran, going to hurt him in elections?
theguardian.com.text:
Outside the Ukrainian educational and cultural center in a quiet Pennsylvania suburb of Jenkintown, on the outskirts of Philadelphia, a banner expressed unqualified gratitude: “Thank you USA for supporting Ukraine.”
Inside, however, the sentiment was altogether different. Irene Skulsky, a retired teacher in her late 70s, voiced indignation at Donald Trump’s sudden turn against her ancestral homeland, which she believed had come close to killing her son, Darko, and a desire to punish his fellow Republicans at next week’s midterm elections.
“When we vote, we have to vote with Ukraine in our hearts,” she told her fellow retirees, gathered to hear a presentation by the Daughters of Knyahynya, a women’s group delivering military equipment to Ukrainian special forces on the frontline. “I know many people here are Republicans, but we can’t go according to party lines now. Ukraine needs us. They need our support. We need to shift the balance of power in Congress and in the Senate.”
Days earlier, Skulsky told fellow members at a meeting of the Ukrainian American Senior Citizens Association, Darko had been sitting in traffic en route to work in Kyiv when Russian drone missiles slammed into five cars immediately ahead of him.
There had been no prior alert, allegedly as a result of a decision by Washington to suspend its intelligence-sharing arrangement with Ukraine that has acted as an early warning system against missiles attacks since Russia invaded in February 2022.
In recent weeks, Trump – who pledged during his victorious 2024 presidential election campaign to end the Russia-Ukraine conflict within 24 hours of returning to office – appears to have abandoned Ukraine.
He struck a deal with the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, to buy nearly 5m tonnes of diesel, overriding US sanctions on Moscow. He called on Ukrainians to replace the country’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy. His administration was accused of throttling the Ukrainian military’s access to the Starlink satellite internet service.
And while the Trump administration denied that it had stopped sharing intelligence this month, as relations with Ukraine nose-dived, Zelenskyy has said his country received no advance warning from US intelligence networks of two Russian missile attack waves.
Darko escaped injury, but several people in the vehicles in front were killed in the strikes, according to Skulsky. Her frustration spilled over to include Trump’s fellow Republicans, whom she said were “selling our souls” rather than standing up to the president.
“Republicans are afraid of Trump,” she said. “They’re afraid to lose their position. I think their heart is with Ukraine, but they’s sitting on their hands.”
Many American Ukrainians will express their outrage at the polls on 3 November, according to Eugene Luciw, a retired lawyer and local representative of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, an advocacy group.
“For [American] Ukrainians, I believe foreign policy is unquestionably the No 1 issue,” he said. “But I think even the average American without the added affinity of a homeland in Europe is going to see foreign policy as a very important issue.
“It’s beginning to reach people’s minds and hearts that something very important is brewing in Europe. If Ukraine loses this war, we have the beginnings of world war three.”
The most recent Ukraine development is the latest in a trio of Trump foreign policy decisions with the potential to hurt Republicans when Americans head to the polls next week.
More relevant to voters’ living costs – a key issue in this election, according to polls – has been Trump’s protracted war with Iran, and his determination to impose tariffs on imports from much of the world.
The Iran war, launched with Israel in February, shows no signs of ending despite Trump’s early claims that it would be a short-term “excursion” certain to end in the “unconditional surrender” of Tehran’s Islamic regime.
Instead, Trump has reportedly drawn up plans to launch renewed strikes against Iran after the midterms as he seeks to break Iran’s grip on the strait of Hormuz, an energy choke point that was the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s energy supplies before the Tehran regime closed it in response to being attacked.
The strait’s closure has resulted in soaring global oil prices, which have been passed on to US consumers in the form of higher prices for petrol and diesel, which is vital for supply chains and US farmers.
Polls have consistently shown voters’ disapproval of Trump’s handling of the war, and his management of the economy and inflation. Roughly 70% are now critical of both, according to a recent AP-Norc survey.
The war’s economic impact has compounded the inflationary effects of Trump’s tariffs, which has affected the prices of consumer goods and increased costs for manufacturers by increasing the costs of imported raw materials such as steel, copper and aluminum.
The tariff regime has also strained Washington’s relations with once-close allies – perhaps most visibly with Canada, the US’s second-biggest trading partner. Ties between the two neighbors plunged to a new low in August following the collapse of bilateral trade talks.
Following the collapse, the Trump administration imposed tariffs on $20bn of Canadian imports – including cars, forestry and dairy produce – triggering a retaliatory tit-for-tat response from Canada’s government, led by the prime minister, Mark Carney. In Michigan, which shares a border with Canada, even Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers released an ad calling on Trump to end the trade war and declared: “Canada is not our enemy.”
Trump has articulated his vision with characteristic bullishness. After January’s US attack on Venezuela, during which it ousted the country’s president, Nicolás Maduro, he dubbed his strategy the “Donroe doctrine” – a play on the Monroe doctrine, named after the 19th US president, which states that the western hemisphere should be Washington’s exclusive domain.
He bragged about extracting Venezuela’s oil resources and fantasized about making the country “the 51st state” in a speech this week in Corpus Christi, Texas, during which he showed off a tanker he claimed was carrying 1m barrels of oil and repeated a phrase – “to the victors belong the spoils” – that startled foreign leaders when he first uttered it at last month’s gathering of the United Nations general assembly.
There are fears that his neo-imperialist instincts could be applied after the midterms to Cuba, where he has repeatedly pledged to topple the communist regime that has ruled for the past 67 years.
Meanwhile, Trump’s fixation with autocratic leaders has been extended to China’s president, Xi Jinping. Having already met Xi at a summit in Beijing this year before hosting him at the White House, Trump will go to China again next month to meet the Chinese leader.
On a range of issues, he has shown disdain for diplomatic niceties – dispensing with seasoned diplomats to instead rely on Steve Witkoff, a real estate investor and attorney with no background in foreign policy, and Jared Kushner, his businessman son-in-law, as negotiators over matters as intricate as Iran, Gaza and Ukraine.
Yet Trump’s latest Ukraine turn carries special resonance, not least because it risks a dramatic rupture with Washington’s European Nato allies, who are heavily invested in Kyiv’s protection as a first line of defence.
It has highlighted once again Trump’s complex relationship with Putin, an autocratic leader for whom he has repeatedly voiced admiration. It is also a reminder of Trump’s failure to live up to his frequently expressed vow to swiftly end the Ukraine war during the 2024 presidential election campaign.
Trump has blown hot and cold towards Zelenskyy. At an explosive White House meeting in February 2025, he told the Ukrainian leader “you don’t have the cards” – but with a peace deal on terms acceptable to Russia seeming ever more distant, relations seemed to thaw, with Trump even publicly mooting giving Ukraine a license to build its own Patriot missiles.
In recent weeks, however, Trump appears to have definitively ditched the US’s putative ally and sided with Putin.
Economists argue that the volume of diesel covered by his deal with Moscow is too insignificant to reduce diesel prices, which have been inflated mainly by the effects of the Iran war, rather than by the actions of Ukraine.
Witkoff, Trump’s envoy, caused further consternation by praising Putin as a “humanitarian” after the Russian president agreed to release a 74-year-old US citizen, Stephen Hubbard, whom Russia had imprisoned for several years after falsely accusing him of fighting for Ukraine.
The Russia-friendly moves have stunned Ukrainian Americans, many of whom have pro-Republican sympathies dating back to the cold war, when staunchly anti-communist presidents like Ronald Reagan were seen as champions of self-determination for the constituent, so-called “captive nations” that comprised the Soviet Union, which included Ukraine.
“We are befuddled and upset by what’s going on,” said Andrij Chornodolsky, chair of the senior citizens association, who urged his fellow members to call the White House and leave comments criticizing the recent policy moves. “How can you be doing this to us?”
The US is “helping a country that wants to subjugate Ukraine back into a new empire, the Russian empire”, added Chornodolsky, who was equally angry with Republicans who have failed to criticize Trump over his abandonment of Ukraine.
“What are the comments coming out of Congress?” he said. “Silence speaks very loudly. If you do nothing, you agree with the person making the pronouncements.”
There are about 60,000 people of Ukrainian descent in Philadelphia’s metropolitan area, the second-largest such ethnic population in the US after New York. From 105,000 to 122,000 people are estimated to claim Ukrainian ancestry throughout Pennsylvania.
Peter and Orysia Hewuka, long-term Republicans who had both previously voted for Trump, said they were likely to vote for a local Democrat because of Ukraine, even though it represented a psychological hurdle.
“I am very hesitant to vote Democrat. I’m a lifelong Republican,” said Peter, 88, a retired nuclear physicist. “But I can’t vote for people who support what Trump is doing. The Republican party has left us, we haven’t left the Republican party.
“It’s very difficult for me and for a lot of Ukrainian Americans to vote for the Republican party based on what they’ve been doing in the past months.”
Luciw, of the Ukrainian Congress Committee of America, said even Trump’s diehard supporters in the Ukrainian community had been alienated by the diesel deal with Putin.
“From my interactions on social media and elsewhere, I would say more than 75% of those who supported him have now abandoned him because it’s now clear where this is headed,” said Luciw, 68, who described himself as a Reagan Republican, but now also intends to vote Democrat.
“Until the last few weeks, there was a hope that Trump’s swinging back-and-forth on Ukraine was a kind of negotiation … that maybe he would come to terms with things because it looked liked Ukraine was going to win and he would support a winner,” he said. “But the diesel deal reversed all that.”
Mykola Hryckowian, director of the Center for US-Ukrainian Relations, said he voted for Trump three times and been active in an ad hoc group called Ukrainian Americans for Trump – but has since severed his last vestiges of support.
“I went to the polling booth in the last election not knowing who to vote for, thinking I might write in Zelenskyy, but in the end voted for Trump, because I couldn’t vote for Kamala Harris,” he recalled. “Today, I could not vote for Trump.
“But a lot of my colleagues [on the committee] were very staunch, holding onto Trump until the very end. But in these last two weeks, they have turned around and said: ‘This is an abomination’.”
Not all Ukrainians are surprised by Trump’s actions. Mark Andryczyk, a Ukrainian studies scholar at Columbia University and board member of the Ukrainian League of Philadelphia – a cultural group that hosts performances by writers and musicians from the country – said the president’s actions were predictable.
“I never thought Trump would be a good idea for Ukraine,” he said. “You just have to look at how happy Russia was each time he was elected.”
“All his information on the war is basically Russian talking points,” added Andryczyk. “I can’t imagine why anybody would think he was pulling for Ukraine. Perhaps people somehow thought that he wouldn’t be doing this. I would think that their eyes are open now.”
A clear-eyed view of Trump’s foreign policy could reap an electoral whirlwind for Trump’s Republican allies on 3 November, with the pocket-book effects of his tariffs and the war on Iran looming large as voters head to the polls.
Yet such an outcome could be a double-edged sword. Should Trump become hemmed in at home by a Democrat-controlled Congress in the final two years of his presidency, where better to assert his power than the rest of the world?

theguardian.com.title: Mahmood infuriates fellow ministers by failing to reveal impact of UK migration shake-up
theguardian.com.text:
Shabana Mahmood has infuriated ministerial colleagues by failing to share what they see as crucial information about the impact of her migration changes.
Sources say the home secretary has repeatedly refused to reveal how much she expects homelessness to rise as a result of changes to the asylum system.
Home Office ministers will meet their counterparts from other departments over the next few days to thrash out a compromise amid warnings about a potential staff crisis in the care sector.
One person with knowledge of the standoff said: “Shabana has been asked on multiple occasions what the Home Office assessment was of the impact her changes would have on homelessness and community cohesion, but she point-blank refused to engage with it.”
The Home Office says it cannot quantify the exact impact of the proposals because the detail has not yet been finalised. They insist the new system will be designed to minimise any impact on destitution and homelessness.
However, others in government believe the Home Office could give out more detailed information but does not want to admit how much disruption the proposals will cause.
“It has caused a huge amount of frustration among other ministers who are working on the government’s push to end rough sleeping,” said the source.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “This policy went through the normal cross-government process, with information shared through the formal collective agreement process.
“Ending asylum hotels will not leave people homeless. We are moving people into more suitable accommodation while delivering reforms that have already saved taxpayers more than £1bn since the election.”
Mahmood announced her changes to the asylum system last November, including ending permanent leave to remain and the government’s duty to support people who would otherwise become destitute.
The home secretary said her proposals would restore order to the immigration system and help puncture the appeal of hard-right parties such as Reform UK.
In an impact assessment released this month, however, her department admitted homelessness could rise.
“There is a risk that, if repayments materially reduce disposable income, some individuals could experience financial hardship or destitution,” the document said.
“This may increase demand for homelessness services and rough sleeping support, creating additional cost pressures for local authorities.”
The first requests for details about the potential impact were made by Ali McGovern and Miatta Fahnbulleh when they were ministers under Keir Starmer. They were supported by the then housing secretary Steve Reed, who was also understood to have been concerned about a possible rise in rough sleeping.
The three ministers already feared the push to move asylum seekers out of hotels could lead to more people sleeping on the streets.
They said the proposals made last November could prevent the government from hitting its target of halving rough sleeping by the end of the parliament.
McGovern and Fahnbulleh secured a meeting with Alex Norris, then a Home Office minister and now the justice secretary, but felt few of their questions were answered.
The pair were preparing to write a formal letter to the Home Office to demand the information when Fahnbulleh resigned from government in a move that helped bring about Starmer’s departure from Downing Street. The letter was never sent, sources said
An ally of Mahmood pointed to the Home Office’s impact assessment, which says: “Thresholds and repayment rates will be designed to … ensure individuals retain sufficient income to meet basic living standards.
“Given that the design of the recoupment mechanism has not yet been developed, it is not possible to assess the scale of the risk at this stage.”
Ministers say the row has only deepened since Andy Burnham came to power, not least because the prime minister has promised to give every rough sleeper a route off the streets by Christmas, committing hundreds of millions of pounds to do so.
Sources say Angela Rayner, Reed’s successor as housing secretary, also wants to see more details about the impact of Mahmood’s proposals.
The sources say she is particularly concerned about the possibility that moving asylum seekers out of hotels and into houses of multiple occupancy will reignite anti-immigration protests.
Rayner has argued against Mahmood’s proposals for changes to legal migration as well, arguing the government should exempt care workers from plans to make it harder for workers to achieve settled status.
The Guardian revealed this year that Burnham was considering intervening to make sure care workers were exempted and prevent a sudden exodus from the sector.
The issue is set to be decided over the next 10 days after a series of meetings between senior ministers.
A government source said: “The prime minister wants ministers to deal with the detail of this policy, but he has made it clear he supports Shabana but also wants to make sure sectors get the support they need.”

theguardian.com.title: Friday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties?
theguardian.com.text:
Good morning. It was described by many Israelis as the most consequential election in their country’s history. And, as the final votes were tallied, it has delivered a result that presents Israel with a significant dilemma.
Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition has lost its mandate while the opposition has a clear majority: but only if the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, led by retired general Gadi Eisenkot, is prepared to make a governing pact with Palestinian Israeli parties, which have secured a historic result.
But the country that is desperate for change remains bitterly divided. After a campaign mired in racism, during which Israel’s far-right demonised the Palestinian population as the enemy within, Netanyahu has gone further since Tuesday’s vote, claiming that Palestinian-led parties have “stolen the election”, despite Israeli authorities insisting there is no evidence of election fraud.
As coalition talks commence, I spoke to our chief Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison in Tel Aviv, about false narratives and the stark choice facing the country. But first, the headlines.
Five big stories
- UK politics | John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.
- Patrick Stewart | The acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi, died at his home in Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, his longtime spokesperson said.
- Environment | One of the most ambitious nature recovery projects ever undertaken in England can go ahead after campaigners announced they had raised £30m to buy an estate in Northumberland.
- Europe | Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday for at least 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision, as hospitals continued to treat dozens of injured passengers and train drivers went on strike to urge more investment in railway safety.
- US news | The Trump administration has opened a criminal investigation in California over claims that thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in the state, and has begun subpoenaing election officials.
In depth: There is no evidence of election fraud
With the final results released early on Friday local time, Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats, compared with 48 for the grouping led by rival Eisenkot. Palestinian parties won 19 seats, a record high. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions.
With neither bloc reaching the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israeli president Isaac Herzog is expected to invite the party most likely to be able to form a government to start coalition negotiations, and has already urged politicians to have an “open mind” before talks begin. The country potentially faces weeks of rancour and uncertainty.
Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, told Israeli media on Thursday that he was meeting Eisenkot and others for initial talks. If the opposition can’t agree some kind of coalition, or even secure Palestinian support for a minority government, Netanyahu may have a lifeline. He is already pushing for a right-wing governing coalition, and would probably welcome new elections or a lengthy period of uncertainty during which he will stay on as caretaker prime minister.
And yet throughout the campaign, voters’ discontent with Netanyahu was evident.
That didn’t mean a shift to the left: young Israelis are more rightwing than older generations, as Emma wrote about here. The national conversation ahead of the election was dominated by security at home and abroad. Although he was in charge on 7 October 2023, when Hamas attacks resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians, the prime minister tried to shift blame on to the security services.
His opponents pledged a state commission of inquiry into the events of 7 October, and spoke to voters’ concerns about the social toll of three years of multi-front wars, and anger about the draft exemption for ultra-orthodox young men when other Israelis are spending hundreds of days on reserve duty.
Netanyahu’s false narrative
Throughout the campaign, Netanyahu and his far-right allies have framed Palestinian voters – who make up about 20% of the population – as a direct threat to the state, with Netanyahu repeating the slogan “the right or Palestine”, which rhymes in Hebrew.
“It’s both tragic and depressing,” Emma tells me, “attempting to paint Palestinians as untrustworthy citizens with dual loyalties, a racist trope that also appears in antisemitic attacks.”
This tactic extended to election day, when voters received a robocall purporting to come from the prime minister falsely claiming that Palestinian party leaders had been caught with envelopes full of cash. Netanyahu and his allies repeatedly made claims about high turnout in Palestinian areas, in a bid to get his own voters out.
Then on Wednesday night, Netanyahu reacted to the high Palestinian turnout and success of Arab Israeli parties by claiming, again without providing evidence, they had “stolen the election,” calling for the central elections committee and Shin Bet internal security agency to investigate foreign interference in the vote. These claims were amplified by far-right Israeli finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who called for the arrest of Arab Israeli leaders.
He was swiftly accused of using smear tactics to cling to power. Eisenkot warned that Likud and Netanyahu “have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election”. President Herzog stepped in with a rebuke to the prime minister and said “we must avoid tarnishing an entire community”. Meanwhile, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson rejected “ridiculous and dangerous” accusations his country had interfered in Tuesday’s election.
It bears repeating: Israeli police and the central elections committee have said there is no evidence of election fraud.
The Palestinian-led parties who could be kingmakers
There was a surge in support for Arab parties after Palestinian citizens came out in historic numbers to vote.
Many had boycotted previous elections “on the grounds that participating endorses a discriminatory system or because they felt their representatives had little leverage”, Emma explains. But this year, the mood changed: “They’re watching ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, a genocidal war in Gaza, and are under huge pressure inside Israel from an openly racist government, which has allowed organised crime to soar, ramped up home demolitions, and targeted political speech. They felt that, if Netanyahu managed to get another mandate with his far right allies including [extremist security minister] Ben-Gvir, this would only accelerate.”
The Joint List – which represents a number of mainly leftist Israeli Arab-led parties – is led by Yousef Jabareen. He has previously said the Joint List could not join an Eisenkot-led government because of its support for Israel’s military operation in Gaza and southern Lebanon, but has left open the possibility of bolstering a minority government through confidence votes.
The other main Palestinian party, Ra’am, is led by Mansour Abbas, and includes a Jewish former chief of police as number two on their slate, a signal of their commitment to working with Jewish Israelis but also their desire to tackle organised crime, which is a big issue for the Palestinian population.
Ra’am joined Naftali Bennett’s government in 2021, the first time a Palestinian party entered an Israeli coalition, but their pact collapsed after 18 months, partly because of disagreements over the occupied West Bank.
The big dilemma
A survey taken as polls closed on Tuesday showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu.
While Eisenkot has not ruled out cooperating with Palestinians because of their race, he has effectively barred them from a future coalition by laying out conditions for any partner which are politically impossible for them to accept.
Still, Emma notes an inconsistency: Palestinian citizens play a key role in Israeli life, with outsized representation in professions from medics to security guards, including much of the team at Eisenkot’s election night HQ. “You would think some of these parties might ask, if you trust Palestinian citizens to secure your campaign events why don’t you trust them to be part of your government?”
Emma points to a rarely referenced precedent from three decades ago, when Yitzhak Rabin relied on Palestinian support for a minority government as he sought a negotiated end to the Israel-Palestine conflict. Might such a compromise be possible now?
“This whole campaign has been based on Israeli voters urgently wanting change, because Netanyahu has led them to the brink of disaster. And now they have voted, this is an existential moment,” she said
“You have a parliamentary majority to bring about that change. Is your racism ultimately more important to you? What matters more: the desire to exclude Palestinians or the desire to get rid of Netanyahu?”
What else we’ve been reading
- Tim Burrows’ deep dive on how Romford might actually be the birthplace of jungle was surprising and gave me a sense of nostalgia for a time that I wasn’t really part of. Poppy Noor, newsletters team
- The latest instalment of our US politics film series, Anywhere but Washington, really captures the vibe in Texas where all eyes are on a hotly contested midterm Senate race. Michael
- Adrian Chiles on the cryptic sign outside his local pub was a lesson in when not to brag. I now know far more about pub tubes, mould and yeast than I ever cared to know. Poppy
- Andy Beckett’s ode to the British Library comes as some of its silent, free-to-access reading rooms face a #coworking space fate. Fun fact, I once fell asleep for a whole hour inside one … Michael
- Readers’ reactions to the budget was a real take on the different ways people in the country live. Poppy
Sport
Women’s Champion League | Paris Saint-Germain’s Tara Elimbi Gilbert had a late equaliser moments after Khadija Shaw scored a penalty as Manchester City drew their third league phase game in a row.
Cricket | England beat Sri Lanka in the One Day International by 55 runs but still do not progress to the final on Sunday.
Football | Everton beat Newcastle 3-1 with goals by James Garner, Hayden Hackney and Thierno Barry to set up a Carabao Cup quarter-final with Fleetwood Town.

Shock and anger in Spain after deadly train crash
Spain has begun three days of mourning after at least 69 people were killed and more than 100 were injured in a crash between two high-speed trains. The town of Urda has become the site of a major operation, as emergency services continue to search through the wreckage and relatives wait for news of their loved ones. There is growing public anger over the incident, which is the second fatal train collision in Spain in less than a year. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Madrid correspondent, Sam Jones.

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Moving away from diesel-powered ferries to electric vessels has not been an easy task. Batteries are heavy, which means more power is needed to propel electric boats forward through significant resistance. But more companies are finding solutions to the problem and creating workable vessels that reduce emissions.
One such company is Vessev, whose electric ferries rely on underwater wings called hydrofoils that lift the boat above the water. This dramatically reduces drag by up to 66%, making their boats more energy-efficient. Swedish company Candela are designing boats, they claim, which can reduce energy use by 80% compared with conventional vessels of a similar type. “I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Eric Laakmann, the chief executive and co-founder of Vessev, said.
