theintercept.com.title: How AIPAC and AI Spent Their Money This Midterm Election
theintercept.com.text:
It’s a superlative achieved again and again: The current election cycle is the most expensive on record, according to AdImpact, likely to be surpassed only by the next one. North of $16 billion have been raised ahead of Tuesday’s looming elections, with ad spending in House and Senate races topping $4 billion. Mega-donors this election season have overwhelmingly backed Republicans with contributions largely flowing from AI, crypto, and online gambling interests.
The Intercept tracked how super PAC spending is flowing into the midterms and how growing public skepticism of special-interest money in politics is affecting campaign strategies. Hundreds of candidates are still taking donations from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and its super PAC, the United Democracy Project, despite public sentiment turning against the pro-Israel lobby.
“The data overall reveals that [AIPAC is] still spending a ton of money on a lot of races, and more often than not, their candidates are still winning,” Intercept managing editor Maia Hibbett told The Intercept Briefing. “It is still quite meaningful money.”
Artificial intelligence super PACs have also poured tens of millions of dollars into this election cycle, most of it on just a few races in the primaries. The two leading AI super PAC networks, affiliated with OpenAI or Anthropic, dropped a whopping $50.7 million on the primaries, but are noticeably spending much less in the lead-up to the general election, $8.5 million — likely responding to public backlash in the same way that AIPAC has.
“The polls are just so startling on the public’s transformation on AI and data centers over the last year. … The entire life cycle of these AI super PACs, which started about a year ago, has followed that evolution of the public’s opinion,” said Intercept politics reporter Matt Sledge. “One of the things that’s been really interesting in the general election races is … candidates [trying] to paint themselves as the more pro-AI safety, pro-AI regulation candidate.”
This week on the podcast, host Jessica Washington speaks to Hibbett and Sledge about the spending trends in the most expensive election cycle to date and unpack the intended impact.
“No matter which party gets control of either or both houses of Congress, there will be a lot of people elected next week who got there on the backs of Big Tech and special interests,” said Hibbett.
“They’re backing a lot of people in safe seats who don’t really have a tight election,” Sledge added. “The goal may just be to buy themselves a few friends in Congress, because sometimes in Congress, it’s just as good to have a few people who can stop regulation as it is to have people who can shape and actually pass laws.”
For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts.
Transcript
Jessica Washington: Welcome to The Intercept Briefing, I’m Jessica Washington, politics reporter at The Intercept.
On Tuesday, voters will head to the polls to cast their ballots in the most expensive election cycle ever in terms of campaign ad spending, even outpacing past presidential elections. That’s according to AdImpact.
North of $16 billion has been raised this cycle, with ad spending in House and Senate races topping $4 billion. Billionaire Elon Musk has dumped hundreds of millions into races across the country, using his enormous personal wealth to sway the election in favor of Republicans. Musk, who has a home and multiple businesses in Texas, has taken a particular interest in the state’s Senate race between Republican candidate Ken Paxton and Democratic candidate James Talarico.
Most of the money from Musk and other donors has flowed not to candidates, but to powerful super PACs representing a variety of different special interests.
That super PAC spending is the subject of my colleagues, Intercept politics reporter Matt Sledge and senior politics reporter Akela Lacy’s new project, tracking how money is flowing into the midterms.
Maia Hibbett, managing editor for The Intercept, and Matt Sledge join me now to talk about the project and how big money is shaping the midterms.
Matt, Maia, welcome back to The Intercept Briefing
Maia Hibbett: Thanks for having us.
Matt Sledge: Thank you for having us, Jessie.
JW: Maia, I want to start with you. As a part of the super PAC project, The Intercept tracked how millions of dollars flow through the pro-Israel lobby in the United States.
What did the reporting reveal about how the American Israel Public Affairs Committee and affiliated groups like the United Democracy Project mask their influence in U.S. elections in a political landscape where AIPAC’s contributions and endorsements have become largely politically toxic?
MH: The reporting showed that AIPAC and its affiliated super PAC UDP are a little bit weakened, but they’re still pretty dominant.
The narrative out of this midterm cycle, especially during the primaries, was largely focused on a few high-profile races that an AIPAC-backed candidate lost — and that was a huge shock. These big upsets were AIPAC or UDP or a related group that, we can talk about a little bit later, had poured money into, and then the candidate didn’t succeed.
But if you look at it in the aggregate, what the data overall reveals is that they’re still spending a ton of money on a lot of races, and more often than not, their candidates are still winning. It is still quite meaningful money. And even though AIPAC has been discussed as going underground, they are still directly invested in a lot of races.
JW: I want to get into AIPAC’s shifting strategy and their latest announcement on that. But first, Matt, I wanted to talk about your reporting. AI super PACs have poured tens of millions of dollars into this election cycle.
What do we know about the people and companies behind these super PACs? This may seem obvious, but what are they hoping to gain with this level of spending? Are there specific examples of friendly legislation these varied interest groups are hoping their candidates will see through if they win?
MS: To answer your second question, I think it’s really more about setting the tone for future regulation at the federal level. You have two big super PAC networks. One is affiliated with OpenAI, and they broadly favor a laxer regulatory scheme for AI. Then there’s another network that’s affiliated with Anthropic that paints itself as supporting a stricter regulatory scheme.
Skeptics will point out that these networks are both backed by big AI companies. So at the end of the day, they’re probably going to favor regulation that is favorable to the AI companies. I get into this a little bit in my story, but, just in the last few months, there’s also been this constellation of other smaller groups that are sometimes backed by individual employees at these firms or just by people concerned about AI that are pushing for stricter regulatory regimes and aren’t as directly connected to one of the big companies.
JW: Matt, I’m curious about the impact on voters here. CNBC analysis from early October found that mega-donors this election season were overwhelmingly backing Republicans with contributions largely flowing from AI, crypto, and online gambling interests: “Fourteen of the 20 largest donors and donor groups this election cycle have exclusively or nearly exclusively backed GOP candidates or aligned groups.”
Matt, are we seeing voters become more receptive to Republicans as a result of all this ad spending? Is it working on the voter base?
MS: It’s always hard to tease out the impact of an individual super PAC or industry, because you have to keep in mind that a lot of the time, if you’re a crypto super PAC, or an AI super PAC — or more recently, a prediction market super PAC — they are not running pro-crypto or pro-AI ads.
They are running ads that look very similar to everybody else’s. Often, they’re doing negative campaigning that campaigns don’t want to do themselves, and they have such vague names that they’re not associated with crypto or AI. So I do think ads have an impact on the races, but overall what we’re seeing in polls is that it’s not a great environment for Republicans.
So it may have served, just writ large, to potentially soften the blow to Republicans this time around. It does help them to have this many corporate allies, but it may still be overwhelmed by a blue tide.
JW: That makes a lot of sense in terms of just, this is a bad environment for Republicans. They have a president who is unpopular. We have an economy that is not amazing right now. It makes a lot of sense that despite all this ad spending, the baseline of the election is not in favor of Republicans.
Maia, I wanted to get back to something that you had said a little bit earlier about AIPAC and their shifting strategy. AIPAC recently announced that they would no longer officially endorse candidates or give money directly to campaigns.
Were we seeing an early signal of shifting strategies from AIPAC during the 2026 midterm elections? And what does this change actually mean for AIPAC’s influence on our elections?
MH: I’m so glad you asked, because we actually noted early in the 2026 cycle that AIPAC was starting to retreat and change its strategy. Our colleague Akela Lacy wrote a story in December 2025, and the headline was, “AIPAC is Retreating From Endorsements and Election Spending. It Won’t Give Up Its Influence.” I encourage anyone to go back and read that story because it was really prescient about what we would see in the cycle to come, which is that AIPAC used to do all of its spending behind closed doors.
In 2022, it made a big splash when it started doing direct spending in that year’s midterms. The group had helped fund some anti-Bernie Sanders ads during the 2020 presidential campaign, but it was 2022 when it went all in, rather than routing its donations through other groups or through dark-money pathways, it just started giving contributions to candidates.
After it spent so much money in that midterm cycle and in last cycle‘s 2024 races, and as public sentiment started to turn against the pro-Israel lobby’s interests and people became very critical of the U.S. support for genocide in Gaza, AIPAC started to essentially return to its roots.
I think this is really interesting because in the press it has been talked about as a very new strategy. But really, it’s more that AIPAC is returning to the way it used to do business.
JW: Is that as effective as a strategy — the old model that they had? Should we expect that it’ll have just as much influence on elections as they did previously?
MH: It’s a good question. I don’t know how effective it will be as a strategy. There’s a lot more scrutiny on AIPAC now than there was a few years ago, and so it’s much more difficult for them to hide what they’re doing because there are journalists like us who are going to try to follow the money and say, maybe you gave to something that’s called Elect Chicago Women, but it’s actually from UDP, which is the super PAC for AIPAC.
I think in some cases, they can’t get away from the public perception that now exists. But on the other hand, there are many voters who might not really pay attention to the name of the PAC that sponsored the ad that they saw, and then go look it up and see where the money came from. So it remains to be seen how effective it will be.
JW: Not everyone is reading The Intercept before voting, as they should, but it’s fine.
Matt, I wanted to get back to you because there’s a lot happening with these big AI super PACs. You noticed in your reporting that, after spending a lot in the primaries in New York in particular, but in other places as well, the big AI super PACs have gone pretty much quiet in the general election.
Are AI super PACs responding to public backlash in the same way that AIPAC is? What have you observed in terms of why they’ve gone a little bit quieter?
MS: In response to your question about backlash, I think the answer is yes.
They’re on this kind of accelerated timeline going through what AIPAC went through over the course of five years but essentially in five or six months. The polls are just so startling on the public’s transformation on AI and data centers over the last year. It’s just such a rapid change in public opinion, and the entire life cycle of these AI super PACs, which started about a year ago, has followed that evolution of the public’s opinion.
It’s just a dramatic decline in spending from the primaries to the generals — even though they still have money they can tap. Leading the Future, which is the OpenAI-aligned network, they started first, and then the Anthropic-aligned network, Public First, they started a few months later as a response to the Leading the Future network.
So it seems like, from what we’ve been able to tell, Leading the Future scaled back on spending as the general election came about, and Public First responded in turn and also scaled back its operations. That doesn’t mean they’re not spending anything, and we have seen a slight uptick in the final few days of this election when ads are probably just less effective than they would have been a couple weeks ago.
One really notable race is now South Carolina, where Leading the Future is helping prop up Sen. Darline Graham, who hasn’t been a great fundraiser on her own. So there’s actually still a world where AI plays a decisive role in this election in terms of control of the Senate.
If Darline Graham narrowly gets away with winning her race in South Carolina of all places, and that narrowly hands control of the Senate back to the Republicans, then you can still say that Leading the Future and the AI industry played a pretty important role in the general race.
JW: Just to be clear, you’re referring to Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham’s sister, correct?
MS: That’s correct.
JW: Maia, speaking of Big Tech, you also edited a story from Intercept reporter Jonah Valdez looking at how tech leaders, including John Hering, are dumping millions into the LA city attorney race to block Marissa Roy, a DSA-backed candidate, from winning. What is going on here — why such an interest in a race most people are likely not paying any attention to?
MH: City attorneys are one of those jobs that, as you said, a lot of voters don’t pay attention to them. I think a lot of people in cities all over the country maybe couldn’t tell you who the top lawyer of whatever city they live in even is. But this is a job that is largely tasked with enforcing regulations and laws and making companies that might be based in that city or might operate in that city comply with them.
Marissa Roy, this DSA-backed candidate, is currently a deputy attorney general for the state of California, and she’s one of the people who helped the state prosecute this historic Meta settlement where Meta ended up having to pay $17 billion for harms to children using its technology.
We don’t know exactly why John Hering and other tech leaders, like the founders of Ring and Tinder and investors in Anthropic and SpaceX, are spending so heavily in this race, but you might be able to conclude that they’re interested in preventing a person who just helped carry out this huge settlement against Meta from becoming the city attorney of LA.
Some of them are funding a group that’s called Neighbors for John McKinney, which is backing the opponent in the race. John McKinney is the other candidate, and he is much less likely to win, but is propped up now by a lot of spending. They frame him as a tough-on-crime candidate; they say he’s going to restore order to LA, help clean it up is the idea.
Like Matt was saying, often these tech investments in races don’t actually foreground the interests of Big Tech, and they don’t say explicitly, “We want to stop this person from coming into office because we’re worried they’re going to regulate our industry.” Instead, they find a different issue and spend money on that.
It’s also worth noting that John Hering, his group, frames John McKinney as a lifelong Democrat and very anti-MAGA, is the language they use. But John Hering himself is a big ally of Elon Musk. He has been an eager investor in his companies. He said Musk was an “American hero” this year, and he has spent pretty heavily also to support Musk’s America PAC and the Trump campaign after previously spending on the Hillary Clinton presidential campaign.
Like many Silicon Valley types, he’s had an evolution. And although he lives in San Francisco, he also spent in favor of Spencer Pratt for LA mayor.
JW: Wow. Yeah, Big Tech has really come a long way from the ’08 years in terms of their relationship with Democrats and Republicans, and propping up Spencer Pratt.
Matt, I want to bring you in and get your perspective and kind of big picture. What has made this election cycle so popular for Big Tech?
MS: When it comes to AI and crypto and the prediction markets, it’s knowing that the next few years are really going to be critical for them in terms of regulation. These are all fairly young industries, and the rules haven’t been set yet. The Trump administration is doing its best to set them, but Congress has not had a final word on any of those industries.
They see a chance to shape the rules in a way that favors them, and they’re just using the old Washington playbook of spending a bunch of money on campaigns and a bunch of money on lobbyists to try to shape the rules in their favor.
JW: Is this just also a matter of them having more money to play with than they’ve had before? Is this something tech probably would have done years ago if they’d had this access to capital? Or is this really, like you said, just they’re aware that there is existential risks to their industry if they don’t?
MS: Tech for the last few decades has had a lot of money. It’s just been a huge part of the U.S. economy. But I think this move into more regulated spaces is maybe what’s newer.
When Microsoft is creating an internet browser or a word processor, that creates potential antitrust issues, and they have to spend political money in that sense. But they’re not playing in the same kind of highly regulated financial spaces, and nobody ever thought that Clippy posed an existential risk to humanity. So we are moving into new territory when it comes to techs.
JW: I miss Clippy. That is my one comment on that.
I want to get both of you back in here. We’ve been talking about some of the biggest donors in American politics today, and a few special interest groups in particular who’ve obviously been experiencing public backlash — AIPAC, AI, and data centers.
What do you make of this new record-level spending in a midterm election in particular? We’ll obviously have more answers on this next week, but from what you’ve observed so far, is it having the intended impact on voters? Maia, let’s start with you.
MH: I think to use the cop-out that we keep coming back to, we won’t really know if it worked with voters until after the results next week. But it’s clear in this midterm cycle and maybe this is a reminder of kind of a perpetual truth in, when it comes to money in politics, that these big spenders are always going to fund candidates on both sides of the aisle. Often election narratives and questions about special interests will really look to one party or the other and try to map this kind of spending onto partisan issues.
While some of that certainly happens, I think no matter which party gets control of either or both houses of Congress, there will be a lot of people elected next week who got there on the backs of Big Tech and special interests.
That is something that voters are more and more aware of and more and more frustrated by, and we did see a lot of rejection of that kind of big-money spending in the primaries. But ultimately, I don’t know how much that narrative has changed.
JW: Matt, I know you’ve seen some specific examples of this impacting elections. Can you talk about that a little bit?
MS: One of the things that’s been really interesting in the general election races is this race from candidates to paint themselves as the more pro-AI safety, pro-AI regulation candidate.
I’ve done some reporting in Michigan’s 7th [Congressional] District, where a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement is trying to unseat an incumbent Republican, and he has from the start really run on being an anti-data center candidate, campaigning with local activists in small towns of a few thousand people.
His Republican opponent is now also trying to paint himself as a data center skeptic — using different language, more language about local control than about big, bad companies.
But there’s been such a backlash that we’ve seen some changing tactics from the big AI super PACs in the runoff. One has donated money to a nonprofit that’s more focused on building support for data centers. Good luck with that, I guess.
And then another, the Anthropic-aligned network, has essentially handed off money to a pro-Scott Wiener super PAC in California that already existed and already has funding from other tech leaders in the San Francisco area. But that donation has generated this whole fight between Scott Wiener and his opponent, Connie Chan, over who is the more pro-AI regulation candidate now. So it’s a lot of candidates fighting to be the more pro-regulation candidate.
Just thinking back to your question about the effect on voters, I think for the super PACs and for their funders, the impact on candidates may ultimately be more important, on elected officials. They’re backing a lot of people in safe seats who don’t really have a tight election. The goal may just be to buy themselves a few friends in Congress, because sometimes in Congress, it’s just as good to have a few people who can stop regulation as it is to have people who can shape and actually pass laws.
JW: That’s a good point. Speaking of the election, which we know is just days away, what are you two going to be following closely next week? Maia, I want to start with you.
MH: There’s obviously a lot to follow next week, and more races than we can keep track of. One I think that will be very interesting that I was thinking about in terms of AIPAC spending — when Matt just mentioned this thing about AI groups backing candidates who are not in close races — is, of course, the Senate race in Maine.
One of the interesting takeaways we found in this AIPAC project is that in the primaries when AIPAC was spending, as it does in, in various races, one of the top recipients of its money was Susan Collins — who at the time did not have a primary challenger, but it spent heavily to support her primary campaign.
So we’ll obviously watch the Collins–Jackson race in Maine. We have a reporter going there. Matt’s going to go to Michigan. We also have a reporter going to Texas to track some of the big Senate races. Depending on how the results look, I think we’ll pretty quickly be pivoting to accountability for, coverage for the people who are elected, who, maybe entered office vowing not to take corporate PAC money or not to take special-interest money, and to keep an eye on those now Congress members and see if they vote like it or if they continue to have that policy once they’ve been elected.
JW: And Matt, what are you following?
MS: As Maia mentioned, I will be in Michigan. Super interested in that 7th District race that I mentioned between Will Lawrence and Tom Barrett. But then the race everybody’s going to be spinning and talking about for weeks probably: the Mike Rogers/Abdul El-Sayed race. It just is going to carry so much narrative heft going forward about what the voters were trying to say.
Where are you going to be, Jessie? What are you going to be up to?
JW: I will be in D.C., and I’ll be looking at what it means to have yet another election with the National Guard in town and essentially in an occupied city.
I’ll also be looking into what it would mean for the district to have a socialist mayor, Janeese Lewis George, who is almost certain to win on Tuesday, particularly when it comes to ICE and the Metropolitan Police Department’s collaboration with ICE. That’s going to be something I’m really keeping an eye on, not just on Election Day, but going forward to see if she can implement some of these really bold ideas that she’s proposing in a city that’s very constricted in what it can actually do because of federal law.
But that’s enough previewing from me. We’re going to leave it there. Maia, Matt, thank you so much for joining me on The Intercept Briefing.
MH: Thanks again.
MS: Thanks for having us.
JW: And thank you for listening. Next week we’ll be back in your feed early with a special midterm election episode, so stay tuned.
That does it for this episode. We want to hear from you. Tell us what you’re following or want to see more coverage of. Email us at podcasts@theintercept.com or leave us a voice mail at 530-POD-CAST, that’s 530-763-2278.
This episode was produced by Laura Flynn. Jordan Uhl is our social media producer. Ben Muessig is our editor-in-chief. Maia Hibbett is our managing editor. Nara Shin is our copy editor. William Stanton mixed our show. Legal review by David Bralow. Slip Stream provided our theme music.
This show and our reporting at The Intercept do not exist without you. Your donation, no matter the amount, makes a real difference. Keep our investigations free and fearless at theintercept.com/join.
And if you haven’t already, please subscribe to The Intercept Briefing wherever you listen to podcasts. Do leave us a rating or a review, it helps other listeners find our reporting.
Until next time, I’m Jessica Washington.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

lemonde.fr/en.title: French economy shrinks 0.1 percent in third quarter
lemonde.fr/en.text:
The French economy contracted in the third quarter, data showed Friday, October 30, and could be "headed for a wall" if the government is unable to get a deficit-reducing budget passed soon, the finance minister warned.
Gross domestic product shrank by 0.1% in the three months to September, the national statistics office Insee said, amid deepening concerns about the state of public finances and growing political tensions ahead of presidential elections next spring. The decline came as inflation accelerated to 3.4% on an annualized basis in October from 3.1% in September, the fastest rate since January 2024, Insee said.
The French economy had already stagnated in the second quarter after contracting by 0.2% in the first. "For three quarters now, there has been no growth," Finance Minister Roland Lescure told France Info radio. "The conclusion to be drawn from all this is that, as of 2026, the French economy is at a standstill," he said. "France is not heading toward a crisis. But if we fail to achieve the turnaround outlined in the budget, we are headed straight for a wall."
Insee calculated that production of goods and services fell by 0.1% from July to September, while household consumption expanded by 0.4%. Investment contracted by 0.6%, and foreign trade also made a negative contribution to growth, shaving 0.6% age points off GDP growth.
Analysts said the GDP data would indeed make it difficult for the government to reach its overall growth forecast of 0.5% for the current year or even the 0.4% anticipated by Insee and the Bank of France. Worries about France's high debt and deficits have sent its government bond yields soaring in recent weeks.
An underwhelming 2027 budget plan last month fanned concerns that government spending would remain high ahead of next year's presidential elections in which the far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, seen as a fiscal populist, stands a chance of winning, according to opinion polls.
France has been rocked by widespread anger over the rising cost of living and inequality, with nationwide demonstrations on October 17 degenerating into some of the country's worst rioting in years.
The Yellow Vest movement and student unions have called for a new day of protests on Saturday.

lemonde.fr/en.title: On Europe's data center construction sites, workers are exploited amid climate of 'terror'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Sandu checked his watch. It was March, and the 34-year-old Romanian electrical tester (names have been changed to protect their anonymity) was finishing a nearly 10-hour workday. He was working on the GBL-6 site in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium – the sixth data center built by Google on its vast European campus. That day, his supervisor asked him to perform two final checks before leaving. "I had no choice," he recalled – colleagues of his had been dismissed for refusing this type of request. Employed on a weekly contract, he agreed.
Sandu had already performed this type of "busbar test" – used to check the integrity of electrical wiring – several times before. Supervisors assured him that the power lines were de-energized. That was not the case for the second test, however. As he handled insulated pliers to connect the cables, a 400-volt, 12,000-ampere electrical arc struck him in the face and on the right side of his body.
"I became completely blind," he said. A witness said that the managers fled the scene while Sandu screamed in pain, lying on the ground. He was taken to the hospital, where doctors placed him in a medically induced coma for five days. According to his medical records, 12% of his body was burned, including his face, neck, shoulder and fingers. He underwent several skin grafts and still suffers from pain, anxiety disorders and other after-effects.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Israel's ceremonial president Isaac Herzog becomes arbiter of a Knesset without a majority
lemonde.fr/en.text:
During his lengthy inauguration speech as head of state on July 7, 2021, Isaac Herzog, freshly elected by the Knesset for a seven-year term, quoted Lebanese poet Gibran Khalil Gibran: "The reality of the other person is not in what he reveals to you, but in what he cannot reveal to you. Therefore, if you would understand him, listen not to what he says, but rather to what he does not say." Five years later, all of Israel is wondering what Herzog is secretly thinking, what he will do behind the scenes, and what he will say publicly as head of state to help the country escape the political deadlock it has been mired in since the election on Tuesday, October 27.
A politician from the left, Herzog typically fills a ceremonial role. His weeks are marked by receiving ambassadors, traveling abroad and giving speeches that the media rarely cover. However, the law grants him a leading role, with genuine freedom of action, when it comes to proposing the name of a prime minister tasked with forming a government after parliamentary elections.
From the official announcement of the results, he has seven days to gather the views of all the party leaders in the Knesset before making his decision. "In cases in which the election results are conclusive, the president enjoys limited discretion. In contrast, when the results are inconclusive, or when there are normative problems related to a candidate, the president’s discretion may be broader," political scientists Dana Blander and Ofer Kenig wrote in the reference book on the presidency published by the Israel Democracy Institute (The Presidency in Israel, 2024).

lemonde.fr/en.title: 11 EU countries vow to release 42.6 million barrels of oil after G7 pledge
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Eleven European countries pledged Thursday, October 29, to jointly release 42.6 million barrels of oil by the end of January, in line with a G7 deal struck this month to ease global energy supply concerns.
"EU member states have reaffirmed their commitment to an accelerated release of 42.6 million barrels from strategic reserves over the next months, and around half of this will be diesel," the EU's energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen told reporters.
Eleven countries, including France, Germany and Italy, said in a statement they would release the oil from their strategic reserves by the end of January 2027, including 20.5 million barrels of diesel.
The announcement comes weeks after the G7 economies said they would release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil after US President Donald Trump threatened a diesel export ban.
The other European countries involved are Belgium, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden. Lithuania also endorsed the initiative, though it did not sign the joint pledge.
The International Energy Agency – to which all the EU nations belong – made a call in mid-October for its members to step up the release of oil stocks ahead of winter.
Trump ramped up the pressure on Europe to release reserves after the US-Israeli war with Iran sent energy prices skyrocketing, coming back to bite him at home with high fuel costs that have become a key issue ahead of congressional elections next week.
The EU said it was taking the impact of the crisis on households seriously but was not worried about supply. "We do not expect the security of supply issue as such. But for the citizens that are struggling to pay the bills, that might not matter," Jorgensen said.

lemonde.fr/en.title: In Morocco, the 'Donald J. Trump Highway' showcases Rabat's ambitions in Western Sahara
lemonde.fr/en.text:
On the Donald J. Trump Highway – the road that leads to Western Sahara, between Tiznit and Dakhla – truck drivers often make their first stop at kilometer 18. Rest areas become scarcer after that, once the asphalt plunges into the desert expanses. In the small douar (rural village) of Bounaamane, nestled among argan trees, a brand-new gas station opened less than two years ago, complete with a convenience store, grill restaurant, butcher shop, café with a terrace and car wash.
On this late October morning, Mohammed, who did not want to give his last name, said he was won over. "Happy, even," he smiled, bundled up in a purple sweater as the sun was still slow to warm the arid lands of southern Morocco. The road, he said, "is a thousand times better than before." For him, journeys have become much less exhausting since the old National Route 1 – "narrow, often covered with sand and worn down by heavy trucks" – was turned into a two-lane road in each direction, with speed limits on some stretches reaching 100 kilometers per hour.
The opening of the new expressway, completed at the end of 2024, reportedly even prompted businesses to use the route again to reach southern Morocco and Western Sahara. Rabat calls this territory its "Southern Provinces," but this is disputed by pro-independence members of the Polisario Front, who are supported by Algeria and classified by the United Nations as a "non-self-governing territory."
"It's undeniable, we save between five and six hours of travel time," said Amer Zghinou, president of the Moroccan Association of Intercontinental Road Transport, reached by phone. "Our savings on fuel are considerable, on the order of 300 to 400 liters of diesel per trip," in other words, almost a full tank – depending on the trucks. "It's quite an achievement," the group leader continued, "which is also helping open up the South."

lemonde.fr/en.title: TotalEnergies posts record profits, fueled by global diesel market turmoil
lemonde.fr/en.text:
In early October, TotalEnergies' CEO Patrick Pouyanné welcomed the "opportunities" created by the upheavals shaking global energy markets. "I prefer the world of disruption to the peaceful world," he said candidly at a major energy conference in London.
There is no doubt that the war in the Middle East is benefiting the French energy giant more than ever. Eight months after the outbreak of the conflict, which has sent hydrocarbon prices and fuel costs soaring, TotalEnergies once again announced massive profits on Thursday, October 29. In the third quarter, its net profit reached $8.3 billion (about €7.45 billion), up 124% from the previous year. This performance added to an already strong first half, during which the company posted a net profit of $11.2 billion (a 72% increase year-on-year).
Since the war began, the oil and gas group has ridden the wave of surging global oil prices. However, it was above all the worldwide strain on refined products – especially diesel – that boosted its profits in recent months, thanks to the dramatic rise in refining margins, the difference between crude oil costs and the value of fuels produced. Its refining and chemicals division reported a record $3.6 billion in earnings – double the previous quarter and five times higher than a year ago.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Christine Lagarde announces departure from ECB, wants 'freedom to engage' on matters other than monetary policy
lemonde.fr/en.text:
A decision to hold interest rates steady at 2.5% and the resignation of its president, Christine Lagarde – who announced that she would leave her post on February 7, 2027, nine months before the end of her term – marked a much-anticipated meeting by the European Central Bank (ECB), on Thursday, October 29. Rather than moving markets, the meeting largely reignited speculation over who would succeed Lagarde at its helm.
As for rates, despite inflation in the eurozone rebounding to 3.8% in September – nearly double the 2% target set by the ECB – the institution's Governing Council decided not to act immediately. Among the reasons cited to support this stance, Lagarde explained that the "second-round effects" of inflation, particularly pressure for wage increases, were, for now, no greater than those already anticipated by the ECB.
Other arguments for this "measured" approach included the fact that inflation excluding energy was "broadly stable," while the climate of uncertainty "is building and increasing." Although the decision was unanimous, it nevertheless sparked debate within the Governing Council, Lagarde acknowledged during her press conference. But the status quo prevailed. The ECB would thus continue to decide on a "meeting-by-meeting" and "data-dependent basis," as is the usual phrasing in Frankfurt, postponing any potential rate hike to December 17, the date of the next Governing Council meeting.

lemonde.fr/en.title: In Lille, a citizens' convention rethinks democracy
lemonde.fr/en.text:
On the weekend of October 10 and 11, a group of randomly selected French citizens gathered in Lille for the second session of the Citizens' Convention for Democracy. The exercise aimed to reclaim a voice in politics, a world away from the tensions fueled by some elected officials and social media. It was also far removed from the violence that, in the following days, would mark the social movement led by French high school students since the end of September.
There were 50 participants from all across France: retirees, job seekers, nursing assistants, entrepreneurs, students. Each had received an unexpected phone call over the summer. This included Anna, an accounting student. "You have been randomly selected to take part in a citizens' convention to improve how democracy works," the person on the line said. "Would you agree to come to Lille one weekend a month between September and December?" At first she declined. Anna felt like she "had nothing to say," she explained. "But then the woman on the phone told me she was specifically looking for people who weren't politically involved." She let herself be persuaded.
On the morning of October 10, at Sciences Po Lille, where the convention was being held, the 22-year-old from Poitiers was still somewhat uncomfortable with everyone addressing one another by their first names, but by that point she felt more comfortable speaking up than she had during the first session. "At each table, a facilitator asks for our opinions and makes sure the more talkative people give others a chance to speak," she said. Among the resolutions to be presented to presidential candidates at the end of the year, one in particular stood out: the inclusion of blank votes and abstentions in vote counts (currently, these votes are possible, but are not reflected in percentages). "Being visible is being heard," she said.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Spain train collision death toll rises to 69
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Spain began demanding answers on Thursday, October 29, after its second high-speed train collision this year killed 69 people and injured scores, with distraught relatives desperately seeking news about their loved ones. One of Europe's deadliest rail disasters this century struck south of Madrid on Wednesday morning when a service by state operator Renfe plowed into the back of a stationary train belonging to private Spanish company Iryo.
Toledo has received 52 of the corpses, overwhelming its morgue's capacity of 30 and forcing the army to set up an improvised facility. Sniffer dogs and thermal drones were searching for bodies at the crash site outside the central village of Urda, around 130 kilometers (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The toll rose from 68 to 69 on Thursday, according to regional authorities. Among the victims was Fatima Banez, a former labor minister for the main conservative Popular Party (PP).
Flags flew at half-mast on public buildings with official ceremonies and public events canceled or scaled back on the first of three days of national mourning. A minute of silence was observed up and down the country, including at Spain's busiest train station, Atocha in Madrid, where some mourners shed tears.
Wednesday's accident happened on a key line linking Madrid to the southern city of Seville, which was also the scene of a collision in January that killed 46 people. It has raised fresh questions about safety on Spain's high-speed rail network, the second-largest in the world after China's.
During a visit to the disaster site, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faces a general election on November 29, pledged "to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again."
King Felipe VI also intervened in the debate after visiting the injured in Toledo, calling for measures "to ensure this does not happen again."
'Searching for culprits'
Transport Minister Oscar Puente said on Wednesday that an automatic control system went down on 69 kilometers of track, causing all trains there to be stopped. But the control center decided to "resume traffic in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable," Puente said, with the Renfe train traveling 25 kilometers before striking the Iryo. The control center "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it," he added.
Sanchez's main rival, PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, accused Puente of "frivolity" by trying to pin the blame on one control center operator. "Political responsibilities cannot wait for an investigation," Feijoo said.
The head of train driver union Semaf, Diego Martin, said "attention is wrongly being focused on searching for culprits" when workers were using "degraded systems."
Renfe train drivers on Thursday maintained a strike that Semaf had called before the accident "to defend rail safety," saying previous commitments on the issue had been broken. Renfe reported "a major impact" on its minimum service requirements as 26.6 percent of the staff concerned joined the industrial action. The Madrid region's sprawling commuter network suffered the most disruption, with 81 percent of its planned services canceled.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'Star Trek' and 'X-Men' star, Patrick Stewart, dies
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Patrick Stewart, the British Shakespearean actor who became a Hollywood megastar through roles in the Star Trek and X-Men franchises, has died at the age of 86, an official statement said Thursday, October 29.
"We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," the statement said.
The actor, who hailed from the northern English region of Yorkshire, trod the boards in Britain with the Royal Shakespeare Company before crossing the Atlantic to enjoy an acclaimed career on the US stage and screen. His best known Hollywood roles were as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in multiple X-Men and related Marvel films.
"His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre," the statement said. "He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction's most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise."
A slew of tributes
The death of Patrick Stewart led to a slew of tributes, including from acting colleagues.
Longtime co-star Hugh Jackman, who played Wolverine, remembered him as both "one of the greats of stage and screen" and "a tremendous friend and man."
"Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did," William Shatner, Stewart's fellow "Star Trek" alum, said in a statement.
George Takei also honored his longtime Star Trek colleague. "Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend," the actor wrote on social media. "He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain."

lemonde.fr/en.title: Trappes shooting suspect, charged with premeditated and attempted terrorist murder, admits to targeting people 'of Muslim or African appearance'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Kevin T., the suspect in the racist attack that left one dead and four seriously injured on Friday, October 23, in a town west of Paris, was charged on Thursday, October 29, for "premeditated murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise," with the aggravating circumstance that the acts were committed due to "the real or perceived belonging to a supposed race, ethnicity, nation or religion," according to the National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office (PNAT).
At a press briefing late Thursday morning, Olivier Christen, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor, revealed several details confirming the racist motive behind the attack and the ideological beliefs of the alleged perpetrator. During police custody, Kevin T. admitted to "specifically targeting" people "of Muslim appearance," "African" or "North African," according to his statements cited by the prosecutor. He said he chose the city of Trappes because, in his words, it was a "haven for Islamists," and denied any terrorist intent, describing his actions as legitimate.
A search was conducted of his home, which he had booby-trapped with two timers connected to electrical outlets. As Le Monde reported on Saturday, this search uncovered a copy of Mein Kampf, as well as a Quran and a Bible. Investigators also found in his apartment 30 stickers reading "Long live France, RN, proud to be French," in reference to the far-right Rassemblement National party; 99 stickers with "100% French/Long live France"; and 98 with the text "Support for law enforcement," according to the prosecutor.

lemonde.fr/en.title: French minister warns of 'very high' violence risk at Halloween protests
lemonde.fr/en.text:
France's interior minister on Thursday, October 29, warned of a "very high risk of public disorder" and announced the deployment of around 70,000 police officers for a new wave of protests this weekend. France has been rocked by widespread anger over the rising cost of living and inequality, with nationwide demonstrations on October 17 degenerating into some of the country's worst rioting in years.
The Yellow Vest movement and student unions have called for a new day of protests on Saturday. The demonstrations come in an increasingly tense political climate, with presidential elections six months away and far-right leader Marine Le Pen leading opinion polls.
"The day of October 31 presents a very high risk of public disorder," Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told reporters. Around 70,000 police officers and gendarmes will be deployed across France, matching the number mobilized a week ago, he said. The security measures introduced last week to protect shops will be strengthened, Nuñez added.
Demonstrations will be allowed, but "not in city centers, where there is a risk of public disorder," he said. "We will tolerate no excesses," he added, pledging an "extremely firm" response.
Nuñez also said that authorities had detected social media calls for Halloween gatherings on Saturday evening calling for a "revolution." He said those appeals were being circulated by radical left groups and some radicalized Yellow Vest activists.
"These gatherings will be banned," he said.
'Dialogue of the deaf'
Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes, large-scale looting and vandalism of public property that erupted on October 17. Although last weekend's rallies were largely peaceful, incidents of street violence still occurred.
The police response has been criticized as heavy-handed and sparked a broader movement against the cost of living and police violence. Several teenage protesters have been seriously injured.
On Thursday, representatives of youth organizations met Nuñez but emerged disappointed.
"We went to this meeting to discuss our demands, but above all the last four weeks of mobilization, which have been marked by unprecedented police violence," said Manon Moret, secretary general of the student union Unef. "This meeting was a dialogue of the deaf."
Some of the attendees accused Nuñez of refusing to acknowledge violence committed against protesters. Louis Letoublon, deputy head of the association Les Lyceens!, denounced "an irresponsible minister, incapable of answering for police repression."

lemonde.fr/en.title: Behind Trump's shift towards Russia, the lucrative business promises of Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's dealmaker
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Kyrylo Budanov struggled to contain his anger. For nearly three hours on October 9, the head of the Ukrainian presidential administration felt treated like a child by Steve Witkoff, Donald Trump's special envoy, who claimed he could teach him how to make money. The meeting at the luxurious Shell Bay golf club in Hallandale Beach, Florida, was nothing like the countless sessions in recent months aimed at building a peace plan between Ukraine and Russia.
"Steve," alongside Jared Kushner, the American president's son-in-law, preferred to talk business that day. The real estate developer dangled the prospect of a grand "regional prosperity plan" for the postwar period, one that would include Ukraine, Europe and Russia. The plan notably involved fully restoring the pipelines that transported Russian gas and oil to Europe via Ukraine. Kyiv would receive dividends, and the project would lower the cost of energy in Europe, Witkoff boasted, convinced he was holding in his hands one of those win-win deals that cannot be refused.
"Our model is not Belarus, but Poland!" the Ukrainian retorted, stunned by a plan that, according to a witness interviewed by Le Monde, would have made Kyiv beholden to Moscow. The meeting was interrupted. Budanov called Volodymyr Zelensky, concerned. The Ukrainian president told him not to let his emotions show. The meeting resumed when, suddenly, someone brought in a note announcing the "deal" that Trump had just made public. The American president pledged to buy nearly five million metric tons of Russian diesel. He was jubilant at the prospect of lowering oil prices to win over voters ahead of the midterm elections on November 3, which the Republican camp is approaching with difficulty.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'They knew the Madrid-Seville line wasn't safe': Spanish press reports first revelations about causes of train crash
lemonde.fr/en.text:
On Thursday, October 29, Spanish newspapers only had room for one story: the rail disaster in Urda (Toledo), that left 69 dead. "A triple safety failure causes another rail massacre," wrote El Mundo in its headline. Daily El País used similar language: "Second disaster on the high-speed network in less than a year." Barcelona-based La Vanguardia, for its part, decried "another unbearable tragedy." Television channels sent crews to the scene, where cranes were working through the night to clear the wrecked carriages, in particular those belonging to the private company Iryo, which was struck by Renfe's AVE train.
"Why did the trains collide?" asked El País, as early revelations about the accident's circumstances multiplied. The online daily elDiario.es reported on the communications between the train drivers and Spanish train infrastructure monitoring body Adif's railway control center at the Atocha station in Madrid. The center had taken over traffic management after a failure of the LZB safety system, which continuously monitors train speed and triggers automatic stops in the event of an anomaly.

welt.de.title: „Man hat uns getötet“ – Kremlkritische Zeitung „Nowaja Gaseta“ stellt Betrieb ein
welt.de.text: Die von Friedensnobelpreisträger Dmitri Muratow gegründete russische Zeitung  „Nowaja Gaseta“ (verlinkt auf https://novayagazeta.eu/)  stellt nach mehr als 30 Jahren und massivem Druck in Russland ihre Arbeit ein. „Man hat uns getötet“, lautet der Titel  einer Erklärung auf der Website der Zeitung.  (verlinkt auf https://novayagazeta.ru/articles/2026/10/30/nas-ubili) „Die russischen Behörden und die russischen Geheimdienste zwangen die Redaktion, die Arbeit einzustellen“, schrieb das Medium darin. Am 9. November mache die Redaktion das Licht aus, fahre die Server herunter und gehe. Die Zeitung gebe es dann nicht mehr. Chefredakteur Sergej Sokolow verbreitete die Botschaft auch in einer Videobotschaft auf der Onlineplattform YouTube „Die ‚Nowaja Gaseta‘ hört auf zu existieren“, sagte er dort. „Die russischen Behörden, die russischen Geheimdienste haben die Redaktion dazu gezwungen, ihre Arbeit einzustellen.“ Die „Nowaja Gaseta“ gehört zu den kritischsten Stimmen in Russland und stand stets unter Druck. Anfang des Monats jährte sich etwa der Mord an ihrer Reporterin Anna Politkowskaja zum 20. Mal. Russische Behörden gingen auch nach Beginn des russischen Angriffskriegs gegen die Ukraine vor mehr als viereinhalb Jahren gegen die „Nowaja Gaseta“ vor. Medium als „ausländischer Agent“ eingestuft Am Vorabend war bekannt geworden, dass die Redaktion ihre Räume in Moskau verlassen muss. Im April waren die Redaktionsräume stundenlang durchsucht worden, im September wurde das Medium als sogenannter ausländischer Agent eingestuft. Auch zuvor war schon ihr 2021 mit dem Friedensnobelpreis geehrter Gründer Dmitri Muratow als „Auslandsagent“ eingestuft worden. Damit brandmarkt Moskau Kritiker. Wer als „Auslandsagent“ gelistet ist, muss mit zahlreichen Nachteilen rechnen. Unter anderem sind ihnen Mieteinnahmen oder Depotzinsen bei einem Sparkonto ebenso verwehrt wie Tantiemen oder sonstige Einkünfte aus intellektueller Tätigkeit. „Mehr als 30 Lebensjahre zusammen mit dem Land und seinen Bürgern werden für uns auf der Straße enden, ohne Existenzgrundlage, unter ständiger Bedrohung durch Repressionen“, schrieb die Zeitung nun.

welt.de.title: Militärchef berät Trump zu Optionen im Iran-Krieg – US-Senator nennt Pläne „wahnsinnig“
welt.de.text: US-Präsident Donald Trump hat sich Medienberichten zufolge bei einem seltenen persönlichen Treffen mit einem ranghohen Militärchef zum weiteren Vorgehen im  Iran-Krieg (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/themen/israel-iran-konflikt/)  beraten lassen. Das „ Wall Street Journal (verlinkt auf https://www.wsj.com/politics/national-security/top-admiral-briefs-trump-on-iran-attack-options-5bd6f13c?mod=hp_lead_pos2) “ schreibt unter Berufung auf US-Beamte, der Chef des US-Regionalkommandos für den Nahen Osten (Centcom), Admiral Brad Cooper, habe Trump am Donnerstag im Weißen Haus unter anderem militärische Optionen im Iran dargelegt. Die US-Zeitung wertete das als mögliches Zeichen dafür, dass ein bedeutender Einsatz der US-Streitkräfte bevorstehen könnte. Das Nachrichtenportal „ Axios (verlinkt auf https://www.axios.com/2026/10/29/brad-cooper-briefs-trump-iran-naval-blockade) “ berichtet, ebenfalls gestützt auf US-Beamte, Coopers Briefing für den Präsidenten habe sich auf die US-Seeblockade gegen iranische Häfen und Küstengebiete fokussiert. Trump wollte demnach vom Centcom-Chef persönlich erfahren, ob die Blockade funktioniere. Cooper habe Trump auch mit Blick auf den Einsatz in der Straße von Hormus auf den neuesten Stand gebracht. Die US-Marine begleitet seit Monaten zivile Schiffe durch die Meerenge, um den Handel mit Öl und Flüssiggas wieder zu ermöglichen. Laut dem Bericht ging es bei dem Gespräch auch um die wirtschaftliche Druckkampagne der USA gegen den Iran. Beide US-Medien berichten übereinstimmend, dass auch Generalstabschef Dan Caine, Verteidigungsminister Pete Hegseth und weitere Kabinettsmitglieder an dem Treffen teilnahmen. US-Senator nennt Kriegsplan „wahnsinnig“ US-Senator Chris Murphy (Demokraten) kritisierte mögliche Pläne für neue Angriffe auf den Iran scharf. „Einige von uns sind über den Kriegsplan informiert worden. Und obwohl ich keine Einzelheiten offenlegen kann, kann ich Folgendes sagen: Der Plan ist wahnsinnig“, schrieb er auf X. Der Plan werde seine Ziele nicht erreichen und „eine neue Eskalationsspirale auslösen“, erklärte der Senator. Einzelheiten zu den möglichen Angriffen oder zur Unterrichtung der Senatoren nannte er nicht. Neue Angriffe oder diplomatischer Durchbruch? Seit Längerem wird über mögliche neue Angriffe der USA und Israels gegen den Iran nach den US-Parlamentswahlen spekuliert, die kommenden Dienstag stattfinden. US-Medien berichteten jüngst allerdings auch, dass Trumps Regierung und regionale Vermittler neue Anstrengungen für eine diplomatische Lösung des Konflikts mit dem Iran unternommen hätten, in die US-Vizepräsident J.D. Vance federführend involviert sei. Die Situation in der Straße von Hormus gilt seit Längerem als einer der zentralen Streitpunkte zwischen Washington und Teheran. Iranische Streitkräfte intensivierten in den vergangenen Wochen ihre Angriffe auf Schiffe in der für den weltweiten Ölhandel zentralen Meerenge. Teheran will Trump vor den Kongresswahlen mit steigenden Energiepreisen unter Druck setzen, die bei seinen Wählern nicht gut ankommen. Der von ihm selbst begonnene Iran-Krieg und die in der Folge gestiegenen Spritpreise sind ein Thema, das Trump im aktuellen Wahlkampf für seine republikanischen Parteikollegen erheblich belastet.

„Das Ganze fällt jetzt auch in den spanischen Wahlkampf“
Stand: 07:35 UhrDauer: 3 Minuten
Nach dem Zugunglück in der spanischen Provinz Toledo, bei dem dutzende Menschen starben, gehen die Bergungsarbeiten weiter. WELT-Reporterin Greta Wagner berichtet.

welt.de.title: „Wir sind bereit“, droht Putin – und warnt vor Eskalation in der Ostsee
welt.de.text: Russlands Präsident Wladimir Putin sieht sein Land für einen Krieg mit Europa gerüstet. „Wir sind bereit, aber wir wollen keinen Krieg mit Europa“, sagte er nach dem Russland-Afrika-Gipfel in Moskau laut der staatlichen Nachrichtenagentur Tass. Sollte es zu einem solchen Krieg kommen, werde es „keine Gewinner“ geben. „Das sollte niemand vergessen.“ Putin behauptete, der Westen habe sein Ziel einer strategischen Niederlage Russlands nicht erreicht. Zugleich erklärte er, Moskau unterstütze Schritte zur Wiederherstellung umfassender Beziehungen zu europäischen Ländern – sowohl mit der EU als auch auf bilateraler Ebene. Positiv äußerte sich Putin über  das jüngste Telefonat mit Finnlands Präsident Alexander Stubb und Norwegens Ministerpräsident Jonas Gahr Støre (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article6ae078eb41a652332eb6d587/ukraine-krieg-putin-telefoniert-mit-finnlands-praesidenten-und-norwegens-regierungschef.html) . Die beiden hätten das Gespräch initiiert. Er wisse, dass sie dafür anschließend  kritisiert (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article6ae191a9f74d161423be0f92/ukraine-krieg-anruf-bei-putin-sorgt-in-europa-fuer-irritationen-frederiksen-kritisiert-alleingang.html)  worden seien, halte ihren Vorstoß aber für richtig. In Europa gebe es Menschen, die einen konstruktiven Dialog suchten, statt Russland eine strategische Niederlage zufügen zu wollen, sagte Putin. Nach seiner Darstellung hatten die beiden Gesprächspartner zu Beginn ausdrücklich betont, in nationaler Funktion und nicht im Namen der EU zu sprechen. Norwegen ist kein EU-Mitglied. Warnung vor Eskalation in der Ostsee Ein Thema des Telefonats war Putin zufolge auch die Sicherheit der Schifffahrt in der Ostsee. Er zog dabei einen Vergleich zur Lage im Persischen Golf und in der Straße von Hormus. „Will irgendjemand, dass sich in der Ostsee dieselbe Situation entwickelt?“, fragte er. Russland wolle dies nicht. Zugleich verband Putin seine Aussage mit einer Warnung: Moskau wolle keine Spannungen in der Ostsee schaffen, werde aber „auf jede Herausforderung reagieren“.

welt.de.text:
Israel steht nach der Parlamentswahl vor einer schwierigen Regierungsbildung. Keines der beiden Lager erreichte eine Mehrheit, wie die Zentrale Wahlkommission des Landes nach der Auszählung aller Stimmen am Freitag mitteilte.

welt.de.title: Endergebnis in Israel steht fest – Rekordwert für arabische Parteien
welt.de.text: Israel steht nach der Parlamentswahl vor einer schwierigen Regierungsbildung. Keines der beiden Lager erreichte eine Mehrheit, wie die Zentrale Wahlkommission des Landes nach der Auszählung aller Stimmen am Freitag mitteilte. Zum Königsmacher könnten nun die israelisch-arabischen Parteien werden, die bei der Wahl vom Dienstag ein Rekordergebnis einfuhren. Das Wahlergebnis lässt zähe Koalitionsverhandlungen erwarten. Bei einem Scheitern drohen Neuwahlen. Unterdessen verschärfte sich der Streit zwischen den gegnerischen Lagern. Der Block von Ministerpräsident Benjamin Netanjahu errang nach Auszählung aller Stimmen 53 Sitze. Das Oppositionsbündnis des Mitte-Rechts-Kandidaten Gadi Eisenkot kam auf 48 Sitze. Für eine Mehrheit im israelischen Einkammerparlament mit seinen insgesamt 120 Abgeordneten sind 61 Sitze nötig. Zum Königsmacher könnten nun die israelisch-arabischen Parteien werden: Sie sicherten sich zusammen 19 Sitze – so viele wie noch nie. Die beiden überwiegend arabischen Listen Ra’am und Vereinte Liste schnitten damit deutlich besser ab als erwartet und könnten zum Königsmacher werden. Die Ergebnisse im Überblick: • Netanjahu-Lager: 53 Sitze • Oppositionslager: 48 Sitze • Vereinte Liste Liste: 11 Sitze • Ra’am: 8 Sitze Für eine Mehrheit im israelischen Einkammerparlament mit seinen insgesamt 120 Abgeordneten sind 61 Sitze nötig. Als Nächstes ist Präsident Isaac Herzog am Zug: Die endgültigen Ergebnisse werden ihm laut Zentraler Wahlkommission am Mittwoch offiziell vorgelegt. Anschließend wird er Gespräche mit den jeweiligen Parteichefs aufnehmen, bevor er einen von ihnen mit der Regierungsbildung beauftragt. Streit zwischen politischen Lagern verschärft sich Das muss nicht unbedingt derjenige sein, dessen Partei an der Spitze liegt, sondern jener mit der besten Aussicht, mindestens 61 Abgeordnete hinter sich zu vereinen. Regieren wird, wem es gelingt, eine mehr oder weniger breite und stabile Koalition zu schmieden. Angesichts der unklaren Mehrheitsverhältnisse könnten sich die Koalitionsverhandlungen allerdings über Wochen hinziehen. Unterdessen verschärfte sich der Streit zwischen den politischen Lagern. Vor dem Hintergrund der historischen Zugewinne israelisch-arabischer Parteien hatte Netanjahus Koalition aus rechtskonservativen und rechtsextremen Parteien bereits am Tag nach dem Urnengang vom Dienstag schwere Anschuldigungen erhoben und dringt nun auf Ermittlungen gegen diese Listen wegen angeblicher Finanzierung aus dem Ausland. „Die Wahlen in Israel wurden gestohlen“, erklärte die Likud-Partei am Donnerstag. Es gehe um einen „Anschlag auf die Demokratie“ mit dem Ziel, Israel zu „islamisieren und die rechte Regierung zu stürzen“. Sie sprach von einem „Raamgate“-Skandal als einem „politischen Erdbeben“. Der rechtsextreme Sicherheitsminister Itamar Ben-Gvir forderte die Festnahme der Chefs der israelisch-arabischen Parteien. Im Mittelpunkt des Streits standen Vorwürfe, wonach Ra’am Gelder aus Katar erhalten haben soll, um damit Stimmenkäufe zu finanzieren. Die Wahlkommission hatte den Geheimdienst mit Blick auf die Vorwürfe am Mittwochabend zu Untersuchungen aufgefordert. Bislang wurden öffentlich keine Belege für die Anschuldigungen vorgelegt. Ra’am-Chef Mansur Abbas wies die Vorwürfe zurück. Auch das Golfemirat Katar nannte sie „lächerlich und gefährlich“. Vorwurf der „widerlichen Kampagne“ Netanjahu sieht sich selbst mit Vertuschungsvorwürfen im Zuge der sogenannten Katargate-Affäre konfrontiert. In deren Zentrum steht die mutmaßliche Bestechung israelischer Beamter aus Katar. Dabei geht es um den Verdacht des Inlandsgeheimdiensts Schin Bet, dass mehrere Vertraute Netanjahus Bestechungsgelder aus dem Golfemirat erhalten haben sollen, um ein positives Image in Israel zu befördern. Oppositionsführer Eisenkot warf Netanjahu im Zuge der Likud-Anschuldigungen gegen die israelisch-arabischen Parteien vor, das Ergebnis der Parlamentswahl infrage stellen zu wollen. „Es ist bereits klar, dass Likud und Netanjahu eine koordinierte, organisierte Kampagne gestartet haben, die darauf abzielt, die Ergebnisse der Wahl zu delegitimieren“, sagte Eisenkot am Donnerstag in einer Videobotschaft. Eisenkots Verbündeter Jair Golan von den linksgerichteten Demokraten warf Netanjahus Block eine „widerliche Kampagne“ vor, die darauf abziele, „den Willen der Bevölkerung, insbesondere der arabischen Bevölkerung, zu delegitimieren“. Der Schin Bet bestätigte, dass die Untersuchung laufe, betonte aber, es gehe nicht darum, „eine ganze Gemeinschaft zu beschuldigen, die auf demokratische und legale Weise gewählt hat“. Auch die Wahlkommission versuchte, die Spannungen zu entschärfen: Ihr amtierender Generaldirektor Dean Livne nannte die Behauptungen, es habe weitreichende Probleme gegeben, „völlig grundlos“. Die Wahl am Dienstag galt als Richtungsentscheidung über die künftige Ausrichtung des Landes sowie über die Zukunft Netanjahus, der mit Unterbrechungen bislang mehr als 19 Jahre lang Regierungschef war. Die Wahlbeteiligung war mit 77,7 Prozent die höchste seit Jahrzehnten. Netanjahu steht unter anderem wegen der Versäumnisse der Sicherheitskräfte beim Hamas-Angriff vom 7. Oktober 2023 massiv in der Kritik.

welt.de.title: Oppositionsführerin Machado bedankt sich bei Trump für dessen „Weitsicht, Mut und Handeln“
welt.de.text: Die venezolanische Oppositionspolitikerin und Friedensnobelpreisträgerin  María Corina Machado  (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article6ade2faf51fb647ba7e7cab7/nach-exil-oppositionsfuehrerin-machado-offenbar-zurueck-in-venezuela.html) hat US-Präsident Donald Trump für den US-Militäreinsatz zum Sturz des damaligen Staatschefs Nicolás Maduro gedankt. „Dank Ihrer Weitsicht, Ihres Mutes und Ihres Handelns am 3. Januar ist das Tor zur Freiheit aufgestoßen worden“, sagte Machado am Donnerstag auf ihrer ersten Pressekonferenz nach ihrer Rückkehr nach Venezuela vor wenigen Tagen. Auf Trumps Geheiß hatten US-Soldaten Maduro und dessen Ehefrau Anfang Januar dieses Jahres in Caracas gefangengenommen und sie in die USA gebracht, wo ihnen der Prozess gemacht werden soll. Für die riskante Aktion hatte Machado den US-Präsidenten bereits in der Vergangenheit mehrfach überschwänglich gelobt; aus Dankbarkeit überreichte sie ihm sogar ihre Nobelmedaille. Bei der Pressekonferenz dankte Machado auch US-Außenminister Marco Rubio. Zu ihrer Rückkehr nach Venezuela sagte die Oppositionspolitikerin, sie wolle „die Gesellschaft mobilisieren“. Mit Verweis auf Rubio erklärte sie, dieser habe einen Prozess angekündigt, der zu einer Demokratisierung und einer Präsidentschaftswahl im Jahr 2027 führen solle. „Der Tag der Wahl ist der Tag der Befreiung“, fügte sie hinzu. Bei der Präsidentschaftswahl im Juli 2024 hatten die venezolanischen Behörden Machado eine Kandidatur untersagt. Damals wurde der langjährige Staatschef Maduro zum Sieger erklärt, dessen Behörden massiv gegen die Regierungsgegner vorgingen. Machado tauchte daraufhin unter. Zu r Verleihung der Nobelmedaille (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article68e8cb83d212ab5081d57269/maria-corina-machado-widmet-friedensnobelpreis-trump-us-regierung-reagiert-enttaeuscht.html)  im vergangenen Dezember kam sie nach einer gefahrvollen Flucht aus ihrem Heimatland zu spät. Anschließend ging sie ins Exil. Trotz Machados offensivem Lob setzt US-Präsident Trump in Venezuela bisher auf Übergangspräsidentin Delcy Rodríguez. Sie erklärte am Donnerstag, Venezuela werde Wahlen abhalten. Einen Zeitrahmen nannte sich jedoch nicht.

welt.de.title: Selenskyj vermeldet Zerstörung russischer Kampfjets am Boden – Moskau reagiert mit Raketen
welt.de.text: Zwei russische Kampfflugzeuge des Typs Suchoi Su-34 sind nach ukrainischen Angaben bei einem Raketenangriff am Boden zerstört worden. „Ich danke euch, Jungs, für das Ergebnis“, sagte Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj in einer Videobotschaft. Zudem sei bei einer weiteren Attacke eine Startrampe für russische Iskander-Raketen beschädigt worden. Nach Angaben der ukrainischen Marine gab es einen Angriff mit Neptun-Raketen auf den Militärflugplatz Marinowka im südrussischen Gebiet Wolgograd. Der Fliegerhorst ist über 450 Kilometer vom ukrainisch kontrollierten Gebiet entfernt. Es wäre bereits der zweite erfolgreiche ukrainische Raketenangriff auf einen russischen Militärflugplatz im Oktober. Das russische Militär äußerte sich nicht dazu. Militärnahe russische Blogger bestätigten den Verlust indirekt. Unter anderem schrieb der Blogger „Fighterbomber“: „Ich hoffe, dass die Erkenntnis, dass die Frontluftwaffe weiter und tiefer zurückgezogen werden muss, die obersten Befehlshaber noch rechtzeitig erreicht, bevor es nichts mehr gibt, was man zurückziehen könnte.“ Su-34-Jets werden für den Abwurf der gefürchteten Gleitbomben eingesetzt. Mit Flügelkonstruktionen ausgestattete Gleitbomben werden aus großer Höhe und Dutzende Kilometer entfernt von der gegnerischen Flugabwehr auf Ziele abgeworfen. Russland greift Kiew erneut mit ballistischen Raketen an Russland hat die ukrainische Hauptstadt Kiew unterdessen wieder mit ballistischen Raketen angegriffen. Es habe einen Einschlag im östlichen Stadtbezirk Darnyzja in einem Lagergebäude gegeben, teilte Bürgermeister Vitali Klitschko bei Telegram mit. Demnach wurde ein Brand ausgelöst. Kurz zuvor waren etwas mehr als ein halbes Dutzend Explosionen im Stadtgebiet zu hören. Bei einem Drohnenangriff auf das ukrainische Atomkraftwerk Saporischschja ist nach Angaben der Internationalen Atomenergiebehörde (IAEA) zudem ein Mitarbeiter getötet worden. Bei dem Opfer handelt es sich demnach um einen Schweißer der zentralen Reparaturwerkstatt der Anlage. IAEA-Generaldirektor Rafael Grossi erneuerte seine Forderung nach militärischer Zurückhaltung rund um das AKW. ​Wer für den Angriff verantwortlich ist, teilte die IAEA nicht mit. Selenskyj  (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/deutschland/article6ae1c453d1f524f7ccaa90d5/hessen-zeichnet-selenskyj-als-symbolfigur-im-kampf-gegen-militaerische-aggression-aus.html) hatte am Donnerstagabend bereits vor russischen Vorbereitungen für einen weiteren Raketenangriff gewarnt. Die Ukraine wehrt sich seit Februar 2022 gegen eine großangelegte russische Invasion.

welt.de.title: „Morgen werde ich abgeschoben“ – Frankreich verweigert Martin Sellner die Einreise
welt.de.text: Der rechtsextreme österreichische Aktivist Martin Sellner ist nach eigenen Angaben von den französischen Behörden an der Einreise nach Frankreich gehindert worden. „Ich bin am Flughafen in Frankreich festgehalten worden. Morgen werde ich abgeschoben“, erklärte Sellner am Donnerstag im Onlinedienst X. „Morgen werde ich abgeschoben. Bald wird man mir auch mein Handy abnehmen“, schrieb Sellner zu einem Foto, das den entsprechenden Bescheid der französischen Behörde zeigen soll. „Man kann Menschen aufhalten, aber keine Ideen. Die Rückwanderung wird trotzdem stattfinden.“ Die „französischen Patrioten“ rief er dazu auf, auf die Straße zu gehen und für ihre Nation zu kämpfen. Eigentlich wollte der 37-Jährige am Freitag  sein Buch „Remigration“ (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/deutschland/article69d7e68d94756c37af5a57ab/duesseldorf-martin-sellner-haelt-migrationsvortrag-in-strassenbahn-unternehmen-ist-schockiert.html)  in einer Pariser Buchhandlung vorstellen und eine Signierstunde geben. Linke Gruppen hatten zu Protesten dagegen aufgerufen. Das Einreiseverbot erfolgt vor dem Hintergrund eines zunehmend aufgeheizten politischen Klimas in Frankreich sechs Monate vor der Präsidentenwahl. Vergangene Woche hatte ein Mann nahe Paris mit einer Maschinenpistole einen Menschen getötet und sieben weitere verletzt. Die meisten Opfer hatten einen Migrationshintergrund. Inzwischen räumte der mutmaßliche Täter  rassistische Motive ein (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article6adb3d27400ffbb8e251b6a4/schuesse-nahe-paris-rassistischer-terroranschlag-stellt-laut-macron-wendepunkt-fuer-frankreich-dar.html) . Als Reaktion untersagten die französischen Behörden am Donnerstag einen rechtsextremen Kongress zum Thema „Remigration“, der am Samstag in einem Pariser Vorort hätte stattfinden sollen. Eine für Sonntag geplante Demonstration in Paris wurde ebenfalls untersagt. Der Präfekt der Region begründete das Verbot des Kongresses damit, dass es auf „einer fremdenfeindlichen und rassistischen Ideologie“ beruhe, derzufolge „Migranten grundsätzlich eine Bedrohung für die Zukunft der europäischen Länder darstellen“. Auch gegen diese Veranstaltung hatten linke Gruppen Proteste angekündigt.

welt.de.title: EU-Hubschrauber stürzt in Bosnien-Herzegowina ab – mehrere Tote
welt.de.text: Beim Absturz eines italienischen Armeehubschraubers der EU-geführten Mission Eufor Althea in Bosnien-Herzegowina sind nach offiziellen Angaben mehrere Soldaten ums Leben gekommen. Bei dem Absturz des italienischen Helikopters vom Typ CH-47 Chinook in der Region Brcko im Nordosten des Landes hätten außerdem mehrere Menschen schwere Verletzungen davongetragen, teilte die EU-Mission am Donnerstag mit. Nach einem Bericht des bosnischen Nachrichtenportals „klix.ba“ kamen vier Menschen ums Leben. Das Portal bezog sich auf nicht genannte Quellen. Elf weitere Personen seien verletzt worden, bei allen Opfern handele es sich um Italiener. Zu dem Absturz kam es nahe dem Dorf Gorice im Gebiet Brcko an der Grenze zu Kroatien. Der Hubschrauber sei bei einem „Routineeinsatz“ in der Region rund 180 Kilometer nordöstlich von Sarajevo abgestürzt, teilte die EU-Mission mit. Keine Zivilisten seien dabei verletzt worden und an ziviler Infrastruktur seien keine Schäden durch den Unfall entstanden. Bei dem Hubschrauber soll es sich um einen CH-47 Chinook handeln, einen großen Transporthubschrauber mit zwei Rotoren. Die EU-Mission (EUFOR) überwacht seit Dezember 2004 die Umsetzung des Dayton-Friedensabkommens, mit dem 1995 der Bosnien-Krieg beendet wurde. Aktuell sind mehr als tausend Soldaten im Einsatz, auch aus Deutschland. Zentrale Aufgabe der Mission Eufor Althea in Bosnien ist das Unterstützen der Umsetzung des Friedensvertrages von Dayton aus dem Jahr 1995. Als Nachfolgemission der von der Nato geführten „Stabilisation Force“ (SFOR) soll Althea in dem Balkanland für Sicherheit sorgen. Weitere Ziele sind die Ausbildung der bosnischen Streitkräfte und die Schaffung eines sicheren Umfeldes für die Entwicklung des Landes. In Bosnien-Herzegowina gibt es mehr als 30 Jahre nach Kriegsende weiter  erhebliche Spannungen (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article251224084/Bosnien-Dann-wuerde-hier-innerhalb-von-einer-Stunde-der-Krieg-ausbrechen.html)  zwischen den Volksgruppen der Serben, Kroaten und der bosnischen Muslime. Vor allem auf Seiten der bosnischen Serben bestehen Tendenzen zu einer Abspaltung beziehungsweise einem Anschluss an Serbien. Die Bundeswehr ist seit August 2022 an der Mission Eufor Althea  mit bis zu 50 Soldaten beteiligt (verlinkt auf https://www.welt.de/politik/ausland/article239811227/Bundeswehr-darf-Auslandseinsatz-in-Bosnien-Herzegowina-wieder-aufnehmen.html) , nachdem sie bereits von 2004 bis 2012 vor Ort war. Das deutsche Engagement umfasst derzeit insgesamt 36 Dienstposten.

welt.de.title: „Polexit“ im Raum – Tusk kündigt „erbitterten Kampf“ gegen EU-Austritt an
welt.de.text:
Polens Regierungschef Donald Tusk weist Überlegungen zu einem EU-Austritt entschieden zurück. Zuvor hatte PiS-Oppositionschef Jarosław Kaczyński einen „Polexit“ ins Spiel gebracht und die Europäische Kommission scharf kritisiert.
